en: I, Ziyi, Abbot of Kaiyuan Chan Monastery in Fuzhou, Master of the Dharma Transmission and Grand Master of the Purple Robe Huītong,
respectfully solicits contributions from the assembly to extend the sacred longevity of His Majesty the Emperor,
to augment the rank and emolument of the civil and military officials, and to complete the carving and production of the Great Canon of the Vairocana Sūtras.
One set of wooden printing blocks. Dated the [blank] day of the intercalary eighth month of the Wuchen year of the Shaoxing era.

The Buddha Śākyamuni of India was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. Ānanda addressed him, saying, "How many Buddhas did the Tathāgata honor and make offerings to in the past while seeking Bodhi?
Under which Buddha did he first plant the roots of all wholesome merit? The Buddha told Ānanda: "I..."
I recall that in the past, during immeasurable kalpas, there was a Kṣatriya king in Jambudvīpa named Mārapramardana who resided in the great city of Padmavatī.
He transformed the world through the ten virtuous paths. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara.

Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, the king went in person to welcome and make offerings to him. At that time, there was a son of a prominent Brahmin family from the south of the Snowy Mountains named Megha.
The youth was the foremost among five hundred Brahmins. At the age of sixteen, he studied the Vedas and other treatises under the Rishi Ratnaśikhin.
Upon completing his studies and bidding farewell to return home, the Rishi said: "Within my dharma-teaching, disciples who have mastered the Way shall attain success."
"You must provide a generous reward. Cloud-Child asked, "I do not know what object would be worthy to repay your instruction.
The Immortal said, "It shall require a golden jar and bowl, along with a staff, an umbrella, and leather sandals, all adorned with gold. Cloud-Child replied, "I now possess only this single body.
If you, O Immortal, permit me to beg for it, I shall come to offer it to you. He then took his leave and traveled to the great city of Śūrpāraka.
Within the city, there was a brahmin named Yajñadatta whose family had been wealthy for generations.
On the final day of a Pañcavārṣika festival (an unobstructed sacrificial assembly), Meghadatta arrived at the gathering.

The assembly, having long admired his reputation, welcomed him with joy and appointed him as the presiding elder (*upasthāyaka*), offering him the foremost hospitality. After Meghadatta had accepted the offerings, he took them and presented them to his own master.
He traveled until he reached the Great City of Lotus. There he saw a magnificent splendor as if a celestial assembly had gathered. He immediately asked the city-dwellers, "What is being prepared?
They replied, "Have you not heard that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara has appeared in the world?

Today, King Jitāri has invited the Buddha to enter the city; therefore, this place is so magnificently adorned. Megha then thought to himself, "I should now go to pay my respects and repay the sage's kindness."

In the evening, he thought again: "In the Buddha-dharma, only the offering of the Dharma is considered most supreme. I am not yet possessed of the Dharma; I should redeem some flowers to present as an offering.
At that time, King Pūru was purchasing incense and flowers to offer to the Buddha and had forbidden their private sale.
When the youth Megha sought to buy them, he could find none at all. Suddenly, in an alleyway, he saw a person in blue robes named Bhadra, who was secretly carrying seven [flowers].
The stem of an utpala lotus was contained within a vase. When Megha-dāraka saw it, he was filled with joy and went out to purchase it with gold coins.
The worthy one said, "The King has prohibited the private sale of flowers. Megha-dāraka said, "I pray you, withhold five of them in secret;
I vow never to forget this. The worthy one asked, "What do you intend to do with them? Megha-dāraka replied, "I have just heard that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara has appeared."

No sooner had he made this vow than the flowers formed a canopy, remaining suspended in mid-air to cover the Buddha’s head.

I pray that Your Majesty will protect the noble son well, so that his blessings and merit may be boundless. Seven days after the Prince was born, Māyā passed away. The King then selected [a wet nurse].

From the midst of the void, a voice proclaimed: "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven, he made a great vow, wishing to deliver all sentient beings.
Now that you have long resided in the royal palace, the time has come; do not be greedy for worldly pleasures. Then he spoke this verse:
Worldly affairs are impermanent, like lightning flashing from the clouds. O Venerable One, the time has now come;

The Prince, having grown deeply weary of worldly splendor, first went out on excursions through the four gates, where he successively beheld birth, old age, sickness, and death. This occurred repeatedly.

He consulted his parents and earnestly sought to renounce the household life; yet, because they were bound by their deep affection for him, they would not grant his wish. That night, the Prince experienced five dreams:
first, he sat upon this great earth with Mount Sumeru as his pillow; then, he scooped up the waters of the four great oceans and placed them upon his hands and feet.
Next, there was a single blade of grass called "Establishment" (*pratiṣṭhāna*), which extended from his navel wheel up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Furthermore, he saw four birds of various colors, each arriving from one of the cardinal directions; upon reaching beneath his feet, they all turned white.
Again, there was a beast with a dark head and a white body that licked the Prince’s feet. Finally, he saw a mound of filth as high and steep as a mountain.
He traveled above, remaining unstained by defilement. A Devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven came again and said, "The eight classes of devas fill the void, supporting the Dharma King;
it is not fitting for you to remain here long. At the third watch of that night, he leaped over the city wall and departed.
He then proceeded to the abode of the great seer Kālāma. The seer asked, "Virtuous one, you have resolved your mind; what do you seek?
The Prince replied, "I see that the world is subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, and is entangled by the cravings of the three realms, unable to escape them.
I desire to attain Buddhahood and deliver those who have not yet been delivered. The seer said, "Excellent! Craving and attachment are the great evil dragons of this world."
The Dragon dwells within the waters of the minds of sentient beings, causing them to lose all wholesome benefits. You, O Benevolent One, have suddenly been able to awaken him;
you are a person of great wisdom. He then spoke this verse:
The supreme among all phenomena is only practice; purity and tranquil concentration do not surpass the mind.
Attachment to affection is the greatest enemy. Regarding all fears, they are old age and death.

There are two meanings: first, the essential nature (*prakṛti*); second, transformation (*nirmāṇa*). As for the essential nature, it refers to earth, water, fire, wind, space, the self, and the signless (*animitta*).
As for transformation, it refers to the sense faculties and their objects, the hands, feet, speech, movement, coming and going, and the mental consciousness.
If one can discern these two meanings and does not give rise to craving or defilement, this is called liberation. Furthermore—
Furthermore, sentient beings do not understand these four kinds of afflictions and thus become greedily attached to the world: first, lack of faith; second, attachment to a self;
third, harboring doubt; and fourth, lack of concentration. Again, a verse was spoken:
The goat is killed because it bleats; The moth throws itself into the lamp because of the color of the fire;
The fish in the water hangs upon the hook because it swallows the bait; Worldly people hasten toward death, led astray by sensory objects. It is further said:
If one can detach from all marks of existence (*nimitta*), one immediately attains the markless (*animitta*). Since there is no longer arising, it is called the "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñā*).
Having heard this, Siddhārtha silently took it to heart; realizing that it was not the ultimate Dharma, he thought, "How could this enable me to attain nirvāṇa?

Fundamentally free from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, And with earth, water, fire, wind, and space in profound stillness, Throughout the three times, there is no teacher’s instruction; Ever pure, one spontaneously realizes liberation.
Next, he went to the place of the two seers, Udraka and Rāmaputra, and said: "Great Seers, what is the nature of the Dharma you practice? The Great Seers replied: [as follows].

If one contemplates correctly with right intention, there is only the subtle and wondrous essential nature, tranquil, stable, and sublime, reaching as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

There, life and longevity are vast and eternal, and it is the abode of sages and seers. Siddhārtha approached those two seers and studied under them for five years; realizing that this was not the ultimate goal, he then—"
He went to the Snowy Mountains and practiced austerities for six years until he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (this is stated here as a general summary).
Accepting the invitation of Mahābrahmā, he proceeded to the Deer Park, where he first taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to the five sages, including Kauṇḍinya and others.

For those of inferior capacity, he preached the Dharma of the Four Truths to enable them to escape the calamity of the fires of the triple world and realize the stage of a Śrāvaka; they were like hares crossing a river by leaping.

Thus, through these twelve conditions of mutual dependence, the cycle of rebirth turns without ceasing. By investigating these factors both forward and backward, one eradicates the root of ignorance and realizes the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
Like a horse crossing a river, those who ride the so-called "deer cart" and possess great roots suddenly open to the true reality (*dharmatā*). To them, Bodhi is directly revealed:

form is emptiness, and one is all. They cultivate the *pāramitā* practices without dwelling in the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), entering the city of omniscience (*sarvajñā*) without failing in the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Next, they ascend the ten stages (*bhūmi*), gradually severing the three delusions, until they achieve the equal, wondrous, perfect, and bright enlightenment, thereby becoming a Great [Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattva was like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, riding upon a white ox-cart.
When the Tathāgata reached the Multi-Treasure Stūpa during his journey, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat with him. He then declared:

"I have secretly entrusted to you the subtle and wondrous Eye of the True Dharma. You must protect it and transmit it to future generations, ensuring that it never be severed. This is the Great Dharma-Eye."

At that time, the Tathāgata again spoke this verse for Kāśyapa:
The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma; without Dharma, even Dharma is Dharma. Now, at this time when the non-Dharma is entrusted, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?
He further said: "I now entrust this saṃghāṭī robe to you. You should protect and uphold it, and transmit it for my sake."
He entrusted [the teaching] to Maitreya Tathāgata and then proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara, where he manifested entry into *nirvāṇa* between a pair of *śāla* trees.

(The *śāla* trees were arranged in four pairs; when the Buddha was about to pass into final extinction, they suddenly joined together to form two, hence they are called "the twin trees. Their color was white as silk, thus they are also named "crane trees. He further addressed Cunda, saying: "The realm of all Buddhas is entirely impermanent;
the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise so. Since the Tathāgata has already, by means of various..."
The Dharma essentials were taught and shown to bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas; all the celestial beings and non-Buddhist practitioners were transformed. Finally, he delivered Subhadra.

As a legacy for future generations, he extensively manifested supernatural transformations, then lay down on his right side with his feet stacked, head toward the north, entering the samādhi of great parinirvāṇa.
Having fulfilled his purpose, he returned to the source. At that time, Mahākāśyapa was outside, arriving last.

Upon his arrival, the Buddha extended both feet from within the golden coffin. After Kāśyapa had paid his respects, the assembly of humans and devas offered sandalwood fuel, yet they were ultimately unable to ignite it. Kāśyapa then requested that the Tathāgata’s fire of samādhi cremate him;
immediately, the golden coffin rose up from its bed of seven treasures, circled the city of Kuśinagara seven times, and returned to its original place.
He entered the Samādhi of the Transformed Fire-light and spontaneously cremated himself. Aniruddha and others collected eight *hu* and four *dou* of relics, which were stored in a golden urn.
King Ajātaśatru and the kings of the eight kingdoms each arrayed their troops to guard them; they then distributed the relics and erected stūpas, which were venerated by humans and devas alike.

The First Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. His surname was Brahmin. His father...
Her name was Yinze (Drinking the Marsh), and her mother’s name was Xiangzhi (Fragrant Will). In the past, during the era of Vipaśyin Buddha, she was a goldsmith who adorned that Buddha’s image.
At that time, a poor woman obtained a single gold coin; beholding the marks of the Tathāgata, she conceived a rare and sublime resolve.

She took it to the goldsmith and requested that he embellish the Buddha image. Subsequently, they both made a vow to be husband and wife in purity for eternal kalpas. It was because of this [that they were so].

Due to these conditions, for ninety-one kalpas his body was entirely golden in color. He was subsequently born in the Brahma Heaven, and next he was born in the kingdom of Magadha, where he was first named Kāśyapa, which translates as "Drinking Light" or "Victorious Radiance. His body possessed a sublime and wondrous radiance;

he was also called Kanakavatsa (Golden Son), taking his name from his golden hue. He was further named Vāseṭṭha. Upon hearing that the Tathāgata had appeared in the world, he resolved to seek ordination.
He aspired to cross over the various realms of existence (*bhava*). The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu. His hair and beard fell away naturally, and the *kāṣāya* robe was donned upon his body.
He maintained the *dhūta* practices, which the Buddha constantly praised. While the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the devas offered flowers.

The World-Honored One held the flowers and showed them to the assembly; Kāśyapa smiled. The World-Honored One addressed the assembly, saying: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the *Nirvāṇa*..."
The Wondrous Mind was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa with the charge that it be propagated for future generations and never allowed to be severed.
He further bestowed upon Kāśyapa the golden-threaded *saṃghāṭī* robe to await Maitreya. At the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa was not present among the assembly;
he had only just returned from outside. Thereupon, the Tathāgata manifested his two feet through the golden coffin to show him.
After Kāśyapa had finished paying his respects, the World-Honored One manifested the fire of *samādhi* to cremate him. Kāśyapa then addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa at the Twin Śāla Trees. We ought to attend to the subsequent affairs; let us convene a council together to propagate the teachings of the Dharma.
Thereupon, he gathered the great multitude, and the proclamation they made was as follows:
"Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter nirvāṇa; those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) should attend the council.

At that time, the sound of these verses pervaded the entire realm of sand-grains (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*). Those who had realized arhatship all assembled at the Piṇḍola Cave (translated as "Seven-Deeds Cliff").
At that moment, Ānanda’s outflows (*āsrava*) were not yet exhausted, so Mahākāśyapa did not allow him to join the assembly. Ānanda thought to himself:
"I have served the Tathāgata without ever committing a transgression. Yet, how could it be that I still possess outflows (*āsrava*) and am not included among the ranks of the noble ones?
Sitting upon this *pāṇḍaka* stone for three days and nights, I have realized the fruit of the absence of outflows. I shall now return to the assembly and strike upon its stone gate.
Kāśyapa said, "You are not yet liberated; why must you come back? Ānanda said, "I have already realized the state of being without outflows. Kāśyapa said, "Then show me [your proof]."
By means of supernatural powers, he dispelled the doubts of the assembly. Ānanda then entered through his own door’s keyhole.

As the sentient beings were filled with doubt, Kāśyapa struck the gavel and requested the Venerable Ānanda, the foremost seat, to preach the Dharma. Ānanda immediately ascended the Dharma seat and said: "Thus have I heard.
After Mahākāśyapa had compiled the Tripiṭaka, he reflected thus: "I shall uphold the transmission received from the Tathāgata."
"The *saṃghāṭī* robe shall remain hidden within Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the three assemblies of the Nāgapuṣpa tree. He then addressed Ānanda, saying:
'You should now know that before the Bhagavān entered parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmacakṣur-kośa*) to me at the Many-Sons Stūpa (*Bahuputra-caitya*).
I am now about to go into concealment on the Peak of the Cock; I transmit this True Dharma to you.'"
Guard and uphold it well, and circulate it for the future so that it shall not be interrupted. Having received my teaching, listen to this verse of mine:
"Every dharma is originally the Dharma; There is no dharma and no non-dharma. How could there be dharma or non-dharma within a single dharma?"
Having received these instructions, Ānanda withdrew into seclusion, and Kāśyapa subsequently passed away.
The second patriarch, the Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan was Kṣatriya; his father was King Droṇodana.
The World-Honored One regarded him as foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī* and constantly praised him.

Furthermore, because he had cultivated great merit in previous lives and had received and upheld the treasury of the Dharma like water being passed from one vessel to another, the Buddha appointed him as his attendant;
thus, he was the World-Honored One’s cousin. Subsequently, after the First Council, Ānanda reflected that the Tathāgata had entrusted the Great Eye of the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa.
"Kāśyapa, Kāśyapa having already entered parinirvāṇa, entrusted [the teaching] to me. Now that I am about to pass away, I have gone to the Nairañjanā River and said:
'Those whom I previously delivered and liberated should now assemble. In a short while, five hundred arhats arrived through the air from the sky. Among the assembly was one named Śāṇakavāsin;
Ānanda, having long known him to be a vessel for the Dharma, then addressed him, saying: 'The Tathāgata, by means of the Great..."
The Dharma-eye treasury was entrusted to Kāśyapa. As he was about to enter nirvana, he secretly transmitted it to me; and now that I am about to pass away, I transmit it to you.
You must skillfully protect and uphold it, circulating it for future generations so that it never be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:
"The Dharma originally entrusted is now entrusted; having been entrusted, it is said there is no Dharma. Each must awaken for themselves;
once awakened, there is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed Śāṇakavāsin, saying: "You shall skillfully perform the work of transformation and continue my propagation. You shall have a successor."

He transformed the Five Indies through his great influence, delivering sentient beings like the Teacher of Gods and Men. Only he lacked the physical marks and signs. His stone chamber was filled with counting sticks.

Ānanda performed eighteen miraculous transformations and entered the *vega-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Agility), whereupon he manifested fire to cremate his own body; humans and devas then shared his relics.
Stūpas and temples were built for each of them during the reign of King Lì (厲王).
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā. His clan name was Vaiśālī;
his father’s name was Vanavāsī, and his mother’s name was Kauśeya. Śāṇa remained in the womb for six years before he was born. In Sanskrit, he is called Śāṇaka.
*Ka* (this is translated as "spontaneous garment"). It is the name of a nine-branched, exquisite herb found in the Western Regions. When a holy Arhat is born, this herb appears;
when Andhaka was born, this auspicious herb manifested in response. Thus, when the Tathāgata traveled to convert beings and arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, [it appeared].
Seeing a lush, verdant grove, he said to Ānanda, "This grove is named Uruvilvā.
One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma in this place.
A century later, Śāṇakavāsin was indeed born; he left the household life, realized the Way, received the Dharma-eye from the Venerable Ānanda, and resided in this grove.
There was a great fire dragon that submitted to the Dharma teachings; consequently, he offered up its land for the construction of a temple.
In the country of Ta-li, the Venerable One obtained Upagupta as an attendant. He then asked him, "How old are you? and he replied:
"I am seventeen years old. The Master asked, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or is your nature seventeen?
He replied, "When my teacher’s hair has turned white, is it his hair that is white, or is his mind white? The Master said, "It is only my hair that is white; my mind is not white.
Guptaka said, "My body is seventeen, but my nature is not seventeen. Knowing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, Upagupta then shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts.
He then declared: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa. It was transmitted from one to another until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it shall not be severed.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
Neither non-dharma nor mind, neither no-mind nor no-dharma—when these dharmas of the mind are thus taught, these dharmas are not the mind.
Having thus entrusted [the teaching], he immediately vanished into the Elephant White Mountain (Hastivāhana) to the south of Kaśmīra. Later, he saw that Guptaka possessed five...
There was a group of a hundred followers who were constantly full of indolence and arrogance. The Venerable One went to them to subdue them and spoke this verse:
"Thoroughly penetrating that which is neither 'this' nor 'that,' The Most Holy One has neither long nor short. You must now abandon your thoughts of contempt and pride."
Having heard the verses, five hundred bhikṣus who had swiftly attained arhatship followed the teaching and practiced accordingly; they all obtained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

The Venerable One then performed eighteen miraculous transformations and entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (the fire-light samādhi) to cremate his own body. Kujūta collected the relics and buried them at Vanga.
Luoshan was during the reign of Emperor Xuan.
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the country of Tāla (also named Upagupta or Utpagupta). His clan name was Śūdra;
his father’s name was Kalyāṇabhadra. He left home at the age of seventeen and realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty. He then traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā. 4.
The multitudes gathered like clouds. Consequently, Māra’s palace shook and trembled;
Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear, and although he exhausted all his demonic powers, he could not find any opportunity, as a garland of flowers remained secretly bound around his neck.

He then looked back at the three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and saw that they had become a garland upon his own neck, infested with maggots, foul, and decaying, yet he could not remove them. Pāpīyān then ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and proclaimed:
The lords of the various heavens sought their deliverance, each saying, "Who among the disciples of the One of Ten Powers can remove these supernatural transformations wrought by you?
Pāpīyas asked, "If that is so, what should I do? The lords of the heavens replied, "You should take refuge in the Venerable One;
he will be able to sever them. Thereupon, they spoke this verse for him:
"If one falls upon the ground, one must rise from the ground; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible.
Pāpīyān, having received these instructions, immediately descended from the celestial palace, prostrated before the Venerable One, and openly confessed his transgressions.
Guptaka said, "From this day forward, will you no longer cause disturbances to the True Dharma of the Tathāgata? Pāpīyān replied, "I vow to turn back."
"Turn toward the Buddha-way and forever sever all that is unwholesome. Guptaka said, "If that is so, you yourself must proclaim the refuge in the Triple Gem.
Following these instructions, the Māra removed all his flower garlands; leaping for joy, he paid homage to the Venerable One and spoke this verse:
I bow my head in homage to the Honored One of Samādhi, the noble disciple of the One of Ten Powers.

I now dedicate these merits with the vow that no venerable one of inferior strength shall remain in this world, so that you alone may guide and transform the greatest number of beings. For every person you convert, place a tally-stick in the stone chamber until they are filled.
They filled the space between them. Finally, there was a son of a householder named Gandhamādana who came to pay homage to the Venerable One, seeking to leave the household life.
The Venerable One asked, "Do you leave the household life with your body, or do you leave it with your mind? He replied, "I have come to leave the household life, not for the sake of body or mind.
The Venerable One asked, "If it is neither for body nor mind, then who is it that leaves the household life? He replied, "As for one who leaves the household life, there is no self."
Therefore, my mind is neither born nor extinguished; this is the eternal Way. Since it is the eternal Way, the Buddhas are not subject to impermanence.

The mind has no form or appearance, and its essence is likewise so. The Master said: "You should attain clear awakening; let the mind spontaneously penetrate through to itself, thereby perpetuating the lineage of the Sages."
He immediately granted him the going forth and the full ordination, and then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa;

it was transmitted in succession down to me. I now entrust it to you. Guard and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it shall not be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
The mind is the mind from the very beginning; the original mind is not a dharma. If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; [but] it is neither mind nor the original dharma.
He further addressed the assembly of incense-bearers, saying: "In your father’s dream, you were born from a golden sun; you may be named Tiṭṭhaka."

(This is known as the "Universal True Measure. The Venerable One then ascended into the void and displayed the eighteen transformations. Returning once more to his original seat, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
Diṭṭhika used the tally-sticks from within the room to cremate his body, collected the relics, and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
During the reign of the Ping dynasty, the Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Dīptaka, was a native of Magadha.
At the time of his birth, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth; before it stood a great mountain, adorned with various jewels, its summit—
Springs gushed forth, flowing profusely in four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Kāśyapa-matanga, who explained it for him, saying:
"The jewel mountain is my own body; the gushing springs represent the inexhaustibility of the Dharma; the sun rising from the roof represents the sign of your current entry into the Way;

and its illuminating the heavens and earth represents the far-reaching transcendence of your wisdom. The Venerable’s original name was Xiangzhong (Fragrant Multitude), but he changed it because of this.
Now, he is thus named. Then, a verse was spoken in praise:

Majestic is the mountain of the seven treasures, From which a spring of wisdom constantly flows; Transformed into the flavor of the true Dharma, It is able to deliver all who possess the karmic affinity.
The Venerable Kūṭadanta replied with a verse:
"My Dharma has been transmitted to you; You shall now manifest great wisdom. Like the golden sun emerging from the house, It shall illuminate heaven and earth."

Having heard his teacher’s sublime verses, Tiṣya paid homage and took them to heart. Later, he traveled to Central India. In that country, there were eight thousand great ṛṣis, with Micchaka at their head.
Upon hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led the assembly to pay him homage and said to him, "In the past, we were born together with you in the Brahma Heaven.
I encountered the seer Asita, who bestowed the ṛṣi-dharma upon me, while you, Master..."
He encountered a disciple of the One of Ten Powers who was practicing *dhyāna*. From this point on, their karmic destinies diverged; six *kalpas* have already passed.
The Venerable One said, "You should abandon your heterodoxy and enter the wisdom of the Buddha. Mīḍhika replied, "In the past, the seer Asita gave me a prophecy, saying:
'Six *kalpas* hence, you shall encounter a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*). Now that we have met, it is not [otherwise]."
"Is this due to past affinities? I pray that the Master, in his great compassion, will grant me liberation. The Venerable One immediately ordained him and conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
The other celestial beings (*ṛṣi*) had just begun to give rise to conceit, so the Venerable One displayed great supernatural powers (*mahābhijñā*).

Thereupon, they all resolved upon Bodhicitta and were ordained at one and the same time. He then said to Mucilinda: "The Tathāgata has entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmacakṣur-garbha*) to Kāśyapa."

Having been transmitted through successive entrustments until it reached me, I now confer it upon you. You must protect and uphold it well, propagating it for the sake of future generations so that it shall never be severed.
Having received my instruction, listen to this verse I speak:
"Penetrating the mind of the fundamental dharma, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma; realizing that awakening is the same as non-awakening, there is neither mind nor dharma.
Having finished this verse, he leaped into the void and manifested eighteen transformations. Entering the *jvālāmukha-samādhi*, he spontaneously incinerated his own body. It was boundless...
Cajja, together with eight thousand bhikṣus, collected the śarīra relics and erected a stūpa for worship on Mount Paṇḍava;
this was during the reign of King Zhuang.
The sixth patriarch, the Venerable Mijia (Mecaka), was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled to various regions to teach and transform beings.
In the kingdom of Northern India, he saw auspicious golden clouds above the battlements and sighed, saying, "This is the aura of the Mahāyāna;
a wondrous person will surely be born who shall become my Dharma heir. He then entered the city.
In the marketplace, he heard of a man holding a wine vessel and went to meet him, asking, "From where have you come, Master? Where do you intend to go? The Master replied, "I come from the mind."
He came forward, intending to go nowhere in particular, and said, "Do you recognize the object in my hand? The Master replied, "This is a vessel for contact that carries purity.
The man asked, "Do you recognize me, Master? The Master said, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, I would no longer be myself.
He spoke again, saying, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your fundamental cause. That man then spoke a verse:
From immeasurable kalpas ago until my birth in this land, my original clan was Bharadvāja and my name was Vāsukī.
My teacher, Diṅnāga, said: "In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through North India, he said to Ānanda: 'This..."
Within this kingdom, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man surnamed Bharadvāja and named Vasumitra.
He shall be the seventh in succession from the Grand Master. The World-Honored One has prophesied to you: "You should leave the household life.

Thereupon, he set down his vessel, prostrated before the Master, and said: "I recall that in past kalpas, I constantly acted as a donor (*dānapati*), offering a precious throne to a Tathāgata. The Buddha—
The Record states: "Within the Dharma of Śākyamuni during the Bhadrakalpa, you shall proclaim the True Dharma. This now accords with the Master’s prophecy; I pray that you grant me deliverance.
The Master then shaved his head and conferred upon him full ordination, whereupon he said to him: "The Tathāgata secretly entrusted the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa.
In this manner it was passed down through successive generations until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must skillfully protect and uphold it, and transmit it."
Transform it and bring it forth; do not allow it to be severed. Receive my teaching and listen to this verse of mine:
"No mind can be attained; What is spoken cannot be called a dharma. If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas."

Having finished the verses, he entered the Lion’s Vigorous Display Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*). Leaping into the air, he manifested the Fire-Light Samādhi (*jvālāmālā-samādhi*), completely incinerating his body.
Vāsulimitra collected the relics and erected a stūpa; this was during the reign of Emperor Xiang.
The Seventh Patriarch, Vāsūmitra, was a native of Northern India. His surname was Bharadvāja. He habitually carried a wine vessel as he wandered through the villages and neighborhoods.
Upon meeting the Venerable Mīḍhaka, who proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past prophecies concerning him, he reflected upon his own prior karmic conditions.

He cast aside his vessel, entered the monastic life, and was granted the Dharma. Traveling to propagate the teachings, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāmala. Before the Dharma seat, suddenly there appeared one...
The wise man introduced himself, saying, "My name is Buddhadeva. I shall debate the meaning with you, Master. The Master said, "O worthy one, where there is debate, there is no meaning;
where there is meaning, there is no debate. If one intends to debate meaning, it will ultimately not be a discourse on meaning. Buddhadeva knew that the Master’s argument was superior.

His mind was immediately filled with reverence and submission, and he said, "I hope that the Master, out of great compassion, will grant me his acceptance. The Venerable One then conferred upon him the tonsure and the full precepts.
He further told him: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa, and it has been transmitted in succession down to me.
I now entrust it to you; you must uphold it well and propagate it for the future, so that it shall never be interrupted."
Receive my instruction. Listen to this verse of mine:
The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, There is neither "is" nor "is not."

Having finished the verse, he entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*). Seven days passed, during which both humans and devas came together to pay him homage, reciting this verse:
"Ancestor of the sages of the Bhadrakalpa, You shall occupy the seventh rank; O Venerable One, have compassion for us."
Please arise from samādhi for the sake of proclaiming the Buddha-ground. Then he spoke this verse:
"The Dharma I have attained is not existent; If one realizes the Buddha-ground, It is because it is free from existence and non-existence."
Having spoken this verse, he returned to his samādhi and manifested nirvana. Buddhadatta then rose from his original seat and erected a jeweled stūpa to enshrine his entire body;
this was the very beginning of the dynasty of the kingdom of Dīnā.
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmarūpa. His clan name was Gautama.

He possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown and was endowed with unhindered, vast eloquence. Having encountered the Venerable Vasumitra, he left the household life and received instruction from him.
Subsequently, while traveling to spread the Dharma, he arrived at the home of Viśākha in the kingdom of Ti-ga. Observing a white light above the house, the Master said: "This family shall..."
An *ārya* had finished speaking. The elder came forth to pay his respects and asked, "What is required?
The Venerable One said, "Your son named Buddhamitra is already fifty years old; he has never spoken a word nor ever stepped in sandals.

He is destined to succeed to the Dharma-treasure; you should allow him to leave the household life. The parents were moved by the Venerable One’s compassionate guidance and subsequently gave their consent. [Thus ends the section on] Buddhamitra.
Upon hearing this, he rose immediately and prepared the rites, then spoke a verse, saying:
"My parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The various Buddhas are not my path;
who is the supreme path?"
The Venerable One replied in verse:
"What you say regarding intimacy with the mind cannot be compared even to that of one's parents. Your practice accords with the Way;
the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek externally for a Buddha with form is not compatible with you."
"I wish to recognize your original mind; it is neither joined nor separated.
Upon hearing these sublime verses from the Master, Vajramitra immediately requested ordination. The Venerable One then conferred upon him the vows of liberation and full admission.
He then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa; it was passed down in succession until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, disseminating it for the future so that it shall not be severed.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one realizes the realm of space, this is the penetration of the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Vajramitra, having received his teacher’s entrustment, spoke a verse in praise, saying:
"Among my teachers and the various patriarchs, you shall succeed to the eighth position; through your Dharma transformation, immeasurable multitudes shall all attain arhatship.
At that time, the Venerable One immediately manifested supernatural powers and entered parinirvāṇa. A stūpa was erected over his original seat to enshrine his remains in their entirety.
Shen (身). This refers to the Jing Dynasty.

The Ninth Patriarch, Vimalamitra, was a native of the country of Ti-ga. His secular surname was Viśāla. He remained in the womb for six years;
consequently, he was named Durlabha (Difficult to Be Born). He encountered the Patriarch Buddhanandi, who was traveling to convert beings when he arrived at his home.

Recognizing that this child was no ordinary person and would surely become a vessel for the Dharma, the Patriarch further explained their past karmic connections to him. For fifty years, [Vimalamitra] never once spoke.

He spoke thus and did not set foot forward; this was surely intended as a sign. His feet neither advanced nor retreated, for the Dharma has no going or staying. His mouth uttered no words, for the principle revealed is emptiness and stillness.

Upon hearing these wondrous instructions, the father finally granted him permission to leave the household life. The Venerable One immediately shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts.
From that time forth, he served diligently at his side, manifesting the majestic deportment of a monk. Thereafter, [the Venerable One] addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata, by means of the Great..."
The Treasury of the Dharma-Eye was entrusted to Kāśyapa; it has been passed down in succession until it reaches me. I now entrust it to you.

The tenth patriarch, Venerable Pārśva, was a native of Central India; his original name was Duṣprasaha. Initially, when the Venerable One was about to be born...
His father dreamed of a white elephant with a jeweled throne upon its back, on which a bright pearl was placed; it entered through the gate, its light illuminating the fourfold assembly.
Upon waking, he was subsequently born. Later, he encountered the Venerable Upagupta and attended him, carrying his towel and water flask, never once sleeping.
Because his side never touched the mat, he was given the name the Venerable Pārśva. When he arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, there was an elder...

I wish to meet a man of great realization who may evaluate this matter. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was resting beneath a tree and pointed with his finger.
The ground turned golden, and he addressed the assembly, saying, "This ground has turned golden because a holy man shall enter this assembly.

Pūrṇayaśas replied, "My mind does not go. The Venerable One said, "Where do you abide? He replied, "My mind does not abide. The Venerable One said:
"Are you not indeterminate? He replied, "The Buddhas are likewise. The Venerable One said, "You are not the Buddhas. He replied, "The Buddhas are also not [indeterminate].
The Venerable One then spoke this verse:

The Master’s seat was upon a golden ground; he constantly expounded the true meaning. Turning his light back to illuminate me, he caused me to enter samādhi.

The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Pūrṇayaśas, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra. His clan name was Gautama.

The Great Being (Mahāsattva) went forward to greet him and paid his respects. Addressing the assembly, he said, "Do you recognize this man? I once dreamed of a great ocean;

'Six hundred years hence, there shall be a worthy one named Aśvaghoṣa in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, who will subdue the heterodox paths, inspire right faith, and establish [the Dharma]...'"
This is the person who composed the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. Aśvaghoṣa posed a question, saying: "I wish to know the Buddha; what is he? The Venerable One replied:
"That which you wish to know as the Buddha, it is precisely that which you do not know. Aśvaghoṣa said: "If one does not know the Buddha, how can one know that it is the Buddha?
The Venerable One replied: "Since you do not know the Buddha, how can you know that it is not? Aśvaghoṣa said: "This is the meaning of the saw. The Venerable One replied: "That is..."
Regarding the meaning of "wood," he asked again, "What is the meaning of 'saw'? [Māṭhara] replied, "It is that which cuts the wood together with the master.
He asked again, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? The Venerable One said, "You have been cut down by it. Aśvaghoṣa, realizing that the Venerable One’s meaning was superior, requested ordination.

The Venerable One immediately shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him. The Venerable One asked, "Do you remember past events? [Aśvaghoṣa replied,] "I do. I was once a king in the kingdom of Vaiśālī..."
"O King, the people of that country are of three classes. The highest class possess bodily radiance; their clothing and food appear according to their thoughts.
The middle class lack bodily radiance and must provide for their own clothing and food. The lowest class are like naked horses.
You, as the King of Vaiśālī, have long been filled with great compassion and possessed divine power; you divided yourself into insects to eat the mulberry leaves."
They spontaneously formed cocoons, and the horse-people of the kingdom took the cocoons to make clothing for themselves. After you passed away from that life, you were reborn in Central India;
because the horse-people mourned you with lamentation and wailing, you were consequently named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry). At that time, you spoke a verse to the horse-people, saying:
In the past, I was born in the Brahma Heaven; when my lifespan there had ended, I descended to be born in the country of Vārāṇasī to share in your sorrow and suffering.
Seeing that you were without clothing, out of a heart of compassion, I divided my body to form a nest-like enclosure, so that you would have no further grief or pain.
The Venerable One then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata personally transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye to Kāśyapa;
it was handed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. You must guard and uphold it well, and disseminate it for the future so that it shall not be severed.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are not separate from one another.

He then transmitted the Dharma of concealment and manifestation—neither one nor two—and having finished transmitting the Dharma, he immediately manifested his supernatural powers and entered parinirvāṇa. The assembly erected a precious stupa to enshrine his entire body. Thus it is said:
The An dynasty was established.
The twelfth patriarch, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. He was also named Saṃgharakṣita;
he was so named because his various merits, both conditioned and unconditioned, were most preeminent. Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Yaśas, he...
Later, in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, a certain old man suddenly appeared before the seat of the Venerable One on the Dharma-ground. The Venerable One said, "This is no ordinary person;
there shall be extraordinary signs. Having spoken, he vanished. Suddenly, from the ground, a golden-colored man emerged, who then transformed into a woman.
She pointed her right hand toward the Teacher and spoke this verse:
"I prostrate to the Venerable Elder, who shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata.
Having spoken this verse, which proclaims the First Principle upon this very ground, he suddenly vanished. The Venerable Aśvaghoṣa said, "A Māra will surely come to challenge me."

The treatise states: After a short while, wind and rain arrived suddenly, and heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness. The Venerable One said, "It is indeed true that Māra has come; I shall dispel him.
He then pointed toward the sky, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its divine majesty and shaking the mountains and peaks. The demonic activities were instantly extinguished.
Furthermore, after seven days had passed, there was a small insect, like a *jiaoming* (a tiny moth), which hid its form beneath his seat. The Venerable One...
He placed it in his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation wrought by a māra who has come to eavesdrop upon my Dharma.
He then commanded the māra to depart, but the māra could not move. The Venerable One addressed him, saying, "By taking refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers.
Thereupon, he returned to his original form, prostrated himself, and repented for his transgressions. The Venerable One asked, "What is your name? Your retinue is vast..."
The youth replied, "My name is Kambala. I have three thousand followers. The Venerable One asked, "Exerting all your supernatural powers, what can you transform?
He replied, "To transform the great ocean would be no difficulty for me. The Venerable One asked, "Can you transform the Sea of Nature (xinghai)?
He asked, "What is meant by the 'Sea of Nature'? I have never known it. The Venerable One then explained the Sea of Nature for him, saying: "Mountains..."
The rivers and the great earth are all established upon it; through this, the samādhis and the six supernormal powers are manifested.
Kāpimāra then gave rise to faith, and his disciples all sought liberation. The Venerable One immediately shaved their heads and conferred the full precepts upon them.

To me; I now entrust this to you. You must guard and uphold it well, transforming others for the sake of the future, so that it shall not be severed.

The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāṇadeva, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra.

Initially a follower of non-Buddhist paths, he had three thousand disciples and was well-versed in various heterodox doctrines. Leading his followers, he traveled to Western India, where there was a crown prince named Meghasvāti.
Having learned the Venerable One’s name, he invited him into the palace to extend his respectful hospitality. The Venerable One said, “The Tathāgata has given this instruction:
‘A śramaṇa must not draw near kings, ministers, or families of influence. The Prince said, “In my kingdom there is a great mountain.
Within that mountain is a stone cave; may you dwell there? The Venerable One then went to it.
After traveling several *li*, a large python came out to meet the Venerable One and coiled itself around his body. The Venerable One then granted it the Three Refuges;
having heard them, the python departed. As the Venerable One approached a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain clothes emerged, joined his palms in greeting, and paid his respects.
The Venerable One asked, "Where do you reside? He replied, "In the past, I was once..."

"O Bhikṣu, I dwelt in the mountain forests, delighting greatly in solitude. When novice bhikṣus came frequently to request instruction, I grew weary of answering them and gave rise to anger and resentment.
At the end of my life, I fell into the body of a python and have resided in this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered you, Venerable One, I have heard the Dharma of the precepts. The Venerable One asked: "Are there any other people on this mountain?"
He replied, "Ten *li* to the north there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas.
That king of trees is named Nāgārjuna, who constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas; I have received it from him. Venerable Sir, you should go there.

When the Venerable One arrived, Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is secluded and solitary, a dwelling place for nāgas and pythons. Great Virtuous One, Most Honorable One, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet to come here?"
The Venerable One said, "I am no one exalted; I have come to visit you, the worthy one.

Nāgārjuna, wishing to take refuge [in him], felt doubt in his mind and asked, "Has this master attained the moistening of the Dharma-nature and clarified the eye of the Way? Is he a Great Sage who continues the True Vehicle?

The Venerable One replied, "Though you speak these words only in your mind, I already know them with my own mind. Simply prepare yourself for the renunciation of the household life; why worry about not being a sage? Nāgārjuna...
Having heard this, he repented and apologized. The Venerable One immediately granted him the tonsure and the full precepts, and then addressed him, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa. In this manner it was passed down successively until it reached me. I now entrust it to you;
you must protect and uphold it, and propagate it for the future so that it shall never be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
The dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). To realize this dharma of the hidden and the manifest is neither folly nor wisdom.
Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations, conjuring fire to cremate his body. Nāgārjuna collected the relics and erected a stūpa. This was King Kaniṣka.
...the dynasty. The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was a native of Western India. He was also named Nāgasena. He first received the Dharma from Venerable Vīra.
Later, he traveled to Southern India. The people of that country were mostly devoted to meritorious deeds and lacked [an understanding of]...
Regarding the nature of wisdom, although Nāgārjuna expounded the Dharma, those who accepted it with faith were extremely rare.

Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they said to one another, "There is a person whose meritorious karma is foremost in the world; yet we speak in vain of Buddha-nature—who among us has beheld it? The Venerable One replied:

The Venerable One replied, "It is neither broad nor narrow; it is immeasurable and without limit; it is without merit and without retribution; it neither dies nor is born.

Hearing these superior principles, they all turned their minds [toward the Dharma]. Then, while seated upon his throne, the Venerable One manifested the form of a full moon, and the assembly heard only the sound of him preaching the Dharma.

The body manifests the form of the full moon, To represent the essence of all Buddhas; In preaching the Dharma, there is no fixed precept, Yet through discernment, it is neither color nor sound.
When the multitude had heard these verses, they all wished to leave the household life. Nāgārjuna immediately shaved their heads and conferred the full precepts upon them.
Previously, there were five thousand non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) in that kingdom who practiced great magical arts and were venerated by the masses;

"This is a wise man who seeks to transform the ignorant. The king said, "One who calls themselves wise should be measured by their wisdom.

Nāgārjuna replied, "Śakra and the Asura King are currently engaged in battle. The king asked, "How can this be verified? Nāgārjuna...
He said, "Wait but a moment. Having finished speaking, he cast aside his spear and severed his own limbs, which fell from the sky.
When the king witnessed this event, he immediately gave rise to faith; [Nāgārjuna] then transformed him completely, leading him to take refuge in the Triple Gem.

Knowing that the king and the assembly possessed true faith, Nāgārjuna further composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, transmitting them to the world. Later, he informed Kāṇadeva...

I now entrust it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it shall not be severed.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
To clarify the principles of concealment and manifestation, he then explained the doctrine of liberation. Regarding all phenomena, his mind attained no realization;

Having transmitted the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi and extensively displayed miraculous transformations. He then returned to his original seat and sat in silent stillness. Kāṇa...
Deva, together with the fourfold assembly, erected a precious stūpa to enshrine [the remains]. This was during the reign of the First Emperor of Qin.
The fifteenth patriarch, the Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India; his secular surname was Viśrāva.
Initially seeking the accumulation of merit, he was also fond of debate. Upon hearing the name of Nāgārjuna, he went to visit him.
As he was about to reach the master’s gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent an attendant to present him with a bowl filled to the brim with water.

When the Venerable One saw this, he immediately cast a single needle into it and proceeded inside. They were delighted by their mutual accord. Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu, where there was an elder.
It was said that Brahmadatta was exceedingly wealthy and possessed great abundance. He had two sons: the first was named Rāhula-yan, and the second was named Rāhula-ta.
In the garden of the elder, a large fungus grew upon a tree trunk; it was exceptionally fragrant and delicious.
Only the elder and Rāhula-ta would take and eat it, and once they had taken it, it would grow back again. None of his other relatives partook of it.
He was able to see. At that time, Rāhulabhadra spoke a verse, saying:
"This tree produces something extraordinary; By eating it, one does not wither away. The wise who understand this cause Should take its ultimate Way as their teacher."
At that time, Kāṇadeva said: "The Tathāgata prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period after his passing, there would be a great Bodhisattva who attained liberation through the ear.
He went to the house of Viśuddhaguṇa and suddenly saw the Venerable One; in his heart he felt rarefied reverence and sought to hear the conditions regarding the 'tree-ear.
The Venerable One asked: 'Did you just now eat rice with a certain bhikṣu? The elder replied: 'I did.'"
"Śramaṇa, he who long ago diligently made offerings has recently entered parinirvāṇa; his stupa still remains.
The Venerable One said to Rāhulabhadra, "Are you not the one who was able to serve and attend that bhikṣu? He replied, "It is exactly as you have described. The Venerable One said:
"You and this child have shared a heart of diligent reverence. Your family members, however, were once possessed of arrogance and were unable to obtain food.
Although that bhikṣu maintained the precepts and was learned, he had not yet realized the ultimate truth; now that his life has ended, he comes to repay his past causes."
"That bhikṣu was born as a tree for you; father and son have obtained food from it, so you ought to repay its kindness.
The Venerable One asked the elder, "How old are you? He replied, "I am now seventy-nine years old. Deva then spoke in verse:
"Entering the Path without penetrating its principle, you return the body [you have received] to the faithful offerings.
At the age of eighty-one, this tree will not grow.
When the elder heard this verse, he marveled and submitted even more deeply, saying: "I am now old and infirm; I cannot serve as your teacher. I pray that you will take my place."
The son followed his teacher and entered the monastic order. The Venerable One said, "Truly, he accords with the Buddha’s prophecy; he is that very person.

He immediately granted him the tonsure and the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Attending upon him, they traveled together to spread the teachings. Upon reaching the city of Pāṭaliputra, they heard that various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.

He replied, "I am destined to attain Buddhahood. The Venerable One said, "Since you say 'I shall attain it,' you truly have not attained it. He then said, "As for me..."

"No, you cannot. "How can you say that? the other asked. The Venerable One replied, "Because you possess a self (*ātman*), you cannot attain it. Because I am without self, I say that I have attained it.
His arguments being thus refuted, he questioned the Venerable One, saying, "What is your name? The Venerable One replied, "My name is Kāṇadeva.
Having previously heard of the Venerable One's reputation, he felt remorse for his previous obstruction and offered his apologies. The Venerable One... [continued].

Having spoken these verses—“I have taught the principle of liberation for those who transmit my Dharma;

regarding the reality of the Dharma, there is nothing realized, no end, and no beginning”—he entered the Samādhi of Agility, emitted a great radiance from his body, and returned to nirvāṇa. The assembly then erected a precious stūpa for him.
This was offered as a memorial. It was during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Former Han dynasty.

The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, was a native of Kapilavastu. While traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
There was a river there named Suvarṇavatī; seeing five Buddha-reflections therein, he said, "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away.
Saṃghanandin resides in that place. As the Tathāgata prophesied, one thousand years hence, he shall succeed [to the Dharma]."
"Saintly state. Having spoken these words, he went upstream until he reached a stone cave in a great mountain, where Saṃghanandi was peacefully established in meditative concentration.
The Venerable One waited for him and asked, "Is your body concentrated, or is your mind concentrated? Saṃghanandi replied, "Both body and mind are concentrated.
The Venerable One said, "If both body and mind are concentrated, how can there be entering and emerging [from concentration]? He replied, "Though there is entering and emerging, it is not lost."
