[The opponent] replied: "Because you have no 'I', your own position is established. [The Venerable] asked: "In which noble one did your teacher train, that he attained this 'no-self' (*anātman*)? [The opponent] replied: "My..."
The teacher Gaṇadeva realized this selflessness. Nanda spoke in verse:
"I bow my head to the venerable Deva, who has emerged from you, O Benevolent One. Because you, O Benevolent One, are without self, I desire to take you as my teacher."
Rāhula replied with many verses:
"Since I am already without a self, you must see my 'I' as the self. If you take me as your teacher, you will know that what is not-self is the self."
Nanda’s mind was suddenly enlightened. He wished for the Master to deliver him, and kneeling on his right knee, he spoke this verse:
"A single bright lamp for the three realms, Turning its light to shine upon me;
The ten directions are all made clear and bright, Like the sun abiding in the void. I have encountered the Great Sage; I pray that I may attain liberation through the Master."
With sincere devotion, he prostrated himself with his head at [the Venerable’s] feet and said, "I pray only that you will deign to accept me.
The Venerable replied, "Your mind is liberated; its intrinsic nature is pure. Having spoken these words, he immediately took a golden bowl in his right hand.

He ascended to the Brahma Palace, took that fragrant food, and brought it to serve the great assembly. However, the assembly feared the golden rice was insufficient, and each harbored feelings of dissatisfaction, unable to partake of the meal.
The Venerable One said, "This is not my fault," and immediately commanded Saṃghanandi to share his seat and eat together with him.
The assembly again marveled at this. The Venerable One said, "That you were unable to eat was because your minds did not understand."
"You should know that he who shared his seat and meal with me was none other than the Tathāgata King of the Pārijāta Tree in the past.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, he descended to manifest in this world. You all, moreover, have already attained the third fruit within the *Ratna-vyūha* Kalpa, though you have not yet realized the state of outflow-free purity (*anāsrava*)."
The assembly said, "Our Master’s supernatural powers can indeed be believed; however, regarding that which is called the 'Buddhas of the past,' we harbor deep doubts.
Saṃghanandin, knowing that sentient beings were conceited, said, "Since the Buddha passed away beneath the twin śāla trees more than eight hundred years ago, people have lacked ultimate faith.
Their right mindfulness has become slight, and they do not revere True Suchness (Tathatā), but cherish only supernatural powers. Having spoken these words, with his right hand...

Gradually advancing into the earth, he reached the boundary of the diamond wheel (*vajramaṇḍala*) and took up the water of ambrosia (*amṛta*). Carrying it in a vessel of lapis lazuli, he returned to the assembly hall.
The great multitude immediately felt deep admiration; they prostrated themselves and repented their transgressions. Thereupon, the Venerable One addressed Saṃghanandin, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma (*saddharmākṣi-kośa*) to Kāśyapa; it has been transmitted in succession down to me."
I now entrust this to you. You should protect and uphold it, and propagate it for the future so that it does not become extinct.
A verse says: In the Dharma, there is truly nothing realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has neither the marks of existence nor non-existence;
How could internal or external [distinctions] arise?
Having heard this, Saṃghanandi immediately praised him from his seat with these verses:
“Excellent, O Great Sage! Your mind is as luminous as the sun and moon; With a single ray of light you illuminate the world, And there is no darkness of Māra that is not extinguished.”
Having transmitted the Dharma, he sat peacefully and manifested his parinirvāṇa. The assembly enshrined his entire body and erected a stūpa; this was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Former Han.
The seventeenth patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of a prince of the Jewel-Adorned City (Śrāvastī).
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents in verse, saying:
"I prostrate to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I bow to my Mother of My Own Flesh and Blood. I now wish to leave the household life."
Out of compassion, his parents heard these verses and earnestly tried to dissuade him. He then made a vow, saying, "I shall now abstain from food until my life comes to an end.
Thereupon, they permitted him to leave the palace and enter the religious life. They ordered the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin to come to the palace to guide him. Nineteen years passed; [the Venerable One...]
He would often think to himself, "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, the light of heaven descended like a torch, and he beheld a great road, level and smooth.
He walked slowly for several *li* until he reached a great mountain, at the foot of which was a stone cave. Thereupon, he entered into meditative stillness within it.
When the father lost his son, he immediately sent out many seekers to search for him, but they did not know his whereabouts. The Venerable One—
Later, while traveling through the country of Mathurā, a gentle breeze suddenly swept over the assembly, bringing a sense of refreshing coolness and comfort.
The crowd did not know its cause, but the Venerable One said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue. A Sage shall soon appear in the world to continue the ancestral lamp."
Having finished speaking, he used his supernatural powers to gather the great assembly and ascend a high peak named Ratnaka.
The Venerable One said, "On this mountain summit there is a purple cloud shaped like a canopy; a holy person dwells here.
The Venerable One saw a youth holding a round mirror who approached him directly. The Venerable One asked, "How old are you? He replied, "I am one hundred years old. The Venerable One...
The other said, "Your years are still few; why do you speak of a hundred years? He replied, "I do not understand the principle; it is precisely a hundred years.
The Venerable One asked, "Are you skilled in wit? He replied, "The Buddha has said:"
If a person lives for a hundred years Without understanding the pivot of all Buddhas, It would not equal living for a single day And attaining decisive realization.
The Master said: "You who hold the mirror, what does your mind clarify? He replied:
The great round mirror of all Buddhas is without flaw or obscuration within or without. Two people saw it together;
their minds and eyes were identical.
Their parents marveled at this and sent them forth to leave the household life. The Venerable One immediately shaved their heads and conferred the full precepts upon them, naming them Gayāśīrṣa.
At that time, the wind blew and the copper bells rang out. The Venerable One asked, "Is it the bells that ring, or is it the wind?
Gaya replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that ring; it is my mind that rings. The Venerable One said, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that ring; whose mind is it that acts thus?
Gaya replied, "Because both are utterly tranquil, it is not a state of meditative absorption (samādhi). The Venerable One said, "Excellent! You shall be the one who continues my lineage."
"Son, to whom shall I entrust you? He replied, "The Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa;
thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, disseminating it for the future so that it never comes to an end.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:
The mind-ground is fundamentally without birth; the ground of practice arises from conditions. Conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another, and the same is true for flowers and fruits.

Having thus transmitted the Dharma, he climbed a tree and passed away. The assembly deliberated, saying: "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree; its spreading shade shall provide shelter for future generations."

His descendants were to enshrine his entire body for burial on a high plateau; however, when the multitude’s strength proved insufficient to lift it, they instead erected a stūpa directly beneath the tree.
This occurred during the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Former Han dynasty.
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His surname was Udraka; his father was Devagupta and his mother was Bhadra.
She dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. He was born after exactly seven days, his body as translucent as lapis lazuli.
He never required washing or bathing, for he was naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood he preferred solitude and stillness, and his speech was unlike that of ordinary children.

Carrying a mirror, he went forth on his travels and encountered the Venerable Nandī. Upon reaching the kingdom of Mahācīna, he perceived an extraordinary fragrance emanating from the house of a certain Brāhmaṇa.
As the Venerable was about to enter that house, the master of the house, Kumāralāta, asked, "Who is this group of people?
He replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Kumāralāta’s heart and mind were struck with awe; he immediately closed the door. The Venerable...
Recently, [the Venerable] knocked upon its door. Rādhā said, "There is no one in this house. The Venerable asked, "Who is it that answers 'there is no one'?
Upon hearing these words, Rādhā knew he was an extraordinary person. She quickly opened the bolt and invited him inside.

The Venerable said, "The Tathāgata prophesied that a thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being would appear in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and flourish the profound transformation. Now you have encountered him."

I, responding to this auspicious destiny, have here caused Kumārajīva to awaken to the wisdom of past lives (*pūrvajātismara-jñāna*). He has entered the path of extinction by leaving the household life, having donned the robes and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Thereupon, I said to him: "The Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma (*saddharmacakṣur-garbha*) to Kāśyapa;
it was transmitted in succession down to me. I now entrust it to you. You must skillfully protect and uphold it, and disseminate it for the future. Do not... [let it perish].
I cause them to be severed. Receive my instruction and listen to this verse of mine:
Where there is a seed and a field of mind, Causes and conditions can bring forth the sprout. When conditions do not obstruct one another, Birth will arise;
where they do not, there is no birth.
After the Venerable One had transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the air and manifested the eighteen transformations. He then cremated his own body, and a stupa was erected for his relics;
this was precisely the era of the Emperor.
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of the Great Yuezhi.

In a former life, he was a *deva* lord of the *Īśvara* heaven. Upon seeing the jeweled necklaces (*vibhūṣaṇa*) of a Bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a mind of attachment and fell to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

There, hearing Śakra expound the Dharma, he was reborn in the Brahma heavens. Because his faculties were sharp, he was skilled in discoursing on the essentials of the Dharma; thus, the various devas honored him as their teacher.
The Master then traveled to the country of the Yuezhi and later arrived at the kingdom of Central India (Madhyadeśa). There was a Mahāsattva there named Jayata who asked him:
"In my family, our parents have always held the Triple Gem in high esteem; yet they have frequently suffered from chronic illnesses, and whatever they undertake never turns out as they wish.
On the other hand, my neighbors have long followed the occupation of Caṇḍālas, yet their bodies are always robust and healthy, and whatever they do succeeds."

[The interlocutor said: "It is fitting. How fortunate they are, and how guilty I am! The Venerable One replied: "Why should you doubt this? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil spans three lifetimes.
Ordinary people merely see that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune;

they then conclude that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and blame are empty. Little do they realize that shadow and echo follow one another, without the slightest discrepancy, even across hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
"Even through kalpas, it shall not be worn away or extinguished. When Jayanta heard these words, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. The Venerable One said:

"Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clearly understood that karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*), delusion exists because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*), and non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*).
The mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without superiority."
"Emptiness! It is profoundly still and spiritually luminous. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may become equal to all Buddhas.
All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions. Śāṇakavāsin received these words and grasped their meaning;

immediately, his latent wisdom was awakened, and he earnestly sought ordination. Once he had received full precepts, the Venerable One told him: "The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived. As it was, so...
I have now come to entrust the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa. It has been passed down in succession until it reaches me; I now entrust it to you.
Guard and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it shall never be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:

"In the nature of things there is fundamentally no arising; it is spoken for the sake of those who seek [the truth]. Since there is nothing to be attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts as to whether it is resolved or not?
The Master said, "These are the words of the Tathāgata Gadgadasvara regarding the purity of seeing one's nature. You should propagate them. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Immediately upon his seat, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly and entered parinirvāṇa.
Śāṇakavāsa erected a stūpa to honor him; this was during the time of Wang Mang.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep, and he transformed and guided immeasurable beings.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha, where he frequently proclaimed the teachings of the sudden [Dharma]. There, the assembly of students there valued only dialectical debate.
The leader among them was named Vāsukapāṇḍu. He always ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day;
he was pure and free from desire, and was thus a refuge for the multitude. When the Venerable One was about to deliver him, he first asked that assembly:

"Can this universal practitioner of dhūta asceticism, who is able to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied: "The Way is realized through practice; he will certainly obtain the state of an Arhat."
[The Buddha said: "The fruit [of this practice]. The Venerable One replied: "This dhūta practitioner is far removed from the Way; before long he shall fall. The assembly asked:
"What virtues does the Venerable One possess that he should disparage our teacher? The Venerable One replied: "I do not seek the Way, nor am I inverted.
I do not perform prostrations, nor am I arrogant. I do not sit for long periods, nor am I indolent. I do not eat only once a day, nor..."
"Eating without mixing [foods], not knowing contentment, and having no craving—having no expectations in the mind is called the Path.
When Pūrvavāsika heard this, he attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and, filled with joy, praised the Venerable One, speaking in verse:

I bow my head to the Honored One of Samādhi; He does not seek after the path of a Buddha, Nor does he perform prostrations, yet no pride or inverted views arise within him. He does not sit in idleness, But eats without attachment;
though slow, he is not indolent, And though swift, he is not restless. Now I have encountered this Venerable One.

Prostrating and relying upon his teacher’s instruction, the Venerable addressed the assembly, saying: "Do you understand my words? The reason I act thus is because their aspiration for the Way is so earnest."
"A string that is too taut will snap; therefore, I did not praise you, so as to cause you to abide in the ground of peace and bliss and enter into the Buddha-wisdom.
He then addressed the mendicant Sarvaga, saying: "When I just now rebuked you before the assembly, was it not distressing to your heart?"
He said: "I recall that in a past kalpa, I was born in the Land of Peace and Bliss as a disciple of the wise Moon-Pure (Candraprabha).
He prophesied that I would realize the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin. At that time, a Bodhisattva named Great Radiance appeared in the world.

Because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him. The teacher rebuked me, saying: 'You honor your son and slight your father; how can you be so base? At that time, I considered myself to be without fault."
"I beg the Master to instruct me. The Master said, "You prostrated before the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha and leaned your staff against the wall while painting the Buddha’s face.
Because of this arrogance, you fell away from the two fruits [of the Path]. Since I have repented my fault, I have heard all manner of evil words, which were like the wind or an echo.
I only pray that the Venerable One, out of great compassion, will deign to instruct me with the wondrous Dharma. The Venerable One said, "You have long cultivated the roots of virtue."
"You shall succeed to my lineage. The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye secretly to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, disseminating it for future generations so that it never be severed.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
"Under these words, one accords with the unborn, Identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm.

If one can understand in this way, having fully penetrated both phenomena and principle, the Venerable One, after transmitting the Dharma, did not rise from his seat but suddenly returned to quiescence. His body was cremated, and his relics were collected to erect a stupa.
This was during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
The twenty-first patriarch, Venerable Vasubandhu, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha;
his father was named Jyotiṣka, and his mother’s name was Yaṅyi. Although the family was wealthy, they had no son, so his parents prayed at a Buddhist stūpa in their quest for one.
He succeeded [to the lineage]. One night, his mother dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dim; upon waking, she became pregnant.
After seven days had passed, an arhat named Bhadrayaśas came to her home and asked:
I have traveled through the four lands and followed this light until I arrived here. Who are you, residing in this house, who has caused the birth of a holy son?

Light-Cover (Prabhācchada) performed a prostration. The assembly of worthies sat upright and accepted it; Light-Cover alone stepped forward to bow, and the assembly of worthies rose from their seats to avoid his path. Light-Cover—
Not fathoming the reason for this, he took a precious jewel and knelt to offer it. Once the venerable assembly had accepted it, they showed no sign of declining or expressing thanks.
Unable to restrain himself, Kāśyapa asked, "I am a man, yet my prostration was disregarded; what virtue does my wife possess that the Venerable Ones avoided her?
The venerable assembly replied, "We accepted your prostration and received the jewel only to bestow blessings upon you. Your wife is carrying a holy child."

"When born, he shall become a bright lamp for the world; therefore, I avoid him. It is not that I hold women in high regard. The assembly of worthies further said, "Your wife shall give birth to two sons.
One shall be named Vāśpa-bandhu, who is the one we revere. The second shall be named Cūḍapanthaka (translated here as 'Wild Crow Son').
Long ago, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat, a cūḍapanthaka bird nested upon his head. After the Buddha..."
He attained the Way. The bhikṣuṇī received her retribution by becoming the King of Nādi. The Buddha prophesied:
"In the second five-hundred-year period, you will be born in the city of Rājagṛha into the family of Viśākha as a biological sibling of a noble one; now there is no discrepancy.
Having fathered two sons, when the Venerable Vāsabhaṇḍu reached the age of fifteen, he paid homage to the arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life, moved by [the arhat's]...
The *bāha* bodhisattva conferred full ordination upon him. They arrived at the kingdom of Naṭika. Its king was named Nityeśvara and had two sons:
the first was named Mahāla, and the second was named Maṇḍala. The king asked the Venerable One, "How does the local custom and climate of Rājagṛha differ from this place?
The Venerable One replied, "In that land, three Buddhas have appeared in the past; now, in Your Majesty’s kingdom, there are two."
The Master [Vasumitra] exhorted him, saying: "Who are these two masters? The Venerable One replied:

"The Buddha prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period, there would be a Great Being of supernatural power who would leave the household life to succeed the Sage; he is the king’s second son. Although my virtue is meager, I shall be included in his record.
The King said: "It is truly as the Venerable One has said; I shall renounce this son to become a śramaṇa. The Venerable One said: [Proceed as you wish.]
"Excellent, Great King! You are able to follow the Buddha's intent. He then told him: "The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the great Dharma-eye secretly to Kāśyapa.
In this manner, it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it well."
Transmit this flow into the future so that it shall not be severed. Receive my teaching and listen to my verse:
"Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded; why do you not awaken to this? To penetrate the Dharma within them is neither of this age nor of antiquity."
After the Venerable had transmitted the Dharma, he entered parinirvāṇa in profound stillness. The assembly reverently offered incense to cremate his body, collected the relics, and erected a stūpa;
this was during the reign of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Mañjarī, was the son of King Nitya-vaśavartin of the country of Nādi.
At the age of thirty, he encountered the Venerable Bhāṣu and traveled to Western India.

The king of that land was named Prāpti, who belonged to the Gautama clan and had taken refuge in the Buddha Vehicle, practicing with diligent perseverance. One day, while on his path of practice, a small [light] appeared.
There was a stūpa that [the King] wished to take for worship, but the assembly was unable to lift it. The King immediately convened a great assembly of the three groups:
those of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), those engaged in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and those of incantations (*vidyā-mantra*). None of them were able to move it.

The Venerable One then explained to the King in detail the origins of the stūpa and its present manifestation, stating that it was brought about by the power of the King’s merit. (The account of King Aśoka’s stūpas is not recorded here at length. Upon hearing this explanation, the King said: "This is truly a Most Holy One."

"Difficult to encounter! Worldly pleasures are not long-lasting. He immediately passed the throne to the crown prince, retired to his grandfather to leave the household life, and subsequently realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The Venerable One comforted and instructed him deeply, saying: "While you reside in this kingdom, you must skillfully deliver others. Now, there is one of great Dharma-capacity in a foreign land;

I shall go to transform him. [The disciple] said: "The Master manifests traces throughout the ten directions; with a single thought, you may arrive there. Why trouble yourself to travel? The Venerable One—
The other said, "Indeed. At that time, while Harelana was reciting verses from the Sūtras for King Ratnamudrā, he suddenly remarked, "The Patriarch Maṇḍara is approaching.

Then the King and Harelana both paid homage from afar. The Venerable One immediately took leave of the bhikṣu who had attained ordination and departed for the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna), where he accepted the offerings of the King and Harelana. Later, Harelana...
He asked the Venerable One, "I have resided in the forest for nine *śveta*s (in India, one year is called one *śveta*).
I have a disciple named Nāgaputra, who was intelligent from his youth; though I have investigated him throughout the three periods of time, I cannot know his origin. The Venerable One said:
"In a past kalpa, this son was born into a Brahmin family in the land of Miàoshàn. He once offered sandalwood to a Buddhist monastery to serve as a mallet for striking the bell;
he was endowed with sharp intelligence and was held in high esteem by the multitude. The Venerable One said, 'I possess the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma;
you should listen and receive it. Thereupon [the son] said, 'The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma to Kāśyapa.'"
Passing down in succession from one to another until it reaches me, I shall now transmit it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it does not perish.
Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:
The mind turns according to the myriad objects; where it turns, its nature is truly profound. Following the flow, if one recognizes the nature, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
Having thus transmitted the Dharma to Mañjarī, he immediately leaped from his seat into the void, manifested eighteen transformations, and returned to his original state.
He passed away while seated in the full lotus posture. Helena and King Baoyin, among others, together offered fragrant wood for the cremation, collected the relics, and erected a stupa;
this was during the reign of Emperor Huan.
*The Extensive Record of the Lamp*, Volume Four;
*The Extensive Record of the Lamp*, Volume Five. [Compiled by Shi] of the Song Dynasty.
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hualena, was a native of the country of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna). His secular surname was Brahmin. His father...
Qiansheng’s mother was named Jinguang. Her family was wealthy but childless, so she prayed before the golden pillars of the Seven Buddhas.
Subsequently, Jinguang dreamed of a divine youth holding a golden ring who said to her, "I am coming. Upon waking, she became pregnant.
One day, a śramaṇa came to her house and said, "The virtue and deeds of the child you carry are beyond the knowledge of this world; he shall be a Śākyamuni."

The testamentary record states: "When the Buddhist teachings flourish, you should protect them with a pure mind. On the day of his birth, celestial flowers rained down and the earth manifested gold and jewels.
When the king heard of this, he prepared his carriage to go and see; he then took the child back to the palace to raise him.

A thousand court ladies all wished to nurse and care for him, but as they could not decide whom to entrust him to, the Venerable One transformed himself into a thousand sons, each placed within the embrace of a court lady.
His appearance was no different [from before], which the King deeply marveled at as extraordinary. He then spoke this verse:
"I now have no prince; It is because I wish to receive you that you have manifested these supernatural powers.
Your display of such powers makes my mind unsettled. If you truly possess supernatural powers, You should manifest your original body."
"You who possess no supernormal powers," he said, having finished the verse "The Palace of the Thousand Sons.
The thousand sons who had been transformed vanished as white light. The son of that Brahmin was already at home;
at seven years of age, while wandering through the villages, he saw the vulgar sacrifices of the common folk and entered the shrine, shouting at them: "You!"

He falsely proclaimed calamities and blessings, deluding and confusing people; every year he abolished the sacrificial animals, causing great injury. When he had finished speaking, the temple image suddenly collapsed.
Consequently, the local community called him the "Holy Son. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life and received full ordination.

At thirty, he met the Venerable Mañjarī. While traveling to Central India to propagate the teachings, he arrived at a kingdom ruled by a king named Abhayasāgara, who held deep faith in the Triple Gem.
After the Venerable had expounded the True Dharma for the king, two individuals dressed in vermilion and white robes suddenly appeared and prostrated before him.
The king asked, "Who are these people? The Master replied, "These are the Sun and Moon Devas. In the past, I..."
"I previously preached the Dharma for him; therefore, he has come to pay his respects. After a short while, he was no longer seen, and only a wondrous fragrance was perceived.

The King asked, "How many suns and moons are there in total throughout the lands? The Venerable One replied, "In each world-system transformed by a thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, there are ten billion Mount Merus, suns, and moons.
If I were to explain this extensively, I could not finish. Upon hearing this, the King was filled with joy. At that time, the Venerable One...
The elder brother of this dragon prince, Upāriṣṭa, died young. His elder brother Siṃha had served as a brahmin;
now that his brother was deceased and his younger brother had likewise passed away, he took refuge with the Venerable One and asked: "I wish to seek the Way. How should I apply my mind?"
The Venerable One said, "If you wish to seek the Way, do not apply the mind. He asked, "If there is no application of the mind, how can one perform the work of a Buddha?
The Venerable One replied, "If you have any application, it is not merit. If you have no action, that is itself the work of a Buddha. For the Buddha has said:
'Whatever merit I have performed, it is devoid of the notion of "mine. Having heard these words, Siṃha immediately..."
"Enter the Buddha-wisdom. At that time, the Venerable One suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of atmospheric phenomenon is this?
Shishizi replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth; furthermore, there are five paths of black vapor stretching across its midst.
The Venerable One asked, "What is the omen of this? He said, "I do not know. The Venerable One said, "Fifty years after my passing, in the north..."
"Difficulties shall arise in the land of India. The infant is within your body; I am about to pass away.
Now, the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, which has been transmitted from Kāśyapa down to me, I now entrust to you. You must protect and uphold it well."
Spread this far into the future so that it shall not be severed. You have received my teaching; listen to my verse:
"When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable. When it is clearly understood that nothing can be attained, One does not speak of 'knowing'."

The Venerable One manifested eighteen miraculous transformations and then entered parinirvāṇa. After the cremation was completed and the relics were distributed, everyone wished to erect a stūpa for them.
The Venerable One appeared once more in the sky and spoke this verse:
"One dharma encompasses all dharmas; all dharmas are subsumed within one dharma. My body is neither existent nor non-existent;
how could it be divided?
When the multitude heard this verse, they built a stūpa at the site of Dhātu.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Bhikṣu Siṃha, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brahmin. From his youth, he was intelligent and perceptive.
While traveling in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was one named Parika who had originally practiced dhyāna-vipaśyanā; thus, there were five groups:

those of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), those of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), those who clung to signs (*nimitta-grāhin*), those who abandoned signs (*nimitta-tyāgin*), and those who remained silent (*amauna*). The Venerable One rebuked and converted them, and these became the four assemblies.
Everyone submitted with hearts full of respect. Only the meditation master Dharmadatta, upon hearing that the fourfold assembly had been reprimanded, came there in a state of indignant agitation.
The Venerable One said, "Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration; why have you come here? Now that you have arrived, how can you still claim to be practicing concentration? He replied:
"Although I have come here, my mind is not distracted; concentration follows the person's habituation—how could it depend on the location?

The Venerable said, "Since you, O worthy one, have arrived, your habituation has also arrived; since there is no fixed location, how could it depend on the person's habituation? He replied, "Because concentration is habituated by the person."

"It is not that non-humans practice concentration; rather, although I have come here, they constantly practice concentration. The Venerable One said, "It is not that non-humans practice concentration;
it is that concentration practices the person. When you first came, who was practicing that concentration?

He replied, "Like a pure, bright pearl, with no obscurations inside or out—if concentration is fully realized, it must necessarily be like this. The Venerable One said, "If concentration is fully realized, it is just like a bright pearl."
"Now that I see you, O Benevolent One, you are no longer among those who lack the jewel. He said, "That jewel is luminously transparent;

both inside and out it is entirely settled. My mind is undisturbed, just like this purity. The Venerable One said, "That jewel has neither inside nor outside; how could you, O Benevolent One, achieve such settling?
Impure things are not subject to agitation; this 'settling' is not true purity. Having received the Venerable One's instruction, Dharmadatta’s mind-ground was opened and clarified.
Now, as the Venerable One had already gathered a community of five disciples and his fame spread far and wide, he was seeking a dharma heir.
He encountered an elder who led forth his son and asked the Venerable One: "This boy’s name is Sthavira; from the moment of his birth, his left hand remained clenched in a fist.

Now that he has grown up, he is still unable to open it. We pray that the Venerable One will reveal the cause of this in his past lives. Upon seeing him, the Venerable One immediately reached out his hand.
The Master said, "Give me back my pearl. The youth immediately opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder.
The Venerable One said, "In a previous life, I was a monk named Po-she. Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea, I received this pearl as an offering."
"Hand it over. Now return my pearl; this is but natural. Thereupon, the elder relinquished his son and he went forth into homelessness.
The Venerable One immediately conferred full ordination upon him. Because of these prior causes and conditions, he was named Vasiṣṭha. The Venerable One then said to him:
My teacher, Halim, made a prophetic prediction: that you would encounter hardship before long.
The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the Right Dharma Eye has been transmitted from Mahākāśyapa down through successive generations until it reached me; I now entrust it to you. You must protect it.
Spread this far into the future; I likewise entrust to you the saṃghāṭī robe, so that the eye of the True Dharma may never be severed.
Receive my instruction and listen to my verse:

"When correctly explaining knowledge and vision, knowledge and vision are both concentrated within the mind; when the mind is present, there is knowledge and vision, and knowledge and vision are right here and now.
Having spoken these verses, the Venerable One sent him to another country. He received many instructions and traveled directly to Southern India. The Venerable One [then] found it difficult...

He could not escape by any means and remained alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) in his native land named Māmukta and Durlabha, who had studied various magical arts and intended to conspire a rebellion.

They then stole the appearance of Buddhist disciples (śākyaputrīya), secretly entered the royal palace, and said: "If this does not succeed, the blame shall fall upon the sons of the Buddha. Since they themselves had committed this sorcery, the calamity...
In an instant, the matter was ruined. The King, truly enraged, said: "I have long placed my heart's devotion in the Triple Gem; why has such malice been plotted against me to this extent?
He immediately ordered the destruction of the monastery and the expulsion of the Śākya community. Furthermore, he personally took up a sword and went to the Venerable One’s location, asking:

"Has the Master realized the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*)? The Venerable One replied: "I have already realized the emptiness of the aggregates. The King asked: "Since you have realized the emptiness..."
"Empty! You may give me your head. The Venerable One said, "The body is not mine; why begrudge my head? The king then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable One's head.
White milk gushed forth to a height of several feet, and the king’s right arm also fell to the ground, where it remained for seven days before he died.
Crown Prince Prabhāvatī sighed and said, "Why did my father bring this calamity upon himself? At that time, there was a white elephant...
The mountain hermit, who deeply understood cause and effect, immediately proclaimed the past causes for Kuśa in detail, saying:

"In a distant eon, your father established a Pañcavārṣika festival (translated here as 'Unrestricted Feast'). At that time, the Venerable Siṃha was a householder who delighted in discussing profound principles.
He led a great multitude of his disciples to the assembly grounds, where he engaged in debate with him; thus, the householder truly possessed [virtue]."
Feeling ashamed, he secretly poisoned his father’s food and sent it to him; the father was subsequently murdered. This is the present King.
As for the layman, he is none other than the Venerable Siṃha. When causes and conditions converged, there was not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy.
Consequently, a stupa was erected over the remains of the Venerable Siṃha. The Venerable Siṇha entrusted the mind-dharma and the robe of faith to Upagupta (Vaspa-si-da).
Aside from the direct lineage, there were twenty-two collateral descendants over four generations of Dharmadatta.
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Kaśmīra; his family name was Brahmin.

His father was named Jixing (Silent Practice) and his mother Chang’an (Ever-At-Ease). Initially, the mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently became pregnant. Upon his birth, he clenched his left hand into a fist.
He encountered the Venerable Siṃha, who revealed his past causes and secretly transmitted the Heart-Seal (*cittamudrā*) to him. Later, he traveled to South India and reached Central India.

There, the king’s name was Jiasheng (Victorious Over Kāśa), who offered him ritual greetings and provisions. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner known as Wuzizun (Venerable Selflessness).
Previously, the King had held him in high esteem. Envious of Bodhidharma’s arrival, he wished to debate with him, hoping that by winning, he might consolidate his own position.
Thus, before the King, he said to Bodhidharma, “I understand the art of debate; it does not require words. Bodhidharma replied, “If you do not speak, how can there be debate?
The outsider said, “One simply grasps the meaning. Bodhidharma asked, “What constitutes ‘meaning’? He replied:
[The monk] said, "Non-mind is the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can there be meaning? [The monk] said, "I speak of non-mind; this should be called my meaning.
The Patriarch said, "Your speaking of non-mind should be called 'not meaning. My speaking of 'non-mind' should be called 'not meaning.
[The monk] said, "If it is the meaning that is not the name, who can discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "You say the name is not the meaning; what kind of name is this name?"
The man said, "I am here to debate the non-meaning. The Master replied, "Since the name is not a name, the meaning is also not a meaning.
Who is it that debates? What is there to be debated? After this exchange, the outsider was silenced and submitted with faith.
At that moment, the Master suddenly turned north, joined his palms, and stood saying, "My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, has encountered a peril today. He then took his leave.

The King traveled south and reached Southern India, where he lived in seclusion within the mountain valleys. The king of that land was named Devaśrī (Heavenly Virtue), who welcomed him and offered him sustenance.
The king had two sons: one was fierce and violent yet possessed of great physical vigor, while the other was gentle and mild but constantly afflicted by illness.

The Patriarch then explained the law of cause and effect to them, and they immediately resolved their doubts. Furthermore, there was a master of incantations who harbored resentment toward the Patriarch.
Dao then secretly placed medicine within the food. When the Master ate it, the other was struck by misfortune. He subsequently sought refuge with the Master and left the household life;

the Master immediately conferred the full precepts upon him. Later, when the Crown Prince achieved victory and ascended the throne, he again believed in non-Buddhist paths and brought trouble upon the Master.

The crown prince was named Amṛtodana. Having offered remonstrance, he was imprisoned. Yù (Jewel) immediately asked the Patriarch, saying, "In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive teachings have long been absent.
As for that which you, Master, have transmitted, to what school does it belong? The Patriarch replied, "In the King’s realm, there has truly been no false dharma from time immemorial."
"What I have attained is the very lineage of the Buddha. The King asked, "Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa has long since passed, from whom did you receive it?
The Patriarch said, "The Mahāsattva Kāśyapa personally received the Buddha’s seal; through successive transmission it reached the twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃha.
From him I received it. The King asked, "I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha could not escape execution; how was he able to transmit it?"

The Dharma was passed to the successor. The Patriarch said, "When my teacher’s time of peril had not yet arisen, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the dharma-verses to manifest the lineage of transmission.
The King asked, "Where is that robe? The Patriarch immediately took the robe out from his bag and showed it to the King. The King ordered it to be burned;
its five colors remained vivid, and even when the fuel was exhausted, it remained as it was. The King then felt remorse and paid homage to the Lion [of the Dharma]. Since the true successor...

The Emperor then pardoned the Crown Prince. The Prince subsequently requested to leave the household life. The Patriarch asked the Prince, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so?
He replied, "My leaving the household life is not for any other purpose. The Patriarch said, "If it is not for any other purpose, then for what purpose is it?
He replied, "It is for the sake of the Buddha’s work. The Patriarch sighed in admiration and said, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as heaven; he will surely become a sage."

When he descended to manifest in this world, [the Master] immediately granted him permission to leave the household life. At the time of his receiving full ordination, the great earth shook, and many miraculous signs appeared.
The Patriarch then addressed him, saying: "I have already grown old and infirm; how could I remain for long? I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
You must protect and uphold it well, disseminating it for future generations so that it shall not be severed. Having received my teaching, listen to me..."
The verse says:
The Sages speak of knowledge and vision; regarding their respective objects, there is nothing that is not such. I have now realized the true nature:
there is neither path nor principle.

Mida heard the verse and again addressed the Patriarch, saying, "The robe of faith should be transmitted. The Patriarch said, "This robe was used as a provisional means of verification because of the difficulties [faced by previous patriarchs].
Since you will face no such difficulties, why should you need this robe? Your transformation shall spread throughout the ten directions, and people will naturally turn toward you in faith.
The Patriarch then manifested the eighteen transformations and emitted a great radiance; he transformed himself into the fire of samādhi and consumed himself. The King and his ministers...
The people collected the relics and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was the crown prince of King Guṇasena of South India.
Having received ordination and attained the Dharma, he traveled to East India. There, the king’s name was Sthira, and he followed non-Buddhist teachers.

When the Brahmin Cūḍapanthaka and the Venerable One were about to arrive, the King and the Brahmin both beheld a white vapor penetrating from the upper to the lower regions. The King asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Brahmin, knowing in advance that the Venerable One was entering the kingdom and fearing that the King might convert to the virtuous path, replied: [The Brahmin said: "O Great King, this is not a good omen. It portends that a great calamity will soon befall Your Majesty. The King asked, "What kind of calamity? The Brahmin replied, "A great fire shall break out and consume the entire city. The King then asked, "Is there any means to prevent it? The Brahmin said, "If Your Majesty orders the city to be sprinkled with water, it may be averted. The King immediately commanded his ministers to prepare a vast quantity of water and to sprinkle it throughout the city. At that moment, the Venerable One arrived at the city gate. The King went out to meet him and asked, "Venerable One, why did you come so late? The Venerable One replied, "Great King, I have come because I heard that the city was being sprinkled with water. The King asked, "For what purpose? The Venerable One said, "I heard that a great fire would break out and consume the city; therefore, I came to extinguish it. The King said, "Venerable One, the fire has already been extinguished by my ministers. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the fire has been extinguished, the smoke remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city again. The Venerable One arrived once more and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the smoke remained. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the smoke has vanished, the smell persists. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city yet again. The Venerable One arrived for a third time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the smell persists. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the smell has vanished, the heat remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city once more. The Venerable One arrived for a fourth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the heat remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the heat has vanished, the ashes remain. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a fifth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the ashes remain. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the ashes have vanished, the ground remains parched. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a sixth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the ground remains parched. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the ground is no longer parched, the dust remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a seventh time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the dust remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the dust has vanished, the wind remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for an eighth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the wind remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the wind has vanished, the clouds remain. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a ninth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the clouds remain. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the clouds have vanished, the rain remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a tenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the rain remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the rain has vanished, the thunder remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for an eleventh time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the thunder remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the thunder has vanished, the lightning remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a twelfth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the lightning remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the lightning has vanished, the dragon remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a thirteenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the dragon remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the dragon has vanished, the palace remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a fourteenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the palace remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the palace has vanished, the throne remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a fifteenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the throne remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the throne has vanished, the King remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a sixteenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the King remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the King has vanished, the Queen remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a seventeenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the Queen remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the Queen has vanished, the Prince remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for an eighteenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the Prince remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the Prince has vanished, the people remain. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a nineteenth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the people remain. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the people have vanished, the earth remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a twentieth time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the earth remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the earth has vanished, the ocean remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a twenty-first time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said the ocean remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although the ocean has vanished, Mount Sumeru remains. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one last time. The Venerable One arrived for a twenty-second time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the Venerable One said Mount Sumeru remains. The Venerable One said, "Great King, although Mount Sumeru has vanished, the sun and moon remain. The King then ordered his ministers to sprinkle the city one final time. The Venerable One arrived for a twenty-third time and asked, "Great King, why are you sprinkling the city again? The King replied, "Because the V

"This is merely a portent of Māra; what auspicious sign could there be? He then gathered his followers and deliberated, saying, "Now that Subhūti is about to enter the capital city, who among us can thwart him?
A disciple replied, "Each of us possesses incantations capable of shaking heaven and earth and entering fire and water;
why should we have any cause for concern? When the Venerable One arrived, he first saw black vapors over the palace walls.
He then said, "This is but a minor difficulty. He went straight to the king's presence. The king asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master?
The Master replied, "I shall deliver sentient beings. The king asked, "By what method do you deliver them? The Master replied, "Those who are stubborn and fierce I transform through firmness;

those who are gentle and pliant I discipline through gentleness. When the Brahmin heard these words, he could not contain his anger and immediately used his illusory powers to conjure a great mountain that stood before him.
The Venerable One appeared above their heads; as they looked up, he returned to the top of the assembly. The Brahmins were struck with terror and threw themselves upon the Venerable One.

Out of compassion for their ignorance and delusion, the Venerable One miraculously caused the mountain to vanish instantly. He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the King, leading him toward the True Vehicle.
Furthermore, the Venerable One said to the King: "In this kingdom, there shall be a holy man who will succeed me. At that time, there was a *bhikṣu*...
There was a son of a brāhmaṇa who was already twenty years old. Having lost both his parents in childhood, he did not know their names or lineage.

Sometimes he called himself "Āmuktamāla" (The One Adorned with Necklaces), so people called him the "Boy Āmuktamāla. He wandered through the streets and villages, begging for his daily sustenance, much like the monk Sadāparibhūta.
When people asked him, "Why do you walk so hurriedly? he replied, "Why do you walk so haughtily? Or when they asked, "What is your clan? he replied:
"You share the same clan as me. When the King saw the Venerable One coming out in the same carriage, the Youth Maṇibhadra prostrated himself before him.
The Venerable One asked, "Do you remember past events? He replied, "I recall that in a distant kalpa, we lived together;
you expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, while I recited the profound *Sūtras*. Today’s encounter is surely in accord with our former causes. The Venerable One said:
The man further said to the king, "This boy is none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
After this holy one, two more individuals will appear: one shall convert the southern land of India, and the other’s karmic conditions lie in China.
Within four or five years, he will return to this region; thus, based on his past causes, he is named Prajñātara. He then continued: "As it is said..."
In the past, I transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa. In this manner, it was passed down successively until it reached me. I now entrust it to you;
you must protect and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it never be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:

The Treasury of the True Nature of the Mind-ground has neither head nor tail; it responds to conditions to transform sentient beings, and for this skillful means, it is called the Honored One of Wisdom.
Having transmitted the Dharma, he took leave of the King, saying: "My work of transformation is now complete; I shall return to quiescent extinction. I pray that the King..."

Having provided external protection for the Mahāyāna without fail, he returned to his original seat, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. He transformed into the fire of samādhi to cremate himself;
his relics were collected, enshrined in a stupa, and interred. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to Southern India to propagate the teachings.
There, a king named Gandhāra—who venerated the Buddha and the Sangha—offered him a priceless jewel.
The king had three sons, the youngest of whom was a bodhisattva. Desiring to test what [the prince] had attained, the Venerable One then...
Śikhidatta asked the three princes, "Is there anyone capable of matching this pearl, so perfectly bright?
The first prince, Candravimalatāra, and the second prince, Guṇaratnatāra, both replied, "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures; truly, nothing surpasses it.
Were it not for the power of your noble Way, who could receive it? The third prince, Bodhitāra, said, "This is..."
Worldly treasures are not the supreme; among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme.
This is worldly radiance, yet it is not the supreme; among all radiances, the radiance of wisdom is supreme. This is worldly illumination, yet it is not the supreme;
among all illuminations, the illumination of the mind is supreme. The light of this jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the radiance of wisdom to be clearly discerned.

In this regard, once one has made this distinction, one immediately recognizes the pearl; once the pearl is recognized, its preciousness is clarified. If its preciousness were self-evident, the jewel would not be a jewel;
if the pearl were self-evident, the pearl would not be a pearl. One must rely on the "wisdom-pearl" to distinguish the worldly pearl;
the jewel is not a jewel by itself. One must rely on the "wisdom-jewel" to clarify the Dharma-jewel. Thus, the teacher possesses the Way.
The Dharma Jewel immediately appeared. When sentient beings awaken, the jewel of the mind becomes self-luminous. The Venerable One praised his discernment and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what thing is without characteristics? He replied: "Among all things, non-arising is without characteristics.
He asked again: "Among all things, what thing is the highest? He replied: "Among all things, the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) is the highest. He asked again.
"Among all things, which is the greatest? He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the greatest. The Venerable One knew him to be a noble being;
however, as the time had not yet come, he remained silent and waited for him. When the incense arrived and the King grew weary of the world, the entire assembly wailed and lamented.
Only the third son, Bodhitara, sought to leave the household life and thus threw himself upon the Venerable One, who immediately—
He was granted the tonsure and received full ordination. Once the auspicious time had arrived, the Venerable One addressed him, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma to Kāśyapa; thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you.
You must uphold and protect it well, disseminating it for future generations so that it shall never be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:"
The various seeds arise from the mind-ground; Due to conditions they arise again. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected;
When the flower opens, the world arises.
Having thus entrusted the Dharma, the Venerable One immediately emitted a great radiance from his seat. He leaped into the void and transformed himself into fire.
The body was cremated, and the assembly collected the relics to erect a stupa; this was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty.

The twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma, was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan name was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. He encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, who arrived in his native land and received offerings from the king.
Consequently, he was tested by being asked to distinguish the bestowed precious jewels with his elder brothers, thereby illuminating the nature of the mind.
Later, the Venerable One said to him, "You have already attained a thorough understanding (*pramāṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*). Now, 'Dharma' carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration.
You should be named Dharma. Consequently, he changed his name to Bodhidharma and addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"I shall travel to which country? I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Venerable One said, "You must not travel far yet. Stay for sixty-seven years in Southern India;
then you shall go to China. Be careful not to travel too soon; there you will be pitied under the sun.
Bodhidharma asked, "Are there Great Beings there who are capable of being vessels for the Dharma? Within a thousand years, will there be obstacles? The Venerable One said, "I..."
More than sixty years after his parinirvāṇa, that country will face difficulties. You, Wenbu, can personally subdue them through your own virtue.
You must not remain in the south, for its people there cherish only worldly achievements and do not understand the principles of the Buddha. Even if you were to go there, [they would not heed you].
Nor may you remain for long. Listen to my prophecy:
"Traveling along the road, crossing water, one encounters sheep again; Alone and weary, one secretly crosses the river at sunset.
How pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses! Two young cassia trees shall flourish for a long time."
He asked again, "What further events will there be after this? The Venerable One replied, "From now on, after one hundred and fifty years, there will be a minor calamity. Listen to my prophecy:"
"Auspicious within the mind, yet ominous without; a monk’s quarters beneath a stream, a name that does not suit.
Because he encountered a venomous dragon, a martial son was born; suddenly meeting a small mouse, his stillness shall be endless.
He asked again, "What further matters will there be after this? The Venerable One replied, "From this point forward, one hundred and sixty [years]."
At the end of the year, there will be a minor difficulty. Father and son shall succeed one another, yet it shall not last long. He shall live for one, two, three, or five years;
once this period has passed, there will be one who perceives his intent and heeds my prophecy, saying: [text missing].

Suddenly encountering deep water on the road, Casually seeing a tiger and then meeting a pig; Though the little calf has horns, When the dragon emerges from the clear stream, all must yield. He asked again, "What will it be like hereafter? [The Master] said, "Two hundred and twenty years hence, one shall see a person beneath the forest trees. When [the monk] was about to speak, [the Master] struck him. The monk bowed and departed. Later, he went to Mount Tiantai and became a monk under Master Zhixian. He lived in seclusion for many years and did not emerge. One day, while walking in the mountains, he suddenly encountered a tiger. He called out, "Great Master Baizhang! The tiger immediately vanished. He then composed a verse: "From the time I left the Master’s gate, I have wandered through the mountains and rivers. Today I encounter this fierce beast, Yet I do not fear its claws and fangs. If you wish to know my name, It is the Dharma-heir of Baizhang. He then went to Mount Luofu and lived there for several decades. During the Tianxi era of the Song dynasty, he passed away at the age of ninety-nine. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Luofu. It is said that whenever the weather was fine, his voice could be heard from within the stupa chanting the *Heart Sutra*. When the stupa was opened, nothing was found inside except for a single shoe. People of the time marveled at this as a sign of his spiritual power. His dharma heirs included Master Xinghua Cunjiang and others. His lineage flourished greatly in the world. This is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan). It is said that when the monk first arrived at Baizhang’s place, he had already been practicing for thirty years. The Master said to him, "You have been sitting in meditation for thirty years; what have you attained? The monk replied, "I have only attained the state of non-attainment. The Master said, "You have attained something, yet you say you have attained nothing. You have attained nothing, yet you say you have attained something. What is this thing you have attained? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "You have attained a dead tree stump. The monk then prostrated himself and withdrew. The Master said, "This fellow has finally attained something. Later, the monk went to Mount Tiantai and lived in seclusion for many years. One day, while walking in the mountains, he suddenly encountered a tiger. He called out, "Great Master Baizhang! The tiger immediately vanished. He then composed a verse: "From the time I left the Master’s gate, I have wandered through the mountains and rivers.
