Having attained the fruits of the Path, listen to my prophecy:
"Though Zhendan is vast, there is no other road; one must rely on the feet of a grandson to travel upon it.
A golden rooster will release a single grain of rice from its beak to provide offerings to the Arhat Sangha of the ten directions."

He asked again, "What will happen after this? He replied, "Three hundred and eighty years hence, there will be a bhikṣu who learns in secret but employs his knowledge openly. I shall record this by means of three prophecies."
In the eighth month, the ancestral vessels of Shang flew with sound; great fortune arrived as auspicious birds were not startled.
Cradling a rooster, he rose again for the assembly; holding dragons and serpents in his hands at the two pillars.
The visiting lord’s cap was temporarily removed; the mosquito-like insect could no longer leave its form.
An elephant from the Eastern Sea returns, tearing through rocks with its swelling trunk; In both places they receive grace, neither of which is slight.
The sun and moon move together as if unmoving; Then there are no crowns upon their heads as they ascend the mountain.
Furthermore, a gift of one peak is added to the verdant crags; Only when jade instructs people to recognize it does it truly bear a name.
The Venerable One said, "A great vessel shall appear; upon meeting the clouds, he will ascend. My Way shall not sink, for your mind has found its resting place.
Bodhidharma then asked, "What will happen after this? He replied, "Four hundred and sixty years hence, you will meet a man who wears no clothes."
Desiring to create an obstacle, listen to my prophecy:
On the high peak, no one is present; even if one sheds their clothes, Though the small snake is venomous, it can do nothing.
In the center of the well, the sky is near; The tiny novice monk possesses a great capacity.
The Venerable One said, "This minor difficulty shall be resolved by the youth clad in black. He asked again, "What will happen after this?

He replied, "Six hundred years hence, the 'Tree that Does Not Grow' (Ajātaśatru) will create obstacles. Although he shall cause such difficulties, two persons will appear and the situation shall naturally become peaceful. Listen to my prophecy:"
Though the great waves are high, they are not worth knowing; A hundred years pass and the ordinary tree grows only dry branches.
One bird flies south, yet returns to the north; Two people go east, yet turn back toward the west. The Venerable One said:
"The Monk in White has preached the Dharma immeasurably. If you understand this prediction, then return and do not face away. Furthermore:
Question: What will happen after this? Answer: Eight hundred years hence, four dragons shall together create a single calamity.
Listen to my prophecy:
"Pitiful, the bright moon alone occupies the heavens; The four dragon children each depart for themselves."
Rushing to and fro in the four directions—east, west, south, and north—the sun shines level overhead across the boundless expanse.
The Venerable One said:
"These words of my record: long waist and short legs; palms joined toward the heavens; turning the head, one loses their companion."
His body is clad in red robes, yet they appear like plain white silk; he stands before one's eyes, yet it is as if he were not seen.
Contemplate this well: when the water is clear, the moon appears.
He asked again, "What follows after this? [The Master] said, "Three thousand years hence, there will be a total of thirteen hardships. His...
There are nine major difficulties and four minor difficulties. Listen to my prophecy:
A bird comes and perches upon the high hall, as if wishing to startle; White clouds enter the earth, yet their color remains green.
The golden dragon is in the heavens, and the sun and moon are bright; Will the waters of the East Yang Sea be clear or not?
Holding a rosary in hand, now heavy, now light; Though lacking eyes and heart, the turning [of the beads] is vividly awake.
Lacking ears and eyes, yet skillfully observing and listening; The body is fundamentally empty, yet possesses form.
Not speaking of surname or name, but merely marking the names with slips; The mind seeks out scrolls, yet mistakenly reads the sutras.
"His mouth speaks of kindness and fortune, yet his heart is devoid of feeling; whether going or coming, his body never rests.
The Venerable One said, "In the future, many hardships shall all lie within these ten lines. Although I have extensively sealed [this teaching], you have not seen it.
The Master respectfully received this instruction and served by his side with diligence for nearly forty years, until the Venerable One was about to pass away from the world.
There was the Tripiṭaka Master Bhadra, to whom Dharmayaśas had once sent inquiries.
Bhadra had a disciple named Na-lien-xie-she (Narasīha), who frequently discussed the scriptural teachings with the lay follower Wan Tianyi. Tianyi then asked Narasīha:
"May I hear about the successive stages through which the holy assembly of the Western Regions has propagated the Dharma? Narasīha replied: "The patriarchal masters, beginning from Kāśyapa..."
The Tradition: Bodhidharma, the disciple of the twenty-seventh patriarch Prajñātāra, arrived at Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty and stayed at Shaolin Temple.
Daoyi asked, "After the Northern Masters have passed away, who will succeed them? Yeshe replied:
The Honored and Victorious One now conceals the ancient; he who was without arms now possesses arms again. When the Dragon arrives, he shall bestow the treasure;
one who offers tribute shall subdue those with loathsome names. Yi said: "After this master, who will be the successor? Ye-she replied:
He arose, seeking what was not obstructing him; the teacher said, "I have cast the rope. On the road he encountered a monk, whom he prostrated at the feet;
the six limbs were divided and refined, and he questioned him again. Yaśas said:
The three and four [elements] are entirely without self; Across the water, one receives the lamp of the mind. The Honored One’s name transcends all measure;
From anger, no increase arises.
Yi asked him again. Yaśas replied:

The offerings presented were of poor quality; though he spoke with diligence, he was not truly diligent. When the person who had offered the auspicious field asked why he had merely written down these four-line verses, Yaśas replied: [The original Chinese text: 奉物可曾物 言勤又不勤 唯書四句偈為對瑞田人懿復問之。耶舍曰。 [Translation: "The offerings presented were of poor quality; though he spoke with diligence, he was not truly diligent.
When the person who had offered the auspicious field asked why he had merely written down these four-line verses, Yaśas replied:"
Able to conceal matters within the heart, he spoke them by the banks of the Han River.
Probing for the moon in the water upon the lake waves, it was about to illuminate two or three people. Yi asked him again. Yaśas replied:
Having received Maitreya’s words, he left his hometown and traveled day by day. Upon arriving in Liang, he moved closer to the road;
the remaining days of his journey were calculated for the celestial path. Yi then questioned him again. Yeśa replied:

The profound principle arises from the earth of Stillness; the Honored One who penetrates all is likewise honored. Standing shoulder to shoulder with the Triple-Howl clan, a single hair grows beneath his foot.
It is also said:
The Assembly of Spirits feels ashamed before the Heavenly Grace; Twenty-six people have sprouted forth. In the Dharma there is no flavor;
upon the stone lies merit.
It is also said:
Originally a great tiger-man, he has now transformed into a lion’s discourse. The government bestowed upon him the title of Tongxiang of Maling;
it is also said he was the thirty-third [patriarch].
"Nine women transcend the human relations; eight individuals sever marriage. As for 'Decaying,' it means adding six feet;
among the assembly, he is the Honored Ancestor.
It is also said:
Zouwu shares borders with Chao; the offspring of the goose and crow emerge from their bodies. Though the two heavens possess resonance, the three transformations are silent and free of dust.
It is also said:
What was spoken as "few" has never been few; what was called "flowing" does not flow. As for the grass, if its tip is removed, three or four will continue to grow.
Ye-she said: "I have recorded this prophecy to mark the future. Two hundred and eighty years hence, there shall be a great [being]..."

The King reverently honored the Triple Gem; as the sovereign led and his ministers followed in harmony, the seas were tranquil and the rivers clear. May those who possess ears take note of these preceding records.
At that time, Master Shuyin flourished with many sages, while Wantian Yiyang respectfully upheld the holy prophecy, wearing it upon himself without weariness.

It was compiled into fascicles. Later, when the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra passed away at Mount Lu, Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty dispatched an envoy to transmit this prophetic text, which was then included in the *Xu fǎzhuàn* (Continued Biographies of the Dharma). At that time, Bodhidharma was propagating the teachings in his own country.
There was one named Buddhayaśas, a follower of the Hīnayāna, who had divided the path into six schools; each adhered to their own interpretations and developed their respective methods of conversion.
The six schools were: first, the School of Characteristics; second, the School of Non-characteristics; third, the School of Samādhi and Prajñā;
fourth, the School of Precepts and Practice; fifth, the School of Non-attainment; and sixth, the School of Quiescence. Bodhidharma said, "Now these six schools are forever entangled in false views.
Having spoken thus, he went to the place of the first school, the School of Characteristics, and asked: "What is the name given to all dharmas?"

"Regarding the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): among those present, a senior elder named Sarvada replied, 'Among all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), that which does not mutually interact with other characteristics is called the true nature.
The Teacher said, 'If one clarifies the true nature, it is that all characteristics do not mutually interact.'"
"What, then, is fixed? He replied, "Among all characteristics, there is truly nothing fixed. If characteristics were fixed, how could they be called 'real'?
The Master said, "The fact that all characteristics are not fixed is precisely what is called the 'true characteristic. You are now not fixed; how then can you attain it?"
He said, "My words are not fixed; I do not speak of characteristics, yet I shall speak of characteristics. The meaning is likewise so. The Master said, "Your words are not fixed;
they should be the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because they are fixed and yet not fixed, they are not the true characteristic.
He said, "Since what is fixed is not fixed, it is not the true characteristic. Knowing that I am not [fixed], it is neither fixed nor changing. The Master said, "You are now unchanging."
"What is meant by 'true reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)? That which has already changed and that which has already passed—its meaning is likewise so. He said, "That which does not change must exist;

because of its existence or non-existence, it is therefore called the changing true reality, establishing its meaning through this certainty. The Master said, "True reality is unchanging; if it changes, it is not true reality."
Regarding existence and non-existence, what is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)? Śāvala perceived that his teacher was a sage; his understanding was profound and his realization subtle.
He then pointed with his finger toward space and said, "This is the world of marks, yet it can also be empty. Can my body become like this?
The Master replied, "If you understand the true mark, you will see that it is not a mark. If you comprehend that it is not a mark, then even its form..."
However, within form (*rūpa*), one should not give rise to the essence of form; because within that which lacks characteristics (*animitta*), there is no obstruction to existence.

If one can understand it thus, this is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). When those people heard this, their minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it with faith.

Then they went to the second school, the School of Non-characteristics (*animittavāda*), and asked: "You speak of non-characteristics; by what should they be realized? Among those people was one of wisdom...
The man replied, "I clarify formlessness (*animitta*), because the mind does not manifest. The Master asked, "If your mind does not manifest, how can you clarify it?
He replied, "I clarify formlessness; the mind does not dare to abandon it. At the time of clarifying, there is also no one who 'should' do so.
The Master said, "Regarding all that exists and does not exist, the mind neither grasps nor abandons, and yet there is no one who 'should' do so. Who, then, clarifies formlessness?"
Therefore, he said, "Even when entering the Buddha-samādhi, there is nothing to be attained; how much more so for the formless (animitta), which one wishes to know?
The Master said, "If you do not even know the forms, who can speak of existence or non-existence? If there is nothing to be attained, what is it that is called samādhi?
He replied, "I say that I do not realize anything; I realize that there is nothing to be realized. Since it is not [a conventional] samādhi, I call it samādhi. The Master said, "It is not samādhi."

"How shall one name this? Since you have not yet realized it, what realization can there be for one who has not realized? When Pāratī heard his master’s analysis, he immediately awakened to his original mind.
He prostrated in gratitude to the master, repented of his past errors, and the master prophesied: "You shall attain the fruit; you will realize it before long.
There is a māra in this land; you shall subdue him before long. Having spoken thus, he went to the abode of the third master, Dinghui (Dinghui Zong).

He asked, "In your study of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), are they one or two? A certain *pālanda* among that assembly replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two.
The Master said, "If they are neither one nor two, why call them concentration and wisdom? He replied, "Abiding in concentration, it is not concentration;
dwelling in wisdom, it is not wisdom. One is precisely not one; two is precisely not two. The Master said, "In that case..."
"One and not one; when two, they are not two. Since these are neither fixed concentration nor wisdom, by means of what concentration and wisdom could they be defined?

He replied, "Neither one nor two—this is what concentration and wisdom can know. That which is neither concentration nor wisdom is likewise so. The Master said, "Since wisdom is not concentration, how then can it be known?
If it is neither one nor two, what is concentration and what is wisdom? When Bharadvāja heard this, his doubts were completely dispelled like ice melting away.
Upon arriving at the abode of the fourth master, the Master of Precepts and Conduct, he asked: "What is called 'precept' (*śīla*)? What is called 'conduct' (*caryā*)?
Regarding these precepts and conduct, are they one or two? A wise man among that assembly replied: "'One-two' and 'two-one'—both are produced from that;
relying on the teaching without defilement is what is called precepts and conduct. The Master said: "When you say 'relying on the teaching,' this is precisely defilement."
"Defilement! Both [inner and outer] are simultaneously destroyed. How can you say you rely on the teachings? These two are contradictory; they do not reach the level of practice.

When inner and outer are not clear, how can it be called precept (śīla)? He said: 'I have both inner and outer. Once he has fully understood this, and having attained thorough penetration, it is itself the practice of precept.
If one speaks of contradiction, then both are right and both are wrong. When speech reaches purity, it is the precept and it is the practice."—The Master.
He said, "If it is both 'is' and 'is not,' how can you call it pure? Since you have attained penetration, why speak of internal and external?
When the worthy one heard this, he immediately felt ashamed and submitted. He then proceeded to the fifth school, the School of Non-Attainment (Wude), and asked, "You say there is non-attainment;
what is attained through non-attainment? Since there is nothing to be attained, there is also no attainment of attainment. Among that assembly was one named Baojing, who replied, "I..."

[The opponent] says: "One speaks of non-attainment (*anupalabdhi*). It is not that non-attainment is non-attainment; rather, one must speak of the attainment of attainment (*upalabdhy-upalabdhi*). Non-attainment is itself attainment. The Master said:

"If attainment is already non-attainment, then attainment is also non-attainment. Since you speak of the 'attainment of attainment,' what is it that this 'attainment of attainment' attains? The opponent replied: "When one perceives attainment, that is non-attainment. This non-attainment is itself attainment.
If one perceives non-attainment, this is called the 'attainment of attainment. The Master said: "Since attainment is already non-attainment, then non-attainment is non-existent."
"Attainment? Since there is nothing to be attained, what could possibly be attained? Upon hearing this, Baojing’s doubts and delusions were instantly dispelled.
He proceeded to the sixth school, the School of Quiescence (Jijingzong), and asked: "What is meant by 'quiescence'? Within this Dharma, what is it that is still and what is it that is quiescent?
A householder there replied: "That this mind does not move is called 'quiescence' (ji). That it is unstained by phenomena is called 'stillness' (jing)."

The Master said, "If the fundamental mind were not inherently quiescent, it would require the support of stillness. Since it is quiescent from the beginning, what need is there for stillness? He replied, "All dharmas are fundamentally empty;
because they are empty of emptiness, they are called 'quiescent' within that emptiness of emptiness. The Master said, "Emptiness itself is already empty, and all dharmas are likewise so.
Quiescence is without mark; what is there to be stilled, and what is there to be quiescent? Upon hearing this ocean of meaning, he was suddenly enlightened as if opening wide.
The ice melted away. Subsequently, the group of six monks all vowed to take refuge [in the Triple Gem]. King Kṛkin ascended the throne, yet he held the Triple Gem in contempt and disparagement.
He would often say, "My ancestors all believed in the Buddha-way," and further claimed, "I myself am the Buddha; why seek it elsewhere?
The doctrines of karmic retribution for good and evil are all fabrications devised by those of great cleverness. The elders of the kingdom, who had served under previous kings—
Those who offered respectful worship were all dismissed. When Dharmarāja learned of this, he immediately thought of two leaders within the school of the signless (animitta-vāda):
one was Bhāradvāja, who had a karmic affinity with the king; the other was Saṃjaya, who was not lacking in intelligence and eloquence, yet lacked prior causal conditions.
At that time, the followers of the six schools also each thought to themselves, "The Buddha-dharma faces a crisis," and having spoken thus, they each departed.
Bodhidharma performed the rites of salutation and inquiry. Zongsheng said, "I consider myself shallow and insignificant; how could I dare to decline your request to go?
Bodhidharma said, "Though you possess discernment and wisdom, your power of the Way is not yet complete.

Zongsheng suspected, "This master fears that I might see the King and perform great Buddhist services, whereby my fame and reputation would become so prominent as to eclipse his majesty. Even if he possesses such merit and wisdom as to become king, I am but a śramaṇa."

"Once you have entered my gate and received the Buddha’s instructions, how could it be difficult to subdue me? Subsequently, [the monk] proceeded to the King's presence and extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma regarding the suffering and happiness of the world, and the good and evil of humans and devas.
The King engaged him in a back-and-forth exchange of questions and inquiries, saying: "As for what you now understand..."
"Where does that Dharma reside? Zongsheng replied, "It should accord with the Way in governing and transforming the people. The King asked, "As for the Way you possess, where does that Way reside?
The King said, "The Way I possess is intended to eliminate heterodox teachings. As for the Dharma you possess, whom do you intend to subdue?
Bodhidharma, knowing that Zongsheng was about to fall into error, told Pratītyasamutpāda (Boluo-ti): "Zongsheng has not received my instruction."
He secretly transformed the King; in a mere moment, the King’s arguments were exhausted. "You may depart at once.

Pāṭaliputra received this command and proceeded to the front of the palace, where he stood silently. At that time, while the King was interrogating Zhongseng, he suddenly saw Pāṭaliputra arrive before him.
The King asked, "Which is heterodox and which is orthodox? He replied, "I am neither heterodox nor orthodox; I have come to rectify both heterodoxy and orthodoxy. The King’s mind—
“If it is correct, I am neither wrong nor right; if my doctrine is superior, you shall immediately be expelled. Pāṭidīpa said, “If Your Majesty possesses the Way, why would you expel a śramaṇa?
Although I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me to the test. Enraged, the king asked, “Who is this Buddha?”
The Master replied, "To see one's nature is to be a Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see his own nature?
He replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? He replied, "It resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning? I do not see it now."
The answer was: "The activity is seen now, yet Your Majesty does not see it yourself. The King asked: "Is it present within me? The answer was:
"If Your Majesty engages in activity, all things are so; if Your Majesty does not engage in activity, the essence is likewise difficult to perceive. The King said: "When it is actually being used..."
He asked, "Where does it appear? He replied, "When it appears, there shall be eight [instances]. The King said, "I pray that you will explain this to me.
Thereupon, Pratītya spoke in verse:
In the womb, it is the body; dwelling in the world, it is called a person. In the eye, it is called seeing; having ears, it is called hearing.
In the nose, it discerns fragrance; in the mouth, it engages in discourse. In the hands, it grasps and seizes; in the feet, it moves and runs.
It manifests everywhere, encompassing all within the sands of the universe, yet it is gathered and received within a single minute speck of dust.
"The wise know this as the Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the spirit-soul.
Having heard this verse, the King repented and apologized for his previous errors. As Zongsheng had already been expelled, he thought to himself: "I am now a hundred years old."
"At eighty, I have committed wrongs; I cannot endure my own reproach. What face would I have to live? Having finished speaking, he threw himself from a precipice.
Suddenly, a divine being caught him and placed him upon a rock. The divine being spoke a verse to Zongsheng, saying: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
The Master lived for one hundred years; at eighty, he was still diligent. Because he drew near to the Most Honored One, he cultivated himself and entered the Way.

Although he possessed some wisdom, he did not once give rise to reverence or esteem toward those venerable ones who held many views of "self" and "mine," yet he practiced meritorious deeds four or five times.
Because their minds were not tranquil and they were arrogant despite their intelligence, they have reached this state where even kings do not respect them;
one should know that such results will be experienced.
From now on, do not be negligent, for before long you shall perfect your wisdom. All the sages dwell within the mind, and the Tathāgata is likewise so.
Upon hearing the verse, Zongsheng was filled with joy and immediately sat down in meditation amidst the cliffs. At that time, King Yijian again asked Bodhidharma:
"Worthy one, you possess such wisdom and eloquence; whom do you take as your teacher? He replied, "The one under whom I have gone forth as a monk is my teacher, the King’s uncle, Bodhidharma.
When the King heard his teacher's name, he was struck with awe for a long while, and subsequently issued an edict to his close ministers to grant him special honors.
He was invited. Dharmatrāta followed the messenger to the palace and performed repentance for the king. The king then issued an edict for Zongsheng to return to his own country.

A high minister reported, "Zongsheng was exiled and perished on a high cliff. The Master said, "Zongsheng is very well; he is resting peacefully among the crags. Simply dispatch a messenger to summon him.
The king immediately followed these instructions and sent a messenger into the mountains. Indeed, they found Zongsheng sitting upright and composed.
Chanji said, "I am deeply grateful for Your Majesty’s intention; I vow to dwell among the rocks and springs. Bodhidharma was Your Majesty’s uncle and the teacher of the Six Companions;
I pray that Your Majesty will revere him so as to bring blessing to the imperial foundation. The Master then asked the King, "Will you come when Zongsheng arrives?

The King replied, "I do not know yet. The Master said, "A second summons shall suffice. After a short while, the messenger returned, and it was indeed just as the Master had said. The Master then took his leave of the King, saying:
"You have cultivated virtue so well; will you not recover quickly? Seven days passed, and he subsequently fell ill. The court physicians examined him, but there was no sign of improvement.

The king urgently dispatched a messenger to inform the Master, saying: "The King’s illness is grave; he is on the verge of death. I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will show compassion and come from afar to rescue him.
When the Master arrived at the King's quarters, he comforted him and inquired after his ailment. At that time, Zongsheng received a second summons from the King.
He then withdrew to a separate cave. Pārāśara, who had long enjoyed the king’s patronage, also came to inquire after his illness.

Pārāśara asked, "This king is now at the point of death; to which realm will he be reborn? Dharmatrāta replied, "If, at the moment of death, a person's head is cold while their feet remain warm, they shall fall into hell.
If both the head and feet are cold, but the chest and heart are particularly warm, they will be born in the human realm. If the eyes are warm..."
"One whose other parts are cold shall be reborn in the heavens. One whose only warmth is between the abdomen and whose other parts are cold shall be reborn among the hungry ghosts.
This is called the method for observing the five aggregates; you should take note of it. Now, as this king’s head is cold and his feet are warm, he will certainly enter hell.
Pāṭaliputra asked, "What should be done to ensure he avoids this retribution of suffering? The Master then commanded the prince to become king.

He pardoned the offenders and bestowed his grace. He venerated the Triple Gem and further performed a rite of repentance, saying: "May all transgressions be extinguished. Thus he spoke three times. The King then felt some relief.
The Master, perceiving that the conditions for China were ripe, went to the King’s presence to console and encourage him, saying:

"You should diligently cultivate pure deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem. My departure is not late; within nine months, I shall return. When the King heard the Master’s words, [he was moved].

Tears flowed from his eyes as he said, "What sin does this land commit? What auspiciousness does that realm possess? Since you, my younger brother, have already responded to your karmic conditions, it is not for me to remain.

I only pray that you will not forget your fatherland; may your elephant-mounted carriage return at an early date. The King immediately prepared a great ship and personally led his ministers and officials to escort him to the seashore.
Once they reached the South Sea, Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu.
He immediately dispatched a messenger with an imperial decree for him to proceed to the capital. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived at Jinling.
The Emperor went out to the suburbs to meet him and subsequently invited him to reside in a separate palace hall. At that time, Master Zhigong was restoring Gaozuo Temple;
he asked the temple master, Lingguan, "Do you know your name, Lingguan? He replied, "An ordinary mind cannot fathom it. Zhigong said, "From the west, a Mahayana Bodhisattva has now entered."
He was inside the city for no long time before he departed.
Listen to my prophecy: Looking up, I see two panels; Bending the waist, one grasps the hook. The nine birds have all been shot;
Only one head remains. If it arrives, it does not stay; To achieve it, one must rely on the sword. It does not stop upon meeting the dragon; It flees as soon as it encounters water.

Upon hearing this, Lingguan silently took it to heart. While Dharma was in the royal palace, the Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, the monasteries I have built, the scriptures I have transcribed, and the monks I have ordained are beyond counting; what merit do these bring? The Master replied, "There is no merit whatsoever."
The Emperor asked, "How can these lack merit? The Master replied, "These are merely the minor fruits of humans and devas; they are causes with outflows (āsrava). Though they exist, they are not real.
The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? He answered, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil."
Such merits as these were not sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
The Master replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization.
The Master, perceiving that his opportunity was not yet ripe, secretly crossed north of the Yangtze River and arrived at Luoyang, where he took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.

He sat facing a wall and never spoke at all; no one could fathom him. At that time, there was a monk named Shen Guang, a man of vast learning and open-minded spirit who had long resided in the Yi and Luo regions.
He had read widely across many books and was skilled in discussing the profound principles of the Way. He often sighed, saying:

"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi—though their rites, arts, customs, and regulations are refined—their writings on the *Zhuangzi* and *Yi jing* do not exhaust the wondrous truth. Recently, he heard of the Great Being Bodhidharma.
Dwelling at Shaolin, the Sage was not far away; he was destined to reach the profound realm. Thus, morning and evening, he attended upon the Master.

The Master would often sit upright facing a wall, and no instructions were heard. Baoguang reflected to himself: "In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow and spread their hair over the mud.
If the ancients were still like this, what kind of person am I? On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, Baoguang...

When he reached the steps, it was raining and snowing heavily. [Nanyue] stood firm and unmoving until the accumulated snow reached his waist. The Master, taking pity on him, asked, "You have stood long in the snow;
what do you seek? Guang wept and said, "I pray that you will show me your compassion. The Master said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way requires diligent effort over vast eons.
One must be able to perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How could it be attained with a small intellect or a frivolous mind?"
Out of arrogance, he wished to aspire to the True Vehicle; his diligent toil was merely in vain.

Upon hearing the Master’s exhortation, he secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Master. The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way..."
"For the sake of the Dharma, one loses all form. Since you have now severed your arm before me, your request may be granted.
The Master thereupon changed his name to Huike. Daowu Guang said, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Master said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
Daowu Guang said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest for me. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall give it to you."
"Peace," Huiguan said. "I have sought the mind and it is utterly unattainable. The Master replied, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
Later, Emperor Xiaoming heard of the Master’s extraordinary deeds and dispatched envoys bearing imperial edicts to invite him three times in succession. The Master did not descend from Shaolin;
the Emperor’s admiration increased all the more, and he personally bestowed upon him two monastic robes (*māṇava-kāṣāya*), a golden bowl, a silver water-purifying flask, and silk brocade.
[The Master] spoke of silk and other matters. From that time on, nine years passed. When he wished to return to India, he addressed his disciples, saying:

"The time has come. You all, why not each speak of your realization? Niti Zongchi came forward, prostrated, and said: "According to what I have seen, the four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist.
At this very moment, there is not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind. The Master said: "You have attained it."
“My skin. Daoyu came forward to prostrate; according to what he saw, it was like Ānanda beholding the land of Akṣobhya Buddha—seen once, never again.
The Master said, “You have obtained my flesh. The Second Patriarch came forward to prostrate three times and stood in his place.
The Master said, “You have obtained my marrow. He then told him: “The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye...”
From Mahākāśyapa, it was transmitted in succession down to me. I now entrust it to you; you must skillfully protect and uphold it, and propagate it for the future so that it shall not be severed.
Along with this, I confer upon you the *kāṣāya* robe as a token of the Dharma. The Master said: "The Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with and realize the mind;
externally, the *kāṣāya* is conferred to establish the fundamental tenet. For in later generations, people will become degenerate and harbor doubts."
They vied with one another. [One] said, "I am a man from the Western Heaven; you were born in this land. On what basis did you obtain the Dharma?

By what means did you realize it? He then conferred upon him this robe and the Dharma. Hereafter, difficulties will arise. Take both this robe and my verse of the Dharma and use them to demonstrate that his transformation was unimpeded.
Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the robe shall cease to be transmitted; the Dharma shall circulate throughout the sands of the world.
Within the realms, those who understand the Way are many, but those who practice the Way are few. Those who discourse on principle are many, but those who penetrate principle are few.

There are more than ten million who secretly accord with and silently realize it; you should propagate this teaching and not disparage those who have not yet awakened. A single thought that turns the mechanism [of the mind] is identical to original attainment. Listen to my verse:
"I originally came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings; when one flower blooms, five petals unfold, and the fruiting of the result is accomplished naturally.
The Master further said: "Since I arrived here, I have been poisoned five times. I have often gone out myself to test it, placing a stone [in the water]."
The rock split. It was because I originally departed from South India to come to this Eastern Land that I beheld the grand atmosphere of the Mahāyāna;

thus I crossed seas and deserts to entrust the Dharma and seek its heirs. Though our meeting had not yet been harmonized and I remained as dull-witted and reticent as a fool, I have now found you to receive the transmission.
"My intention has already been fulfilled. Having said this, he went with his followers to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen and stayed for three days.

There was Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng, who had long admired the Buddha Vehicle. He questioned the Master, saying, "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, you are revered as the Patriarch;
what is the nature of that Way? The Master replied, "It clarifies the mind-source of the Buddha, being equal and without error; practice and understanding are in accord."
"This is called the Patriarch. He asked again, "What is beyond this? The Master said, "One must clarify one's own mind and know its past and present;
one does not loathe existence or non-existence, and takes nothing from the Dharma. One is neither wise nor foolish, neither deluded nor awakened. If one can understand it thus," [he continued].

Therefore, he was called the Patriarch. He further said, "I, your disciple, have taken refuge in the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom has been clouded and dull, and I remain deluded regarding the True Principle.
Having just heard your words, Master, I do not know how to apply them. I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and reveal the essential tenets.
Knowing his earnest supplication, the Master spoke this verse:
Neither do they behold evil and give rise to aversion, nor do they observe good and strive to cultivate it;
neither do they abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, nor do they cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment.
They transcend all measure in attaining the Great Way, and they surpass all limits in penetrating the Buddha-mind and delivering beings.
Not sharing the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages, he was transcendentally named the Patriarch.
When Xuanyi heard the verse, his feelings of sorrow and joy were intertwined, and he said, "I pray that you, Master, will remain long in this world to transform and guide all sentient beings.
The Master said, "I shall depart immediately; I cannot remain for long. To shake off these myriad differences, one encounters much suffering and hardship. Xuanyi said:
"I do not yet know who you are; I pray that you will deign to reveal your name. I, your disciple, shall remove this affliction for my master.
The Master said, "I have transmitted the Buddha’s secrets to benefit deluded disciples. To harm another for my own peace is certainly contrary to principle.
Xuanyan said, "If you, Master, do not speak, how can you manifest the power of your penetrating transformation and contemplative insight? He then uttered a prophecy: [The prophecy follows.]
The river raft parts from the jade waves; the torches of the pipes unlock the golden chains. Two or three travel together, and for ninety [days], there is neither "other" nor "self.
Having heard this, Xuánzhī could not fathom its source; he silently committed it to memory, paid his respects, took his leave, and departed. He passed away during the Shùn era of the Wèi dynasty.
In the Bingchen year, he was buried at Mount Xionger. Three years later, Wei Songyun, while returning from a mission to the Western Regions, encountered the Master on the Pamir Mountains.
He saw the Master holding a single shoe in his hand and departing alone with graceful ease. Songyun asked, "Where are you going? Bodhidharma replied, "To the Western Heaven.
He further told Songyun, "Your sovereign has already grown weary of the world. Upon hearing this, Songyun was utterly bewildered; he took his leave of the Master and headed east.
When he returned with his report, Emperor Ming had already ascended to heaven. Upon the accession of Emperor Xiaozhuang, Daoyun submitted a detailed account of the matter.
The Emperor ordered the tomb to be opened; there was only an empty coffin, with a single pair of leather sandals remaining. The entire nation was struck with wonder and admiration.
By imperial decree, the sandals were taken and enshrined for veneration at Shaolin Temple. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, they were stolen by a follower of the Way.

He resided at Huayan Monastery on Mount Wutai; his current whereabouts are unknown. Initially, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty encountered the Master, yet their karmic affinity was not fully realized.
Master Zhigong once remarked: "The Emperor met him, yet did not meet him. This [Master] is the one who transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal and is the very embodiment of Avalokiteśvara.

Later, when the Emperor heard of the account concerning Song Yun, he personally composed an inscription for the Master’s memorial stele. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Yuan (Complete).
The Master Jue’s stupa is named Kōngguān (Empty Contemplation).

The twenty-ninth patriarch, Grand Master Huik’e, was a native of Wulao. His surname was Ji, and his father’s name was Ji.
Before he had a son, [the father] often thought to himself, "Our family honors goodness; how could we not have a worthy son? After he had prayed for a long time, one night—

He was moved by a miraculous light that illuminated his room, and his mother consequently became pregnant. When he grew up, she named him Guang (Light) in accordance with the auspicious sign of the light illuminating the chamber.
From childhood, his aspirations were extraordinary; he studied the *Shi* and *Shu* extensively and was particularly proficient in Buddhist studies.

Disregarding worldly possessions, he delighted in wandering among mountains and rivers, eventually arriving at Xiangshan Temple on Longmen in Luoyang, where he left home under the guidance of Chan Master Baojing.

Having received full ordination at home, he further frequented lecture halls to extensively investigate the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. At the age of thirty-two, he returned to Mount Xiangshan.
Suddenly, a divine being said to him, "You are about to receive the fruit of enlightenment; why do you linger here? The Great Way is not far away."
"You shall go to the south. Daokuang realized this was divine assistance, and he consequently changed his name to Shenguang (Divine Light).
On the following day, he felt a headache as if it were being pierced by needles. His master wished to treat it, but a voice from the air said, "This is the transformation of the bones;

it is not a common pain. Daokuang then reported the matter in detail to his master. When the master examined his cranial bone, it appeared like five peaks rising in prominence. Thereupon, [the master] said:
"Your signs are auspicious; you shall surely attain realization. As for the divine command that you go south, this is the Great Being Bodhidharma of Shaolin who shall be your teacher.
Huiguo received these instructions and traveled to Mount Shaoshi. There, he attained the Dharma, transmitted the robe, and changed his outward appearance.

This is fully recorded in the *Dharmapada* (Chapter on Dharma). Since the Great Master entrusted his transformation at Shaolin and returned to the West, he had already propagated the true wind of the Dharma and was seeking a successor.
During the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, there came a lay practitioner whose name and lineage were not disclosed;

having arrived, he performed the rites of salutation and asked the Master, "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic ailment of wind; I pray that you will perform a rite of repentance for me. The Master said, "Bring..."
"Sin has arrived. I shall grant you repentance. The layman said, "I have searched for my sin, but it is utterly unfindable. The Master said, "I have finished granting you repentance from your sin.
The layman immediately went forth under the Master, received full ordination, and was given the name Sengcan.
From that time on, his illness ceased. After three years had passed, the Master addressed him, saying: "Bodhidharma came from afar from Central India with the True Dharma..."
The Eye-Treasury has been secretly entrusted to me; I now transmit it to you, along with the robe of faith of the Dharma.
You must guard and preserve it so that it does not come to an end. Listen to my verse:
Originally there must be earth as a condition; based on the earth, flowers grow from seeds. Originally there being no seeds, flowers likewise cannot grow.
After the Great Master had transmitted the Dharma of the robe, he further said: "Having received my teaching, you should dwell in the deep mountains; you should not yet go forth to transform others."
When they encountered national calamity, [Daofu] Can said, "Since you, Master, have foreknowledge, I pray you will grant me instruction.
The Master said, "This is what the prophecy of Prajñātāra predicted: 'Though auspicious within the mind, it is ominous on the outside.

I have calculated the years, and it falls precisely upon you. You must carefully reflect on my previous words and avoid falling into worldly disaster. However, I too have karmic burdens from past lives."

"Now I must repay him. Go well and act virtuously; wait for the right time to transmit [the teachings]. Having said this, he immediately went to the capital of Ye, where he concealed his brilliance and blended in with the common crowd, altering his appearance and demeanor.
When people asked him why he was acting in such a manner, the Master replied, "I am merely disciplining my own mind;
what concern is it of yours? He also discoursed on the Dharma at Guancheng Temple, and those who listened gathered like a forest. At that time, there was a man named Bian...
As for Dharma Master He, he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at the temple gate. When his disciples heard their teacher expounding the Dharma, they gradually began to emerge from the crowd.

Bian He could not contain his indignation and instigated a slander against the district magistrate, Zhai Zhongkan. Zhongkan, deluded by these perverse arguments, subjected the Master to illegal treatment.
The Master accepted this with a serene countenance, submitting to it in accordance with the Way. Those who recognized the truth called this "repaying a debt. At that time, his age was... [year].
He was one hundred and seven years old, which corresponds to the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty. Later, he was buried seventy *li* northeast of Xuan in Fuyang, Cizhou.
Emperor Dezong of the Tang posthumously conferred upon him the title of Grand Master (Dazushi). Shi Falin composed a stele inscription stating:
"Zhi Zhongkan was a cow in his previous life. His driver, resentful of its panting, killed it. This cow is now the County Magistrate."
Furthermore, you were once my driver; your past debt must now be repaid.
As for the thirtieth patriarch, Master Sengcan, it is unknown where he was from. Initially, as a layman (*baiyi*), he visited the Second Patriarch.
Having received ordination and the transmission of the Dharma, he lived in seclusion at Mount Wangong in Shuzhou. It happened that Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou dynasty destroyed...

The Buddha-dharma was extinguished. During the Kaihuang era, there was a novice monk named Daoxin who was fourteen years old. He came to pay his respects to the Master and said, "I pray that the Upādhyāya will, out of compassion, grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. The Master asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one. The Master said, "Since no one has bound you, why do you seek liberation? Daoxin was greatly enlightened by this. He remained with the Master for twenty years and eventually attained the Way. Later, he resided at Shuangfeng Mountain in Huangmei County, where he propagated the teachings for over forty years. His disciples numbered in the thousands. When he passed away, he was seventy-nine years old. He was posthumously titled Great Master Dajian. His stupa was named "Vimala. His dharma heirs were Huineng, Hongren, and others. They all received the transmission of the robe and bowl and became patriarchs. Thus, the lineage of the Sixth Patriarch was established. It continued through Huairang, Mazu, Baizhang, Huangbo, Linji, Xuefeng, Yangqi, Yunmen, Fayan, Dongshan, Caoshan, Deshan, Linji, Yantou, Xuansha, Fenyang, and finally Dahui. From the time of the Sixth Patriarch until the present day, the succession of the Dharma has been unbroken. This is called the Southern School of Chan. As for the Northern School, it originated with Shenxiu. He was a disciple of the Fifth Patriarch. He resided at Nanyue Mountain in Hubei Province. His followers were numerous. However, because he taught that the mind must be cultivated and polished to attain Buddhahood, he was criticized as being inferior to the Southern School. Eventually, his school declined and was eventually lost. Thus, the two schools of Chan flourished and declined during the Tang dynasty. It was only in the Song dynasty that the Southern School alone remained. This is the general history of the transmission of the Dharma. Now, let us return to the story of the Sixth Patriarch. After Daoxin had left, the Master remained in seclusion. One day, a monk named Huiming came from the north and asked, "What is the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West is to see the nature and become a Buddha. The monk said, "If one sees the nature and becomes a Buddha, what about me? The Master said, "You have already become a Buddha. The monk said, "How can I know that I have already become a Buddha? The Master said, "If you do not know that you have already become a Buddha, how can you say you have seen the nature? The monk was greatly enlightened by this. He remained with the Master for ten years and eventually attained the Way. He later resided at Mount Nan in Hubei Province and propagated the teachings for over thirty years. His disciples numbered in the thousands. When he passed away, he was sixty-five years old.

He was posthumously titled Great Master Dayi. His stupa was named "Donglin. His dharma heirs were Huineng and others. Thus, the lineage of the Sixth Patriarch was firmly established. This is the story of the transmission of the Dharma from the Fifth Patriarch to the Sixth. It is a testament to the fact that the essence of the Buddha-dharma lies in seeing one's own nature and attaining liberation. If one seeks outside of oneself, one will never find it. Therefore, the Master said, "Who has bound you? This single phrase cuts through all delusions and reveals the true nature of reality. It is the very heart of the Chan school. Those who hear it and understand it will immediately realize their own Buddha-nature. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and patriarchs. May all beings encounter this Dharma and attain liberation. Thus ends the record of the transmission of the Dharma. May it be widely circulated for the benefit of all sentient beings. May they all quickly realize the Way and attain Nirvana. Thus, the Buddha-dharma shall never perish. Amity, peace, and happiness to all. Aum Maṇi Padme Hūṃ. Sarva Mangalam. Śubhamastu. Sarvadā.
