"Regarding 'no one is bound,' the Master said: 'Since no one is bound, this is itself liberation. Why need you further seek liberation?

Under these words, [the student] attained great enlightenment. He served the Master diligently for nine years, whereupon he shaved his head and received full ordination. The Master knew that his conditions were ripe."
He then transmitted the Dharma-garment and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now transmit it to you, together with the Dharma-robe of Bodhidharma, to serve as a token of faith in the Dharma."
Circulate this for posterity so that it shall not be severed. Listen to my verse:
"Though the seed of the flower depends on the earth, From the earth the flower is produced. If there were no one to sow the seed, The flowering earth would be entirely without growth."
The Master further said, "The Great Master Ke transmitted the Dharma to me, after which he went to the capital of Ye and only passed away some thirty years later.
Now that I have found you, why do you linger here? He then departed for Mount Luofu, where he remained for three years before returning to his former dwelling place.
One day, the officials and commoners rushed forward; after he had extensively established offerings of alms (*dāna*), he manifested his passing beneath a great tree.
This was precisely the fifteenth day of the tenth month during the Daye era of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty. The assembly enshrined his entire body and erected a stupa for him.

Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jianzhi, and the stupa was named Jueji. Fang Guan, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel and Third Rank of the Chancellery, composed the inscription.
Epitaph. Li Chang, the former Governor of Henan during the early Tang dynasty, had long admired the patriarchal style and delved deeply into the profound principles of the Way.
During the Tianbao era, he encountered Shenhui of Heze and asked: "Where was the Great Master of the Third Patriarch interred?
Some say he entered Mount Luofu and did not return; others say he passed away at Shanyu. I do not know which account is correct. Shenhui replied: "Master Can returned from Mount Luofu..."

At Shangu (Valley Mountain), he attained parinirvāṇa more than a month after his realization. Today, the tomb of the Third Patriarch still exists at Shuzhou, yet Huichang had not previously believed this to be true.
Upon being demoted to the position of Vice Governor of Shuzhou, he inquired of the monks of Shangu Monastery, saying, "I have heard that there is a tomb of the Third Patriarch behind the monastery;
is this so? At that time, the senior monk Huiguan replied, "It is indeed there. Huichang was filled with joy and [discussed it] with the local officials.
They went together to pay their respects. Furthermore, they opened the tomb and took out the true likeness [of the Master], which was then cremated. They obtained countless *śarīra* relics;
one portion was used to erect a stupa, another portion was entrusted to Heze Shenhui to verify his previous words, and the remainder was kept with the body.
Later, a vegetarian feast was held at his private residence in Luoyang to celebrate this event. At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master Gaṇa and others from the Western Regions were present.
During an assembly, Chang asked the Tripitaka Master, "How many patriarchs are there in India?
Kanadeva replied, "From Kāśyapa down to Prajñātāra, there are twenty-seven patriarchs. If one includes Venerable Siṃha, there are forty-nine patriarchs in total.
If one counts from the Seven Buddhas to the present, excluding lateral branches, there are thirty-seven generations. Chang asked again:
An elder of virtue in the assembly said, "I have seen charts of the patriarchs that cite fifty or more ancestors;
yet as for the divergent branches and lineages, the ancestral clans are not fixed, and some possess nothing but empty names. By what means can one verify [the truth]?

At that time, there was Zen Master Zhiben, a disciple of the Sixth Patriarch, who replied: "This refers to the beginning of the Later Wei dynasty, when the Buddha-dharma had declined. There was a śramaṇa..."
During the period of turmoil, Fotudiao recorded the names of the various patriarchs on a single roll of plain silk;
as he had forgotten their proper sequence, he concealed it within the collar of his robe and hid himself in a mountain cave. Thirty-five years passed until Emperor Wen Cheng ascended the throne.
The Dharma-gate flourished once more. Tanyao, whose reputation and conduct were both highly esteemed, was subsequently appointed as the *Sengtong* (Patriarch of the Monks).

He then assembled various *śramaṇas* to deliberate once again upon the compilation [of the scriptures], titling it the *Fufa zang zhuan* (Biographies of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury). There were some minor discrepancies within it, which were truly caused by the state of fear prevailing at that time.

Furthermore, after thirteen years had passed, an imperial edict was issued for Huang Yuanzhen, a *Guoziboshi* (Court Doctor of the National Academy), to [collaborate] with [a master from] Northern India...
The Tripitaka Master Buddhasanta, Ji Fuyan, and others have distinguished the essential tenets and successively recorded the lineage of masters;
thus, there shall be no error.
As for the thirty-first patriarch, Grand Master Daoxin, his surname was Sima. His family had resided in Henei for generations. Later, he followed...
In Guangji County of Qizhou, the Master was born with extraordinary qualities. From childhood, he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he traveled to Jizhou, where he encountered a band of rebels besieging the city for seventy days without resolution. The masses were filled with anxiety and distress;
the Master took pity on them and instructed them to recite the *Mahāyāna*. At that time, the rebel horde perceived what seemed to be divine soldiers within the battlements, and they...
He said, "There must be a great extraordinary person within this city; it is not possible to attack it. He then gradually withdrew his forces.
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, the Master returned to Qichun and resided at Mount Poutou.

One day, while traveling to Huangmei County, he encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and extraordinary, unlike those of ordinary children. The Master asked him, "What is your surname? The boy replied, "My surname is..."
[The boy] replied, "It exists; it is the constant nature. The Master asked, "What is its nature? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Master asked, "Do you have no nature?

He replied, "Because its nature is empty. The Master silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately ordered a monk to go to his home to persuade his parents to let him leave the household life. His parents showed no sign of reluctance and said, "We wish—"
He graciously accepted. The Master then shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts. Thereafter, he addressed him, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa, and through successive transmission it has come down to me.
I now entrust it to you, along with the Dharma-robe of Bodhidharma, as a token of the Dharma. You must protect and uphold it well, and propagate it for the future so that it shall never be severed."
Listen to my verse:
The nature of the lotus seed exists; Depending on the ground, the lotus grows. When the great conditions unite with its nature, That which should grow does not grow.
Having finished the ritual for entrusting the robe, he addressed the assembly, saying: "During the Wude era, while traveling to Mount Lu, I ascended its summit and gazed toward Mount Poutou.
There was a purple vapor like a canopy, beneath which a white vapor divided into six horizontal paths. Do you understand this, or not? The assembly remained silent.
Huineng said, "Could it not be that after the Master’s passing, a separate branch of the Buddha-dharma will emerge? The Master said: [It is so.]
Later, during the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, drawn to the flavor of the Master’s Way and desiring to behold his countenance, issued an edict summoning him to the capital.
The Master submitted a memorial declining the summons, doing so three times in succession, ultimately declining on the grounds of illness. The Emperor again dispatched an envoy with the command:

"If he truly does not rise, then bring his head. When the envoy arrived at the mountain to convey the imperial decree, the Master extended his neck toward the blade; his expression remained solemn and composed. The envoy was struck with wonder.
He submitted a report on this matter. The Emperor, filled with even greater admiration and longing, bestowed upon him precious silks so that he might fulfill his aspirations.
During the Yonghui era of the Gaozong reign, he suddenly issued an admonition, saying: "All dharmas are entirely liberation.

You all must each protect and mind yourselves, spreading this transformation to future generations. Having spoken these words, he sat upright and passed away. He was seventy-two years of age; a stupa was erected at his original site.

At Mount Shuangfeng, on the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stupa opened spontaneously for no apparent reason; the physical features [of the remains] were as if alive.
Thereafter, [the disciples] did not dare to close it again. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred the title Chan Master Dayi and erected a stupa for him, inscribed "Ciyun."
The thirty-second patriarch, Master Hongren, was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. His surname was Zhou. From birth, he was exceptionally intelligent and precocious.
While playing as a child, he encountered a man of wisdom who sighed and said, "This boy lacks seven of the marks of a Great Man;
he does not equal the Tathāgata. Later, he resided at Mount Pòtóu. During the Xiánhé era, there was a layman surnamed Lú named Huìnéng.
He came from Xinzhou to pay his respects. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan. The Master said, "What do you seek?
Nan said, "I only seek to become a Buddha. The Master said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature."
When Huineng said, "If one seeks to attain Buddhahood," the Master replied, "People have north and south, but how could the Buddha-nature be like that?
Recognizing that Huineng was a vessel for the Dharma, the Master rebuked him, saying, "Go and haul wood for the trough!

Huineng prostrated and withdrew, then entered the rice-hulling shed, where he performed labor among the pestles and mortars day and night without ceasing. Knowing that the time for the transmission had arrived, the Master then addressed the assembly, saying:

"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it cannot be grasped merely by memorizing my words. You must take this as your own responsibility. Each of you may compose a verse according to your own inclination.
If the meaning of your words accords with mine, I shall bestow both robe and Dharma upon you. At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly.

Among them, the Elder Shenxiu wrote a verse on a corridor wall, saying: The body is like a Bodhi tree; The mind is like a clear mirror stand. At all times we strive to polish them, And never let dust collect.
The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a bright mirror stand. At all times diligently wipe it clean, And never let dust collect upon it.
As the Master was walking about, he saw this verse and knew it had been composed by Shenxiu. He sighed and said, "If one practices according to this, one will also [attain the Way]."
Neng attained the fruit of a human or celestial being. While he was at the rice-hulling shed, he suddenly heard someone reciting a verse. He asked his fellow students, "What are these lines?
They replied, "The Master is seeking a Dharma heir and has ordered each of you to compose a verse expressing your mind;
this is the one composed by Upādhyāya Xiu. Neng then immediately composed four lines of his own. When night fell, he secretly had someone copy them beside Xiu’s verse.
It is said:
Enlightenment originally has no tree; the bright mirror is likewise not a stand. Originally there is not a single thing—where, then, could there be dust?

The Master saw this verse and asked, "Who wrote this? They have not yet seen their nature. He then removed his sandals, rubbed away the characters, and because of this, the assembly paid it no further heed.
When night fell, the Master went secretly to his own millhouse and asked, "Is the rice white yet?"
Neng said, "I am Bai; I have not yet had my rice sifted. The Master struck the mortar three times with his staff. Neng immediately entered the room after three drumbeats.

The Master told him, "The Buddha appeared in the world for one great matter. It was entrusted to Kāśyapa and passed down through successive generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived in this land.
There, he met the Great Master Huineng, who inherited it, and it has continued down to me."
I now entrust to you this Dharma-treasure and the robe I have transmitted.
You must protect them well yourself and propagate them for the future, so that they shall never be severed. Having received my instruction, listen to my verse:
When sentient beings come to plant seeds, fruits grow back according to the ground. Since insentient things have neither seed nor nature, they likewise have no birth.
[This concludes] the method for the Layman Neng to receive the robe. He asked: "The Dharma has now been received; to whom shall the robe be entrusted? The Master said: "In the past, Da..."
When Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him; therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest his attainment of the Dharma.

Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with you and will no longer be transmitted. You should withdraw to a distant place for now and wait for the time to go forth and transform others.
As it is said: "The one who receives the robe has a life as precarious as a hanging thread. He further said: "One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally."
[The Master] said, "Accomplished. He further said, "When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower opens, the world arises. Huineng asked, "Where should I dwell?

The Master replied, "Stop wherever you encounter a place of rest; hide yourself whenever you meet with an opportunity. After Huineng had prostrated and taken his leave, he took the robe and departed in secret.
That night he traveled south, unknown to the assembly. The next day, the assembly was filled with doubt and wonder. The Master said, "My Way is now being practiced. Why ask any more?"

He asked again, "Who shall receive the robe according to the Dharma? The Master replied, "He who is capable shall receive it. Thereupon, the assembly deliberated that the name of Layman Lu was capable;
however, having already been lost to their search, they secretly learned that he had obtained it. At that time, the monk Huiming pursued him to the summit of Mount Dayu.
Seeing that Huiming was approaching, Lu hid himself amidst the thickets and simply placed the robe on the ground. Huiming tried to lift it, but it would not move. Huiming—
Neng immediately called out, "I have come seeking the Dharma; I do not seek his robe. Neng was able to respond, saying, "Do not think of evil; do not think of good.
At this very moment, return to me the original face of Master Ming. At this, Ming attained great enlightenment.
Neng said, "You must return quickly. When you encounter Meng, stop there; when you meet Yuan, you shall dwell there. Ming then prostrated himself in gratitude.
He returned. Upon reaching the foot of the mountain pass, he encountered a group of people pursuing him. Ming deceived them, saying, "I have come from the pass, but I have seen nothing at all.
The group hesitated and withdrew. Ming later changed his name to Daoming (Dao-ming), presumably to avoid using the first character of his master’s name.
He settled on Mount Meng in Yuanzhou. His master suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "My work here is finished; it is time for me to depart. Immediately—
He entered his room, sat peacefully, and passed away. He was seventy-four years old.

On the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Ren-shen, the second year of the Shangyuan era of the Tang Emperor Gaozong, a stupa was erected on East Mountain at Huangmei. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Daman and named his stupa Fayu (Dharma Rain).
The thirty-third patriarch, Master Huineng, was of the secular surname Lu. His ancestors were originally from Fanyang.
His father, Xingtao, was transferred as an official to Xinzhou in Nanhai during the Wude era and subsequently registered his residence there.

He lost his father at the age of three; his mother remained steadfast in her resolve to raise him. Upon reaching adulthood, the family was especially impoverished, and the Master provided for them by gathering firewood. One day...

Carrying firewood to the market, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he was moved to awakening and asked, "What dharma is this?
From whom did you receive it? The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*; I received it at Huangmei.
The Master immediately informed his mother of his intention to seek out this Dharma, and set off directly for Shaoyang.
In the province, he met the man of lofty conduct Liu Zhilüe and formed a friendship with him.
There was a nun named Wujinzang, who was Zhilüe’s paternal aunt; she regularly recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When the Master briefly listened to her, he immediately explained its meaning for her.

The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Master said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I ask about the meaning. The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters..."
"How could he possibly understand the meaning? The Master said, "The wondrous principle of all Buddhas is not concerned with written words.

The nun was struck with wonder and told her fellow villagers, "Neng is a man of the Way; you should invite him to come so that we may pay our respects. Nearby there is the old site of the ancient Bao Lin Temple."
He had the site restored and invited a master to reside there; the fourfold assembly gathered like a mist, and in no time a precious monastery (*ratnagṛha*) was established.

One day, the master thought to himself, "I seek the Great Dharma; how could I stop halfway? He then proceeded to a stone grotto on the western mountains of Changle County, where he encountered Chan Master Zhiyuan.
He subsequently requested instruction from him. Zhiyuan said, "Observing your spiritual faculties, you are exceptionally sharp and outstanding; you are surely not [an ordinary person]."
"Ordinary person. I have heard that Bodhidharma of the Western Regions transmitted the Mind-Seal to Huangmei.
You should go there to seek his instruction and resolve your doubts. The Master took his leave and traveled to Dongshan in Huangmei;

this was during the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty. Upon seeing him, Master Ren recognized him silently. Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma to him, instructing him to remain hidden between Huaiji and Sihui.

On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Yifeng era (the Bingzi year), he arrived at Nanhai. There, he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Faxing Temple.
The Master [Huineng] observed two dharma masters disputing over the wind and the banner; one of them claimed that it was the wind that moved.
One person said, "The banner moves. Huineng called out, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. It is your own mind that moves.
Upon these words, the two people attained great enlightenment. They asked, "Could you be the Layman Lu? If so, speak quickly! The Master replied, "I am Huineng.
The two Dharma Masters said, "We were sent from the Western Heaven to this land specifically for your sake."

Having undergone tonsure and received full ordination, [he found that] there was still the Precept Platform of Vinaya Master Zhiguang at Fasheng Temple, which had been established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
The record states: "In the future, an incarnate Bodhisattva will receive the precepts upon this platform.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang Dynasty, Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally planted two Bodhi trees beside the platform. The record says:
"One hundred and twenty years hence, there will be a Great Being who receives full ordination beneath this very tree, as if by a prior covenant.
The two Dharma Masters said, "I shall be your preceptor for the tonsure; you shall be my teacher from whom I receive the Dharma.

This was because they were moved by the words concerning the wind and the banner. On the eighth day of the second month the following year, after he had received full ordination, [the Master] said, "I shall not..."
"I wish to reside here. Later, when the Master arrived at Baolin Monastery, Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaoyang, invited him to reside at Dafan Monastery.
In the first year of the Shenlong era of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict was issued stating: "I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to provide for them within the palace.

In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle. Both masters have in turn recommended that there is a Chan Master named Huineng in the south who is secretly [practicing]."

Regarding the method for receiving the robe of the Great Master, you may inquire about it directly with him. Now, I have dispatched the inner attendant Xue Jian to deliver an imperial decree inviting you.

I pray that the Master will look upon me with compassion and proceed swiftly to the capital. The Master submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, expressing his wish to spend his final years among the forested foothills. Xue Jian said:
The Chan masters of the capital all say: "If one wishes to realize the Way, one must necessarily practice seated meditation and cultivate samādhi.
It has never been the case that anyone attained liberation without relying on dhyāna and samādhi. I do not yet know what kind of Dharma you, Master, preach. The Master said:
The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? As the Sūtra says: "If one says that the Tathāgata sits or lies down, this is to walk in a deviant path.
Why is this? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; ultimately there is nothing to be realized—how much less so sitting?
Jian said, "When I return, Your Majesty will surely question me. I pray that you, Master, out of compassion, will instruct me on the essentials of the mind.

The Master said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of succession and replacement. Light and darkness are both inexhaustible, yet they are also exhaustible;
these names are established in mutual dependence. Therefore, a sutra says: 'Dharmas have no comparison, for they do not depend upon one another. Jian said, "Light is used as a metaphor for wisdom."

Darkness is the afflictions (*kleśa*). If those who cultivate the Way do not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter these afflictions, by what means can they escape from the beginningless cycle of birth and death?
The Master said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; they are non-dual and without distinction.

To use wisdom to illuminate afflictions is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of the sheep, the deer, and so forth. Those of great wisdom and superior faculties [do not view them thus]."
"It is not so. Jian asked, "What is the vision of a Mahāyāna practitioner? The Master said, "Luminosity and ignorance—these are the views of ordinary people.
The wise person thoroughly realizes that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is precisely the true nature. As for this true nature..."

It does not diminish when encountering ordinary beings, nor does it increase among sages and saints. It remains undisturbed while dwelling amidst afflictions, yet it is not quiescent while abiding in meditative concentration.
It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes; it is not in between, nor within, nor without.
"Neither arising nor ceasing; its nature and characteristics are as they are now, eternally abiding and never shifting.

Jian said, "When you speak of 'neither arising nor ceasing,' how does this differ from what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) discuss? The Master replied, "As for the 'neither arising nor ceasing' discussed by the non-Buddhists..."
One seeks to extinguish arising by means of cessation, using arising to manifest cessation; yet even now, it is not extinguished, and arising itself is non-arising.

When I speak of "neither arising nor ceasing," it is because there was originally no arising, and now there is likewise no cessation. This is why I differ from the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). As for those non-Buddhists:

He said, "I merely wish to know the essence of the mind through what is expressed by words, phrases, and meanings. Do not deliberate at all upon good or evil, and you will naturally enter [the truth].
Its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. He said, "For the first time, I realize that my original nature is not remote;
nirvana is quiescent, and there is no remaining dharma. Everything is manifest before me. Having spoken, he prostrated, took his leave, and returned to the capital.

A memorial was submitted reporting the Master’s words; an imperial edict was issued in response to express gratitude to the Master, and he was further granted a *mona* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, a precious alms bowl, and silken fabrics.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, an imperial decree changed the name of Gu Baolin to Zhongxing Temple.

On the eighteenth day of the eleventh month of the third year, another imperial decree ordered that the Master’s scripture-copying quarters at Shaoyang Prefecture be extensively renovated and granted the name Faquan Temple.
The Master established Guoen Temple at his former residence in Xinzhou. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Good friends, settle your minds and listen to my teaching of the Dharma. You all, each of you, are Buddhas within your own minds; do not harbor further doubt.
There is not a single thing outside that can be established. Therefore, when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease."

Extinction. If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one must attain the samādhi of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇasamādhi*) and the samādhi of a single practice (*ekakāryasamādhi*).
If, in all places, one does not dwell upon characteristics; if, amidst those characteristics, one gives rise to neither aversion nor attachment, and likewise has no grasping or rejecting;
if one does not think of matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure; remaining at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the samādhi of a single characteristic.
If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a single, pure mind, the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is immovable and truly becomes a pure land.
This is called the Samādhi of One Practice. If a person possesses this samādhi, it is like a seed in the earth:
it contains and nurtures [the potential] until its fruit ripens. A single characteristic and a single practice are likewise so. My preaching of the Dharma now is just like that season.
The rain falls, universally moistening the great earth. Your Buddha-nature is like various seeds; encountering this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout and grow.
Those who receive my intent will obtain the benefit of Bodhi; those who rely on my practice will certainly realize the wondrous fruit.

In the first year of the Tianxian era, he addressed the assembly, saying: "I have received the robe and the Dharma from the Great Master Ren. Now I preach the Dharma for you, but I do not transmit it."
"O monks, your faculty of faith has matured; its moisture and stability are such that you have no doubts and are capable of undertaking this great task. Listen to my verse:
The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the essence of the flowers is suddenly awakened, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously realized."
He spoke again: "The Dharma is non-dual, and the mind is likewise so. The Way is pure and free from all marks.
You must be careful not to contemplate purity, nor to empty your minds. This mind is fundamentally pure; there is nothing to be grasped or rejected. Each of you must exert yourselves."
"Go as you please according to conditions. The Master preached the Dharma to transform the world for forty years.

On the sixth day of the seventh month of that year, he instructed his disciples to go to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou to construct a memorial pagoda. On the first day of the seventh month of the second year of the Xiantian era, [he passed away].
He said to the assembly, "I wish to return to Xinzhou; prepare my boat and oars quickly. The assembly asked, "Master, once you have departed from here, when will you return?
The Master replied, "When the leaves fall, they return to the root; when one comes, there is no mouth. They asked again, "Who shall receive and transmit your Dharma-treasury?
The Master replied, "Those who possess the Way attain it; those who are without mind penetrate it. They asked again, "Will there be any difficulties later on? He said, "There will be."
"Five or six years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a person who comes to take my head. Listen to my prediction:
'On his head he nourishes his parents; from his mouth he must eat his meals. When he encounters the calamity of the flood, he shall become an official by means of willow trees.
Furthermore, seventy years after I have departed, two Bodhisattvas shall come from the east—one remaining at home and one leaving it."
"His family and his own lineage flourished simultaneously; he established our school, restored monasteries, and caused the succession of the Dharma to prosper.
Having finished speaking, he went to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou, where he sat in the lotus posture and manifested parinirvāṇa on the third day of the eighth month of that year.

At that time, the prefectures of Shaoyang and Xinzhou each constructed a stupa and temple, and neither the clergy nor the laity could decide which site it should be dedicated to. The two Regional Inspectors together burned incense and prayed, saying: [The text continues with their prayer.]
The place where the incense smoke led was precisely where the Master intended to return. At that time, the incense rising from the burner surged upward, piercing straight through to Caoxi.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he entered his stupa; his age was seventy-six. Wei Ju, the former Prefect of Shaoyang, composed the inscription for his stele.
The assembly recalled the prophecy concerning his head and immediately ran to secure the Master’s neck with iron plates and lacquered cloth.
On the third night of the eighth month in the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era, they suddenly heard a metallic clanging sound from within the stupa.

The monks rose in alarm and saw a man wrapped in a white turban emerge from the stupa; he leaped over the wall and fled. They then searched through the ritual vessels and implements, but found nothing at all.

Shortly thereafter, he noticed a wound on the Master’s neck. He reported the matter of the robbery in full to the district magistrate, Yang Kan, and the regional governor, Liu Wutiǎn, who both ordered a rigorous manhunt.
On the fifth day, the culprit was apprehended at Shíjiǎo Village and sent to Shāozhōu for interrogation.
It was revealed that his surname was Zhāng and his given name was Hángmǎn; he was a native of Liáng County in Rǔzhōu. He had received the new [scriptures] at Kāiyuán Monastery in Hóngzhōu.
Luosengjin was ordered to take the head of the Sixth Patriarch Master and return to the Eastern Sea to offer it in worship.
Upon hearing this report, Prefect Liu did not immediately impose the punishment; instead, he went in person to Caoxi and asked the Master’s senior disciple, Lingzhao, "How should this be adjudicated?

Lingzhao replied, "If one were to judge according to the principles of state law, it would indeed be appropriate to proceed as planned. However, according to the compassion of the Buddha-dharma, there is no distinction between enemy and kin."

How much more so, then, when he sought only offerings—his offense is indeed forgivable. Prefect Liu sighed in admiration and realization, for he had only then come to know the vastness of the Buddha-dharma;
he subsequently pardoned him. In the first year of the Shangyuan era, Emperor Suzong dispatched an envoy to request the Master’s robe and bowl to be brought back to the palace for veneration.
Then, on the fifth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Yongtai era, Emperor Daizong dreamed that the Great Master Huineng requested his robe and bowl.

On the seventh day, an imperial edict was issued to the Regional Inspector Yang Jian, stating: "In a dream, I was moved by the Venerable Master Huineng’s request that I transmit the Dharma-kāṣāya and return it to Caoxi.
I have now dispatched the General of the Pacification of the State, Liu Chongjing, to receive and deliver it. I regard it as a national treasure.
You shall enshrine it according to the Dharma within your temple and strictly command the monastic community to guard it with vigilance. Do not..."
Whether they were dropped or stolen by others, all were recovered without traveling far. Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dajian;
his stupa was named Yuanhe Lingzhao. The *Nanyue Ji* states: At the beginning of the Jin dynasty, the realm was fragmented as various factions seized military power.

Cao Shuliang was appointed General Who Guards the South (Zhennan Jiangjun) and placed in charge of the affairs of the Commander-in-Chief for Pacifying the South (Pingnan Zongguan). After the Jin successfully reclaimed the territory...
The King conferred the title of Duke upon Shuliang. On the slopes between the two peaks of Mount Shan, Shuliang possessed a private villa;

he donated this land to establish Shuangfeng Caoxi. From this, Caoxi became renowned by name. As for Baolin Monastery, during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, there was a monk who began its construction.
He inscribed on a stone: "One hundred and seventy years hence, a Bodhisattva of Great Power shall preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings."
The person propagated the teachings throughout the four quarters, and disciples gathered like a mist. It was fitting that it be titled "Baolin" (Jewel Forest).

The provincial governor submitted a formal petition, and the Emperor personally inscribed the plaque. In the second year of the Yifeng era, the Great Master took up residence there, fulfilling all his prior prophecies. Later, the nameplate was changed.
During the Shenlong era, it was called Zhongxing and Fajian; three years later, Guangguo; in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era, Jianxing;
during the reign of Suzong, Guoning Temple; and during the reign of Xuanzong, Nanhua. To this day, no swallows or sparrows have nested there.
There was a single robe transmitted by the Patriarch Bodhidharma, made of *kṣauma* cloth from the Western Regions. It was woven from the core of cotton fibers;
those who claim it is silk cloth are mistaken. The garment was dark blue-black in color, with later generations using greenish-blue silk as a lining.

The Emperor Zhongzong bestowed upon him a *monastic mantle*, a precious alms bowl, materials for crafting a true likeness [of the Master], ritual implements, and so forth. His funerary stupa is located at Shengta.

During the Kaiyuan era, Song Jing, the Governor of Guangzhou, paid homage at the stupa. He saw the Elder Lingtao and asked him, "What is meant by 'the patience of the non-arising of dharmas' (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?
Lingtao replied, "To know that arising is already suchness, and that all things are likewise, is called 'non-arising.
To have mastery over arising is called 'patience of dharmas. To know that cessation is not cessation is called 'non-arising. [The text continues: "Excellent..."
Not forgetting the Dharma is called the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). To give rise to the bodhicitta is called non-arising (*anutpāda*).
That the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) do not arise is called the patience of the Dharma. Not being angry when confronted by objects is called non-arising.

Not harassing others is called the patience of the Dharma. Having no deluded thoughts within is called non-arising. Having no defilement without is called the patience of the Dharma. Prajñā has no abiding. This...

It is called "Non-arising. To contemplate and illuminate this with wisdom is termed "Dharma-patience" (dharmakṣānti). Upon hearing this, [Dao]jing received it upon the crown of his head and subsequently performed the rites of a Buddha’s disciple.

At the beginning of the Kaibao era of the Imperial Dynasty, when the Imperial Preceptor had pacified the Liu clan of the South Sea, the remnants of their troops caused disturbances at the master’s stupa and temple.
It was reduced to ashes and embers, yet the true body (śarīra) suffered no damage whatsoever. Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued for its reconstruction;
though the work was not yet complete, Emperor Taizong ascended the throne and took a keen interest in the Chan school, significantly enhancing its magnificence and grandeur.

Now the present Emperor has ascended the throne, and with the Empress Dowager Ming-su assisting in governance and the Empress Ci-feng presiding over judicial decisions, the empire enjoys peace and stability. Yet the Emperor alone has set his heart upon the Dharma of Zen;

this is surely because Heaven has opened his inner mind. He once dispatched an envoy to invite [the Master’s] robes and alms bowl into the palace, where they remained for a long time to be reverently displayed.
I offer this with further precious adornments, hoping that his extraordinary traces may endure forever.

From the year of Gui-chou, the second year of the Xuan-tian era of the Tang dynasty, when the Great Master entered *nirvāṇa*, until the year of Bing-zi, the third year of the Jing-you era, exactly three hundred and twenty-five years have passed.

Chan Master Nanyue Daoyi, whose name was Huairang, was a native of Jinzhou. His secular surname was Du.

He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty. A white vapor was perceived in response to the celestial omens in the region of Ankang. The Great...

The Grand Astrologer, Shi Zhan, observed this and reported it to Emperor Gaozong. The Emperor asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied, "This is a ritual vessel of the state;
it is untainted by worldly glory. The Emperor then issued an edict for Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, to go in person to offer his condolences.
The family had three sons, and the Master was the youngest. At the age of three, he was already remarkably extraordinary;
by nature, he was full of kindness and yielding. His father therefore named him Huairang. When he reached the age of ten, he took pleasure only in Buddhist scriptures.

At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanjing passed by the house and, seeing him, marveled at his qualities. He told the parents, "If this boy leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle."

He extensively saved sentient beings. In the third year of the Chuigong era, at the age of fifteen, he took leave of his parents and went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu, where he followed Master Hóngjǐng to receive the tonsure and enter the monastic order.
In the second year of the Tōngtiān era, he received full ordination. Thereafter, he studied the Vinaya Piṭaka. One day...
He sighed to himself, saying, "As for those who have left the household life, they seek the unconditioned Dharma; among all in heaven and on earth, there is none superior to this.
At that time, his fellow student Tanran, knowing that his teacher’s aspirations were lofty and far-reaching, urged him to go together to visit Master An of Mount Song.
Huian attempted to inspire him, but [Fazheng] did not attain realization. He then went directly to Caoxi to pay respects to the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "I have come from the place of Chan Master Huian at Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? The Master was speechless.
After eight years had passed, he suddenly attained a realization. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so?
The Master replied, "To describe it as a thing is not correct. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still anything to be cultivated or realized?"
The Master said, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; I simply dare not defile them. The Patriarch said, "This very non-defilement is the thought of all Buddhas.
I am thus; you are also thus. The twenty-seventh patriarch of the Western Heaven, Prajñātāra, prophesied of you, saying:"
Though China is vast, there is no other path; One must rely on the feet of one’s descendants to travel it.

In the second year of the Tianjian era, he first traveled to Mount Nanyue and resided at Prajñā Monastery. He instructed his disciples, saying:

"All phenomena arise from the mind; the mind is fundamentally unarisen, and phenomena likewise have no abiding place. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, all actions will be without obstruction.

A monk asked, "When a mirror is used to cast an image, once the image is formed, where does the light go?
The Master said, "When you, Venerable Sir, had not yet left the household life, where did your physical form go? The monk said, "Once it is formed, why does it no longer reflect?
The Master said, "Although it does not reflect, it cannot deceive him by even a single point. [This occurred] when Mazu was at Mount Nanyue.
Behind the Chuanfa Yuan (Dharma Transmission Court), he lived alone in a single hermitage, devoting himself solely to the practice of seated meditation.

He paid no heed to anyone who came to visit him, nor did he acknowledge the Master when the Master went to see him. The Master observed that his spiritual bearing was extraordinary and recalled the prediction of the Sixth Patriarch;

The Teacher said, "If grinding a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha?
The Patriarch then left his seat and asked, "How then is it so? The Teacher replied, "It is like a cow pulling a cart; if the cart does not move, one strikes the cow."
"It is so. To strike the cart is precisely it. He further said, "You study seated meditation; do you study sitting as a Buddha? If you study seated meditation, the Master neither sits nor lies down.
If you study sitting as a Buddha, the Buddha has no fixed form. Within the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as a Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha.

"Is there formation and destruction? The Master said, "If one perceives the Way through formation and destruction, gathering and dispersing, that is not so.
Listen to my verse:
The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When meeting with moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless."

As for what was destroyed and what was established, once the Master had received his enlightenment, he served him for ten autumns; day by day, [the teachings] became more profound and mysterious. When the Master entered the treasure, there were six disciples.
Each was certified with the words: "You six have collectively realized my body; each has accorded with one part.
One person attained my eyebrows—excellent in dignified demeanor (Chang Hao). One person attained my eyes—excellent in looking and glancing (Zhidá).
One person attained my ears—excellent in listening to principles (Tǎnrán). One person attained my nose—excellent in knowing the breath (Shénzhào). One person attained my..."
[The Master] was skilled in eloquent discourse (both stern and gentle). One person grasped my mind; he is Shanwuwei (now known as Daoyi).

Mazu was propagating his teachings at Kaiyuan Temple in Jiangxi. The Master asked the assembly, "Has Daoyi preached the Dharma for the community? The assembly replied, "He has already preached the Dharma for the community.
The Master said, "I have not yet seen him bring back any news. He then dispatched a monk to wait [for him].
When he ascended the hall, [the Master] simply asked, "How is it? He instructed the monk, "Remember the answer and bring it back. The monk followed his instructions;
upon returning, he recounted the exchange to the Master. The Patriarch said, "Since the time of the chaotic beginning, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce."
The Master approved this. On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the third year of the Tiānbǎo era, the Master entered nirvana at Nányuè.

By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dàhuì Zuìshènglún, and a stupa was erected for him. Guī Děng, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, composed the inscription for the stupa.
The Zen Master Daji Mazu of Jiangxi was named Daoyi. He was a native of Shifang County in Hanzhou and belonged to the Ma clan by secular surname.
He left home to become a monk at Luohan Monastery in his hometown. The Master’s appearance was extraordinary:

he had the gaze of a tiger and the gait of an ox, his tongue could extend past his nose, and there were two wheel-shaped marks on the soles of his feet. In his youth, he received the tonsure under Venerable Tang of Zizhou and subsequently received full ordination.

Regarding Master Yuanyou of Yuzhou: during the Kaiyuan era, he practiced dhyāna at the Chuanfa Temple on Mount Heng. There, he secretly received the Great Compassionate Mind-Seal (Mahākaruṇā-citta-mudrā).
A verse concerning his propagation of the Dharma was prophesied by the Indian Prajñātāra, which says:
Having received the words of Maitreya, he left his hometown and traveled abroad day after day. During the Eastern Liang dynasty, he moved closer to the main road;
later, under the Qi dynasty, he first relocated from Fojingling in Jianyang to Linchuan, and subsequently to Gonggongshan in Nankang during the Dali era.
He registered his name at Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling. At that time, Governor Lu Sigong, hearing of his reputation, felt deep admiration for him and personally bestowed upon him secret instructions.
Consequently, scholars from all quarters gathered like clouds at his seat. Thereafter, his Dharma heirs spread extensively throughout the land;
he was then known as Mazu of Jiangxi.
The Master said to the assembly, "All of you, believe that each of your own minds is Buddha; this mind is itself the Buddha-mind.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came personally from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle, the single-mindedness of the One Mind."
I cause you all to attain awakening. Furthermore, I cite the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the minds of sentient beings.
Fearing that you might be deluded and unwilling to have confidence in this Dharma of the One Mind—which each and every one of you possesses—the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"The Buddha’s word takes the mind as its essence; having no gate is the Dharma-gate. Now, those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek, for there is nothing outside the mind.
Apart from the Buddha, there is no separate mind outside of the Buddha. It does not grasp at good, nor does it reject evil.

It relies upon neither of the two extremes of purity or defilement. It realizes that the nature of offenses is empty; in every thought-moment, they are ungraspable because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, the three realms are mind-only. The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by this single Dharma. Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind. The mind is not a mind in itself; it arises through...
Because of form, there is existence; you merely speak according to the occasion. Whether in terms of phenomena or principle, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
It is the same with the fruit of the Bodhi path: that which arises within the mind is termed "form. Because one knows that form is empty, arising is non-arising.
If you understand this meaning, you may then dress and eat according to the occasion, nourishing the holy embryo and passing through life spontaneously.
At that time, what further matters are there? You should receive my instruction; listen to my verse:

"The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion; Enlightenment (bodhi) is likewise simply tranquility. When phenomena and principle are both without obstruction, That which arises is, in its very arising, non-arising."

Question: What is the cultivation of the Way? The Master said: "The Way does not belong to cultivation. To say it is attained through cultivation implies that once cultivated, it can still be destroyed;
this is the same as the Śrāvakas. If one says there is no cultivation, this is the same as an ordinary person. Question: By what kind of insight can one attain the Way?
The Master said: "The self-nature is fundamentally complete. It is simply a matter of not being obstructed by good or evil phenomena."

To call oneself a "cultivator of the Way" while taking up good and rejecting evil, or contemplating emptiness and entering meditative absorption, belongs to the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
If one further pursues it outwardly, one becomes increasingly estranged and distant. Simply exhaust the mental scope of the triple world;

a single thought of delusion is the very root of birth and death within the triple world. If one simply lacks even a single thought, the root of birth and death is eliminated, and one attains the state of the Dharma King.
The supreme jewels. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings—flattery, crookedness, deceit, falsehood, pride, and arrogance—have combined into a single entity.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "This body is merely composed of various dharmas; when it arises, only dharmas arise; when it ceases, only dharmas cease.
When these dharmas arise, they do not say 'I arise'; when they cease, they do not say 'I cease. The preceding thought...

The subsequent thought and the middle thought—moment after moment they do not wait for one another; moment after moment they are quiescent and extinguished. This is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

It embraces all phenomena, just as hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all return to the great ocean and are collectively called "ocean water. Abiding in this single flavor, it immediately embraces all flavors;
abiding in the great ocean, it immediately mingles with all currents. It is like a person bathing in the waters of the great ocean, who immediately uses [the water].

All waters. Thus, while Śrāvakas awaken from delusion, ordinary people are deluded regarding awakening. Śrāvakas do not know that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally devoid of stages, causes and effects, or gradations.
They cultivate causes and realize fruits through the mental constructions of their own limited minds.

Though they may dwell in empty samādhi for eighty thousand or twenty thousand kalpas, even if they have already awakened, they subsequently fall back into delusion. To the various Bodhisattvas, such states appear as painful as the hells; they sink [into them].

It is empty, stagnant, and quiescent. Furthermore, one perceives the Buddha-nature. If it is a sentient being of superior capacity who suddenly encounters the instruction of a good spiritual friend, they may comprehend it at the moment of hearing;

they do not pass through successive stages or levels, but rather awaken suddenly to their original nature. Thus, a sutra says: "Ordinary people possess a mind of reversal and regression, whereas the śrāvakas do not.
Awakening is spoken of in contrast to delusion; since there is fundamentally no delusion, awakening is likewise [non-existent].
It does not stand apart. All sentient beings, from immeasurable kalpas past, have never emerged from the samādhi of dharmatā; they have long remained within the samādhi of dharmatā.
Whether putting on clothes or eating food, speaking and responding to others, employing the six sense organs, or performing any activity whatsoever, [they remain therein].

All is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Failing to understand how to return to the source, you follow names and pursue appearances; thus, deluded sentiments arise falsely, and you create all manner of karma.
If you can, for even a single thought-moment, reflect back upon yourself, your entire being will be the sacred mind. You all, each person, must realize your own mind; do not merely memorize my words.
Even if you were able to explain as many principles as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, your mind would not increase thereby. If you cannot express it at all—
The mind does not diminish. To say it can be attained is your own mind; to say it cannot be attained is also your own mind.
Even now, though you emit light and manifest the eighteen transformations, it is not as good as returning my dead ashes to me. Once soaked, the dead ashes have no power.
