The Master then ordered a monk to deliver a letter to Venerable Qian of Mount Jing. In the letter, he drew a circle.
As soon as Qian opened it and saw it, he asked for a brush and placed a dot in the center. Later, a monk reported this to National Teacher Zhong, who said:

Even Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma. A monk drew four lines before the Master—the top line long and the three bottom lines short—and said, "One must not say that one line is long and three lines are short; it transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
I beg the Master to answer me. The Master drew a single line and said, "One must not speak of long or short; my answer to you is complete. Later...
A monk brought this up to National Teacher Zhong. The National Teacher said, "Why did you not ask me?
The Master asked the monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan.
The Master said, "Is the water in Dong Lake full yet? He replied, "Not yet. The Master said, "After all this time of rain, it is still not full. (Daowu said, "It is full. Yunyan said, "—")
It is profoundly still. Dongshan said, "In what kalpa has it ever been lacking?
Baizhang asked, "What is the essential purport of the Buddha? The Master said, "This is precisely where you let go of body and life.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying, "The Way does not require cultivation; one need only avoid defilement. What constitutes defilement? It is simply the presence of birth and death."
The mind’s fabrications and tendencies are all defiled. If you wish to directly encounter the Way, the ordinary mind is the Way.
What is meant by the "ordinary mind"? It is without fabrication, without right or wrong, without acceptance or rejection, without annihilationism or eternalism, and without ordinary people or sages.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "It is not the practice of ordinary beings; it is not the practice of sages or worthies. This is the practice of Bodhisattvas.

Just as in the present moment—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—responding to conditions and engaging with sentient beings is entirely the Way. The present is itself the Dharma-realm, even unto the wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It does not depart from the Dharma-realm. If it were otherwise, how could one speak of the "Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground," or the "Inexhaustible Lamp"?
All phenomena are the phenomena of the mind; all names are the names of the mind. The myriad dharmas all arise from the mind;
the mind is the root of the myriad dharmas. Thus, a sutra says: "To recognize the mind and reach its source is why one is called a Śramaṇa."
Regarding the gates: the equality of names and the equality of meanings mean that all phenomena are equal, pure and without admixture.

If one attains mastery according to the occasion within the gateways of the teaching, then whatever is established as the *dharmadhātu* is entirely the *dharmadhātu*; if one establishes *tathatā*, it is entirely *tathatā*.
If one establishes principle, all phenomena are entirely principle; if one establishes phenomena, all phenomena are entirely transformations.

Taking one thousand instances as examples, phenomena and principle are without difference; they are all wondrous functions and there is no separate principle apart from them. All arise from the revolving of the mind.
For example, while there are many reflections of the moon, the true moon has no multiplicity; while there are many sources of water, the nature of water has no multiplicity;
while the myriad phenomena of the universe have multiplicity, space has no multiplicity; while the explanations of principles have multiplicity, unimpeded wisdom has no multiplicity.
All these various establishments arise from the one mind. Thus, they may also be established [as such].
Sweeping away [all delusions] is also permissible; all of these are wondrous functions. These wondrous functions are entirely one's own self.

They do not exist apart from the Truth (Tathatā), for wherever they are established, that very place is the Truth. All of them are the substance of one's own self. If it were otherwise, who else could they be?
All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; all dharmas are liberation; liberation is Tathatā; and all dharmas...
It does not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*). Walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are all inconceivable functions that do not depend upon time or season. As the Sūtra says:

"In every place there is a Buddha. A Buddha is one who is capable and wise, skillful in responding to the capacities of beings, able to shatter the net of doubts of all sentient beings, and to bring about liberation from the bonds of existence and non-existence.
When the dualistic sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, both person and phenomena are [transcended].
Emptiness. It turns the peerless wheel, transcending all calculation and measure. Its activities are unimpeded, as both phenomenon and principle are simultaneously penetrated.
Like clouds arising in the sky—suddenly appearing and then vanishing without leaving a trace—and like drawing patterns upon water, which neither arise nor perish, it is the Great Quiescence.
When enmeshed in afflictions, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when free from entanglements, it is named the Pure *dharmakāya*. Its essence neither increases nor decreases; it is able to...
The great can become small; it can be square or round. It manifests forms in accordance with objects, like the moon reflected in water. Its application flows on without establishing roots or sprouts.

Wood exhausts itself in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); it does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The conditioned is the function of the unconditioned; the unconditioned is the support for the conditioned.
Because it does not abide in its support, it is said: "Like space, it has nothing upon which to rely. This is the meaning of the arising and ceasing of the mind.

The meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind. As for the *tathatā* of the mind: it is like a bright mirror reflecting images. The mirror is a metaphor for the mind; the images are a metaphor for phenomena (*dharma*).
If the mind grasps at phenomena, it immediately engages with external conditions, which is the meaning of arising and ceasing.
Not grasping at phenomena is the meaning of *tathatā*. Śrāvakas hear of Buddha-nature with their ears; Bodhisattvas see Buddha-nature with their eyes. They realize that these two are non-dual.
It is called the nature of equality; its essence is without differentiation, yet its functions differ. In delusion it is consciousness; in awakening it is wisdom.
To accord with principle is awakening; to accord with phenomena is delusion. Delusion is to be deluded regarding one’s own fundamental mind; awakening is to awaken to one’s own original nature.

Once awakened, one is awakened forever; one shall never again be deluded. Just as when the sun rises, it does not coexist with darkness, so too when the sun of wisdom rises, it does not coexist with the darkness of afflictions (*kleśa*).
When the realm of the mind is fully understood, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is immediately eliminated.

Once false conceptualization is eliminated, this is precisely the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharmatā*), the originally inherent nature that does not depend on cultivation for its realization. Meditation does not belong to sitting; sitting itself constitutes attachment.

If you perceive this principle, you will truly accord with the Way; you will pass your days in accordance with conditions, your observance of the precepts will grow more refined, and you will accumulate pure karma.
If you can simply act in this manner, what need is there to worry about not attaining penetration? I have stood for a long time; take care.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, the Master ascended Mount Shimen in Jianchang.

While walking in meditation amidst the forest, he saw that the caves and ravines were level and the peaks and ridges were strikingly prominent. He said to his attendant, "This is a place of auspiciousness;
it shall be the place where I bring my life to its end. Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness. The head of the monastery asked, "How is the Master’s health these days? The Master replied:
On the first day of the second month, Fozhao Deguang—known as Niu-tou Fa-jung—bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.

He was eighty years of age, with sixty years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaśa*). During the Yuanhe era, Emperor Dezong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Daji, and his stupa was named "Dazhong Zhuangyan" (Magnificent Adornment of the Great Zhong).
The Chan Master Dazhi of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou was named Huaihai. He was a native of Changle in Fuzhou and his secular surname was Wang.

Having left the mundane world at the age of seven, he became thoroughly proficient in the three studies of the Buddhist canon. During the time that Mazu Daishi was propagating the Dharma in Jiangxi, [Huaihai] devoted himself wholeheartedly to him as a disciple.
Together with Xitang Zhizang and Nanquan Puyuan, he was counted among the "Three Great Beings" who entered the Master’s inner sanctum. One.
One evening, while the three great adepts were attending Mazu as they gazed at the moon, Mazu asked, "What is it like at this very moment?
Xitang said, "It is precisely the right time for making offerings. Shishuang said, "It is precisely the right time for practicing the Way. Nanquan shook his sleeves and departed.
Mazu remarked, "The Sutras have entered the Canon; Chan has returned to the sea. Only Puyuan alone transcends the mundane world."
The Master was Mazu’s attendant. One day, while walking along the road in attendance upon Mazu, he heard the cry of a wild duck.
Mazu asked, "What sound is that? The Master replied, "The cry of a wild duck. After a long silence, Mazu said, "Where has that sound just now gone?
The Master replied, "It flew away. Mazu turned his head and twisted the Master's nose.
The Master made a sound of pain. The Patriarch said, "You say it flew away. At these words, the Master attained realization.
The next day, as soon as the Patriarch ascended the hall and took his seat, the Master came forward and rolled up the bamboo mat; the Patriarch then descended from the seat.
The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters. The Patriarch said, "Just now, I intended to cite a causal precedent for you;
why did you roll up your mat? The Master replied, "Because my nose was aching. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you been?
The Master said, "Yesterday I happened to go out; I did not manage to attend the assembly. The Patriarch gave a shout. The Master—
He then went out. One day Mazu ascended the hall; when the assembly had gathered, he struck the handle of his whisk three times with his hand and immediately descended from the seat.

The Master (Baizhang) silently attained realization. Three days later, he reported this to Mazu. Mazu ascended the hall and told the assembly, "What need have I for further concern? I now have [him]."
Daimo was present. He was the teacher of all of you.
One day Mazu asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from behind the mountain.
Mazu said, "Did you encounter anyone there? The Master replied, "I did not encounter anyone. Mazu asked, "Why did you not encounter anyone?"
The Master said, "If you encounter him, report this immediately to the Abbot. The Patriarch asked, "From where have you received this news?
The Master said, "It is my fault. The Patriarch said, "But rather, it is my own fault.
The Master went to visit Mazu again. Mazu held up his whisk. The Master said, "Is it used right here? Or is it apart from this?"
The Patriarch hung his whisk back in its original place and remained silent for a long while. Then he said, "In the future, when you open your mouth to speak, with what will you show people?
The Master then took up the whisk and held it upright. The Patriarch said, "Is this its use, or is it separate from its use?
The Master again hung the whisk back in its original place. The Patriarch then gave a shout, which left the Master deaf for three days.
He was deaf. Only then did he attain great enlightenment.
A monk entered the Dharma Hall weeping. The Master said, "What are you doing? The monk replied, "Both my parents have passed away."
"Please ask the Master to select an auspicious day. The Master said, "Tomorrow at the first watch, bury it.
A monk asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said, "Sitting alone on Mount Daxiong. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
Xitang asked the Master, "How will you instruct others in the future? The Master rolled his hands out at both sides. Xitang...
[The student] asked, "How else could it be? The Master pointed his head with his hand three times. He ascended the hall and said:
"The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals the true permanence, unbound by words and letters.

The nature of mind is unstained; it is fundamentally perfected from the beginning. Simply leave behind delusive conditions, and you are the Buddha of Suchness. A questioner asked: "According to the sutras, how does one understand..."
"Meaning is the enemy of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. To deviate from a single word of the sutras is to speak like a demon. The Master said:
"To cling rigidly to movement and stillness is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods of time. To seek something else apart from this is likewise to speak like a demon.

Mazu sent someone to deliver a letter along with three jars of sauce to the Master. The Master ordered them to be carried out in front of the Dharma Hall. He then ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered—
The Master took up his staff and pointed to a jar of sauce, saying, "If you can speak, I shall not break it; if you cannot speak, I shall break it.
The assembly remained silent. The Master then broke the jar and returned to his quarters.

He ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master drove them away with his staff. He then called out to the assembly; as they turned their heads, the Master asked, "What is this?"
When Huangbo arrived at the Master’s place, one day he took his leave, saying, “I wish to go and pay my respects to Mazu. The Master said, “Mazu has already passed away.
Huangbo asked, “I wonder what words or phrases he left behind? The Master then related the occasion of Huangbo’s second visit to Mazu, when Mazu held up a whisk.
Upon hearing this account related, Huangbo involuntarily stuck out his tongue. The Master said, “In the future, you must not—”
"Are you going to succeed Mazu? Huangbo replied, "Not so. Today, because of what you have raised, I have come to see the great function of Mazu’s spiritual power.
However, I do not yet know Mazu. If I were to succeed Mazu, my own descendants would later be lost.

The Master said, "When the student's vision is equal to the teacher's, it diminishes the teacher's virtue by half; only when the student's vision surpasses the teacher's is he fit to receive the transmission. "Son," [Huangbo said].
He possessed a vision that far surpassed his teacher. Later, Mount Huangbo asked Yangshan about the circumstances of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu, in which Mazu held up a whisk.
"What was the underlying meaning of these two venerable masters? Yangshan replied, "This was the manifestation of the function of the great capacity.
Mount Huangbo asked, "Mazu produced eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras*; how many among them attained the great capacity?"
"How many people have attained great function? Yangshan replied, "Baizhang attained the great capacity; Huangbo attained the great function;
all others are merely masters who shout the Way. Guishan said, "So it is, so it is."
The Master, having gone out for the communal labor of clearing a field, turned back and asked, "Master Yun, clearing a field is no easy task.
Baizhang said, "The assembly of monks is performing their duties. The Master said, "I am troubled by the exertion of your Way-function. Baizhang said, "How would I dare decline such toil?
The Master asked, "How much field have you cleared? Baizhang made the gesture of hoeing a field. The Master then gave a shout. Baizhang covered his ears and went out.
The Master asked Huangbo, “Where have you come from? Huangbo said, “I have come from gathering mushrooms at the foot of the mountain.
The Master said, “There is a tiger cub at the foot of the mountain; did you see it? Huangbo then made the sound of a tiger.
The Master drew a hatchet from his waist and made a gesture as if to strike him. Huangbo grabbed him and gave him a slap.
The Master gave a late evening discourse from the high seat, saying: "O assembly! There is a tiger cub at the foot of the mountain;
you all must look out carefully when entering or leaving. This old monk was personally bitten by one this morning.
Later, when Guishan asked Yangshan, "What about Huangbo’s story of the tiger? Yangshan said, "How about you, Master? Guishan said, "Baizhang at that time..."
He then brought his axe together and struck him dead. Why did it come to this? Yangshan said, "Not so.
Miaoshan asked, "What about you, my son? Yangshan said, "Not only do I ride the tiger's head, I also know how to grasp the tiger's tail.
Miaoshan said, "Ji (Yangshan), you truly possess words of perilous precipice."

Whenever the Master ascended the hall, there was always an old man who would listen to the Dharma; once the session ended, he would invariably disperse with the assembly. One day, however, he remained behind and did not leave.
The Master asked, "Who is this person standing here? The old man replied, "In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain.
A student then asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall under the influence of causes?"
The old man said, "Does the fruit not exist? The Master replied, "It does not fall away from cause and effect.

The old man said, "Because you did not say it does not fall away from cause and effect, I fell into the body of a wild fox. Now I request the Master to provide a turning word on my behalf. The Master said, "Just ask me.

The old man then asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within cause and effect? The Master said, "He is not deluded regarding cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.

The guest took his leave. The Master said, "I have already escaped the body of a wild fox. I reside behind the mountain; I beg that you allow me to be cremated according to the rites for a deceased monk.

The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly: "After the midday meal, everyone shall be invited to escort the deceased monk. The assembly was all astonished.
After the meal, they went to the back of the mountain, where they indeed found a dead wild fox in a rock crevice. They piled wood and cremated it.
When the Master went up to the hall in the evening, he recounted the preceding karmic cause and condition.
Huangbo then asked, "An ancient person gave one wrong response and fell into the body of a wild fox. But what of those who today respond correctly at every turn?
The Master said, "Come closer, and I will tell you. Huangbo stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm. The Master said, "I took you for a man with a beard!"
[The Master] said, "Red! Furthermore, there is the red-bearded barbarian. At that time, Guishan was serving as the head cook (diànzuò) in the assembly.
Head Monk Sima raised the question of the wild fox and asked the head cook, "What do you say? The head cook shook the door panels three times with his hand.
Sima said, "How coarse! The head cook replied, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of such a principle."
Later, Guishan raised the story of Huangbo’s question regarding the wild fox for Yangshan. Yangshan said, "Huangbo constantly employs this device.
Guishan asked, "Do you say he was born with it, or did he receive it from others?
Yangshan replied, "It is both received through the lineage of a teacher and the penetration of one's own school. Guishan said, "So it is, so it is—Huangbo."
Question: "What Dharma did the ancients of old use to instruct people? The Master remained silent for a long while. Huangbo asked:
"How will your descendants of later generations transmit it? The Master said: "I thought you were a man of some substance. He then returned to his quarters.
One night, Guishan stood in attendance in the abbot’s quarters for a long time. The Master ordered him to poke into the brazier to see if there was any fire.
Guishan poked it and said, "There is no fire. The Master rose himself, poked the embers until he produced a spark, and holding it up, showed it to him, saying, "You say there is no fire;
what is this? Through this, Guishan attained realization. Later, one day, while they were engaged in manual labor...
The Master asked Muzhou Shanzhao, "Is there fire here? Muzhou said, "There is. The Master asked, "Where is it?
Muzhou took a piece of firewood, blew on it, and handed it to the Master. The Master said, "It is like insects eating wood.
Later, while they were working together by request to hoe the earth, a monk heard the sound of the drum, raised his hoe, and laughed loudly, "Ha ha!"
Returning, the Master said, "How brilliant! You have entered through the gate of Avalokiteśvara. Later, he called the monk and asked, "What principle did you perceive just now?
The monk replied, "I was hungry; hearing the sound of the drum, I went back to eat.
The Master laughed heartily.
Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Who are you? He replied: "I am so-and-so. The Master said:
"Do you recognize so-and-so? He replied: "Clearly. The Master then held up his whisk and asked:
"Do you see the whisk? He replied: "I see it. The Master did not look at him.
The Master ordered a monk to go to Zhangjing’s place to see him ascend the hall and preach the Dharma.
You should then unfold your sitting mat, perform a prostration, stand up, take one shoe, brush the dust off it with your sleeve, and turn it upside down to cover [the other shoe].
That monk went to Zhangjing’s place exactly according to his master’s instructions. Zhangjing said, "I, an old monk, am at fault."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Close off your throats, lips, and mouths, and quickly bring forth what you have!
Miaoshan said, "I cannot say it; I beg the Master to speak for me. The Master said, "I do not refuse to speak to you, but afterwards my descendants will perish.
Wufeng said, "The Master must also close off [your own]. The Master said, "In a place where no one is, I shall look up with bared teeth at you."
Yunyan said, “I have attained the Way; I ask the Master to provide an example. The Master said, “Close up your throat, lips, and mouth, and quickly bring forth what you have!
Yunyan said, “The Master has it now! The Master said, “You have lost your own children and grandchildren!
Later, he ascended the hall and said, “I want someone to go deliver a message to West Hall Master. Who can go? Wu... [five characters]... went.
Feng said, "I am able to go. The Master asked, "How will you deliver the message? Feng said, "I will speak it once I have seen the West Hall Abbot.
The Master asked, "What will you say? Feng said, "I will come back and report it to you, Master.
When the Master was a child, he accompanied his mother to a temple to pay homage to the Buddha. Pointing to a sacred image, he asked his mother, "What is this object?"
The mother said, "He is a Buddha. The child said, "His appearance is like that of a human being; I shall also become one like him in the future.

Whenever the Master performed manual labor or took up strenuous tasks, he was invariably the first among the assembly. The assembly could not bear his toil and secretly gathered his tools to urge him to rest.
The Master said, "I possess no virtue; why should I compete with those who labor? Since they searched everywhere for his tools and could not find them, [the Master continued his work].
He likewise did not eat. Thus, the saying that "one day without work is one day without food" spread throughout the world.
The Master entered nirvana on the seventeenth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era at the age of ninety-five.
In the first year of the Changqing era, an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dazhi, and his stupa was named Dasheng Baolun.
As for Chan Master Duanjie of Mount Juefeng at Huangbo in Yinzhou, he was a native of Minzhong. In his youth, he left the household life at Huangbo Mountain in his home province;
a fleshy protuberance between his eyebrows rose like a pearl, his speech was fluent and elegant, and his disposition was profound and serene. Later...

While traveling to Mount Tiantai, he encountered a monk who appeared to be an old acquaintance, so they traveled together. Upon reaching a mountain stream where the water was surging in a torrent, the Master leaned on his staff and stopped.
The monk urged the Master to cross with him, but the Master said, "Please, brother, go ahead. The monk then floated his straw rain-hat upon the water and crossed over.
The Master remarked, "I, however, am traveling with this fellow; I regret not having struck him dead with a single blow."
A monk took his leave to return to Guizong. Guizong asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to the various quarters to study the 'five flavors' of Chan.
Guizong said, "In the various quarters there are five flavors of Chan; here, with me, there is only the one flavor of Chan. The monk asked, "What is this one flavor of Chan?
Guizong struck him. The monk said, "I understand! I understand! Guizong [said], "Stop talking nonsense."
"Way! Way! The monk prepared to open his mouth, and Zongyi struck him again. Later, that monk went to the Master’s place.
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Guizong. The Master asked, "What words or phrases did Guizong say? The monk then recounted the previous conversation.
Thereupon, the Master ascended the hall and, citing this causal occasion, said: "Master Mazu produced eighty-four men of excellence..."
"Knowledge. [The Master] asked, "Each and every one of you is dripping wet; there is only the returning to the source that is slightly better.
While the Master was in the assembly at Yanguan Monastery, Emperor Dazhong was a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*). As the Master was prostrating before the Buddha in the Buddha Hall, the novice said:
"Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek by clinging to the Sangha. Elder, when you prostrate, what do you seek?"
The Master said, "Seek not by clinging to the Buddha; seek not by clinging to the Dharma; seek not by clinging to the Sangha. Always pay homage in this manner.
The śrāmaṇera asked, "What is the purpose of paying homage? The Master then struck him with his palm. The śrāmaṇera said, "That was too coarse.
The Master said, "In what kind of place do you speak of 'coarse' and 'fine' here? He then struck him again.
The śrāmaṇera then ran away.
When the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at Nanquan. One day at the time of the midday meal, he held his bowl and sat upon Nanquan’s seat.
Nanquan came down, saw him, and asked, "In what year did you begin practicing the Way? The Master replied, "Vibhūṣaṇarāja (King of Majestic Sound)."
Previously, Nanquan said, "This is still just a descendant of Old Wang. The Master then stepped down from his seat.
One day, as the Master was coming out [of his quarters], Nanquan said, "With such a large physical frame, you wear such a tiny little hat.
The Master said, "The three thousand great thousandfold world-systems are all contained within it. Nanquan said, "Old Wang! The Master replied, "Yes, Teacher."

Dai Li went forth. One day, while the Master was sitting in the tea hall, Nanquan came down and asked, "Regarding the principle that 'cultivating study with equal wisdom leads to clearly seeing the Buddha-nature,' how is this?
The Master said, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, do not rely upon or depend on a single thing.
Nanquan said, "Is this not your own realization, Elder? The Master said, "I dare not say so."
Nanquan said, "Let us set aside the payment for the rice gruel; who will repay the cost of the straw sandals? The Master then ceased speaking.
Later, Guishan raised this anecdote and asked Yangshan, "Is it not that Huangbo could not outmaneuver Nanquan?
Yangshan said, "Not so. One must know that Huangbo possessed the mechanism of trapping a tiger. Guishan said, "..."

The Master’s realization had grown to such an extent that one day, during a communal work assignment (*pǔqǐng*), Nanquan asked him, “Where are you going? The Master replied, “I am going to select vegetables.
Nanquan asked, “What do you use to select them? The Master held up his knife. Nanquan said, “You only know how to act as a guest; you do not know how to act as a host.”
The Master struck the blade three times.
One day, five newly arrived monks were being examined simultaneously; four prostrated themselves, while one did not prostrate, but stood there drawing a circle with his hand.
The Master said, "Do you know this fine hunting dog? [The monk] replied, "Yes."
[The monk] said, "I have come following the scent of a wild goat. The Master said, "A wild goat has no scent. Where have you been searching?
He said, "I have come following the tracks of a wild goat. The Master said, "A wild goat leaves no tracks. Where have you been searching? He said, [I have come following the tracks of a wild goat.]
"In that case, you are a dead antelope. The Master then ceased speaking.
On the following day, as he ascended the seat, [a monk] withdrew. The Master called out, "The monk who was searching for the antelope yesterday, come forth! The monk came forward.
The Master said, "Yesterday, the old monk did not yet have words for you. What do you say? The monk was speechless.

The Master said, "I thought you were a monk of true substance; it turns out you are merely a śramaṇa of scholastic learning. The Duke said, "The form and shadow are here; where is the eminent monk? The temple master had no reply.
The Duke asked, "Is there perhaps a Chan monk here? The temple master said, "There is one.
The Duke then invited the Master to meet him and repeated his previous question. The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! When Pei Xiu responded, the Master sighed.
The Master said, "Where are you? At these words, the Official attained realization. He then requested the Master to ascend the hall again. Entering the hall, the Master said:
"All of you here are nothing but people who eat dregs of wine. To travel on pilgrimage like this is to make others laugh.
If you were all as casual as this, how could there be a 'today' for you? Do you even know that within the Great Tang Empire..."
"Is there no Zen master? At that time, a monk asked, "If so, why do you say there is no Zen master when you lead a community and guide disciples in all directions?
The Master said, "I do not say there is no Zen; I simply say there is no master.
Later, Guishan cited this anecdote and asked Yangshan, "What is your intention here? Yangshan replied, "The king of geese chooses its own milk."
"Originally not a species of duck. Guishan said, "This is indeed difficult to distinguish.
One day, Minister Pei placed a statue of the Buddha before the Master. Prostrating himself with his knees on the ground, he said, "I request the Master to bestow a name upon it.
The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! Pei responded, "Yes. The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you. The Minister then [departed].
[The Master] paid his respects.
One day, the Official presented a poem. As soon as the Master received it, he sat down and asked, "Do you understand?
The Official said, "I do not. The Master said, "To be this way ignorant is still somewhat better than committing it to paper and ink."
How could there be anyone of my lineage? A poem says:

"Since the Great Being transmitted the mind-seal, With a round pearl upon his brow and a body seven feet tall, He hung his staff for ten years while dwelling by the waters of Shu; Floating his bowl today, he now crosses the banks of the Zhang."
"A thousand dragon-elephants follow your lofty steps; Ten thousand miles away, fragrant flowers form a cause for excellence.
I wish to serve you as your disciple; I do not know to whom you will entrust the Dharma.
The Master replied:
The mind is like the great ocean, without limit; From its mouth it breathes forth red lotuses to nourish this sickly body.
Though it possesses a pair of hands that do nothing, They have never been used to attend to those who are merely ordinary.
Now, one who studies the Way must first eliminate all miscellaneous studies and external conditions; they must resolutely seek nothing and resolutely cling to nothing.
Hearing the profound Dharma is like a clear breeze reaching the ears; it passes by in an instant and is not pursued further—this is what is meant by "profound.
Entering the Tathāgata-dhyāna, one leaves behind the conceptualizations of ordinary dhyāna. From the ancestral masters above, only the single mind has been transmitted, with no other dharma.
Pointing to the mind as Buddha, one immediately transcends both the stages of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment, decisively never flowing down to the [lower] levels.
Second thought: it seems you have just begun to enter the gate of our school. Regarding such a Dharma as this, when someone arrives here at random, how do you intend to study it?

Therefore it is said: "When you give rise to a conceptualizing mind, you are bound by the demon of conceptualization; when you do not give rise to a conceptualizing mind, you are bound by the demon of non-conceptualization;
and when you are neither giving rise to a conceptualizing mind nor not giving rise to one, you are again bound by the demon of neither-conceptualization-nor-non-conceptualization. Demon.
It does not come from without; it arises from your own mind. Only those Bodhisattvas who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) cannot trace its footprints.
If, at all times, the mind maintains a view of permanence, one is a follower of the eternalist heretics (*śāśvatavāda*).

If one contemplates all phenomena as empty and forms a view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*), one is a follower of the nihilist heretics (*ucchedavāda*). Therefore, the triple world is mind-only, and all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

This is still spoken in reference to those with the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If one speaks of the *dharmakāya* as the ultimate fruit, this is said in reference to those of the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ pūjyāḥ*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśa āryāḥ*).
Therefore, on the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), two delusions are abandoned: first, the subtle delusion regarding the knowable (*sūkṣmajñeyāvaraṇa-moha*);

second, the extremely subtle delusion regarding the knowable (*atisūkṣmajñeyāvaraṇa-moha*). Since the Buddha is already thus, what further need is there to speak of the two types of awakening—the equal awakening (*samyaksambodhi*) and the wondrous awakening (*vibuddha*)?
Know this: all people merely desire to move toward light and do not desire to move toward darkness; they merely seek awakening and do not love affliction.

Thus, they claim that the Buddha is awakening while sentient beings are delusion. If one holds such a view, one will continue to transmigrate through the six realms for hundreds and thousands of kalpas without interruption.
Why is this? Because it constitutes slandering the fundamental self-nature of all Buddhas. Therefore...
I have told you clearly: the Buddha is not enlightened, and sentient beings are not ignorant, for the Dharma is neither light nor dark.
The Buddha is not strong, and sentient beings are not weak, for the Dharma is neither strong nor weak.

The Buddha is not wise, and sentient beings are not foolish, for the Dharma is neither foolish nor wise. You emerge from your hiding place and claim to understand Chan; as soon as you open your mouth, you fall ill.
It arises. It does not speak of the root; it speaks only of the branches. It does not speak of delusion; it speaks only of awakening. It has never spoken of the essence; it speaks only of function.
There is, in total, no place for you to engage in discourse. All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, yet now they are not non-existent either.
Conditioned arising is non-existent; conditioned cessation is not non-existent. The root is also non-existent, because the root is not a root. Mind is also not mind, because mind is not mind.
Because of the mind, appearances are also not appearances. Because appearances are not appearances, it is said: "Without phenomena, there is no fundamental mind;

only then does one understand the mind and mental dharmas. Phenomena are themselves non-phenomena; non-phenomena are themselves phenomena. Because there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon, this is the mind and its mental dharmas.
Suddenly, when a single thought flickers up, one realizes it is like an illusion or a transformation; thus, one immediately flows into the past Buddhas. Past...
The Buddha of the past does not exist; the Buddha of the future is not non-existent. Furthermore, he is not called the "Buddha of the future.
In the present, moment by moment, there is no abiding; thus, he is not called the "Buddha of the present.
When the Buddha arises, one should not deliberate whether he is enlightened or deluded, or whether he is good or evil. One must never cling to him or cut him off, even for a single fleeting thought.
It arises. A thousandfold gates and locks cannot restrain it; ten-thousand-fathom ropes cannot bind it.
Since this is so, how can you possibly intend to extinguish it or stop it? I am telling you clearly: O *vijñāna* of the mirage!
How do you intend to sever it? It is like a mirage; even if you search throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it cannot be found. Only then do I say: [it is not real].
Far away! Yet when you look, it is right before your eyes. If you try to pursue it, it moves further away;
just as you begin to avoid it, it comes back to chase you. You cannot grasp it, yet you cannot let it go. Since this is so, know that the nature of all phenomena is inherently thus;
there is no need to worry about it or be anxious over it. As for the saying that the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought...
This is the Sage. It is like the turning over of a hand. This is the ultimate of the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

According to our School, the preceding thought is not the ordinary person, and the succeeding thought is not the Sage. The preceding thought is not the Buddha, and the succeeding thought is not a sentient being.
Therefore, all forms are the form of the Buddha, and all sounds are the sound of the Buddha. To bring this forth—
One principle; all principles are likewise so. To see one thing is to see all things; to see one mind is to see all minds; to see one path is to see all paths.
There is nowhere that is not the Path. To see one speck of dust, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth of the ten directions are all likewise so.
To see a single drop of water is to see the entirety of the worlds of the ten directions. All [is thus].
The nature is water. Furthermore, to see all phenomena is to see the universal mind. All phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet the mind is not non-existent.
That which is not non-existent is wondrous existence; that which exists does not exist, and that which does not exist is existence—this is true emptiness and wondrous existence.
Since this is so, the empty worlds of the ten directions do not transcend my single mind, nor do all lands of fine dust.
The earth does not exist outside of my single thought. If this is so, what can be said of "internal" and "external"? It is like the nature of honey being sweet; all honey is thus.
One cannot say that this honey is sweet while the rest is bitter. Where could such a thing exist? Therefore it is said:
"Space has no interior or exterior; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Space has no middle; such is the nature of phenomena."
From that time forth, sentient beings are themselves the Buddha, and the Buddha is himself sentient beings. Sentient beings and the Buddha have from the beginning been of one and the same essence.

Birth-and-death and Nirvana, the conditioned and the unconditioned, have from the beginning been of one and the same essence. The mundane and the supramundane, even the six realms and the four modes of birth, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, whether possessing nature or lacking nature, are likewise of one and the same essence. As for saying they are "the same," even their names and characteristics are...
Emptiness. Existence is also empty; non-existence is also empty. Throughout all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is fundamentally but one emptiness.
Since this is so, where is there a Buddha who delivers sentient beings? Where are there sentient beings who receive the Buddha’s deliverance?

Why is this so? Because the nature of the myriad dharmas is inherently thus. If one views this as "spontaneity," one falls into the path of the naturalist heretics. If one views it as... [non-existence]... [text truncated].
"I have neither the view of a self nor the view of what belongs to a self; I abide within the stages of the Three Sages and Ten Sages.
How can you now attempt to measure the void with a mere foot or an inch? He has already made it clear to you: phenomena do not reach one another."
Because the Dharma is inherently quiescent, it abides in its own place and is true in its own place. Because the body is empty, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*);
because the mind is empty, it is called the emptiness of nature (*prakṛtisūnyatā*). When both body and mind are entirely empty, it is called the emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatāsūnyatā*).
Even the thousandfold divergent explanations do not depart from your own fundamental mind. As for what is now spoken of as bodhi, nirvāṇa, suchness (*tathatā*), and buddha-nature—these two...
Those who ride upon the Bodhisattva path all point to the leaf as being gold, according to the teaching of the clenched fist.
Yet, when the hand is opened, the entire assembly—whether gods or humans—sees that within the palm there is not a single thing. Therefore it is said: "Originally there is not a single thing;
where could there be any dust? Since there is originally no thing, there is likewise nothing throughout the three periods of time. Thus...
A student of the Way must enter directly with a single blade; only when they perceive this very meaning can they succeed.
Therefore, the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven to this land, traveling through countless kingdoms until he found only Master Ke, to whom he secretly transmitted the mind-seal.
He sealed your original mind: using the mind to seal the Dharma, and using the Dharma to seal the mind. Mind and mind do not differ; it is the mind itself.
Since it is thus, the Dharma is also thus. It is identical with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Within the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, who is the person who receives the prediction? Who is the person who becomes a Buddha? Who is the person who attains the Dharma? He has clearly told you:
Awakening (bodhi) cannot be attained by means of the body, because the body is without marks (animitta); it cannot be attained by means of the mind, because the mind is without marks. It is not...
It can be attained through one's nature (*xing*). Since this nature is precisely the original source-nature, the true and natural Buddha, one cannot attain a Buddha by means of a Buddha;
one cannot attain the signless (*animitta*) by means of the signless; one cannot attain emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by means of emptiness;
one cannot attain the Way (*mārga*) by means of the Way. Originally there is nothing to be attained; even non-attainment is unattainable. Therefore it is said: "Non-existence."
There is but one dharma to be attained: it is simply to instruct you to realize and grasp your own original mind. At the moment of realization, there is no characteristic of "realization";
even the characteristics of neither realizing nor not realizing cannot be found. Regarding such a dharma, those who attain it do so immediately;

yet those who attain it do not cognize it themselves, and those who do not attain it likewise do not cognize it themselves. Such a dharma has existed from the time of the ancient patriarchs until now.
How many people know this? That is why it is said: "Throughout the world, how many have forgotten themselves?

Now, within a single occasion and a single environment, a single scripture and a single teaching, a single age and a single moment, a single name and a single character—you must grasp this before the gates of the six sense faculties.

"How does this differ from a mechanical wooden man? Suppose a person were to emerge who does not form conceptual interpretations based on names or characteristics—I say that even if one were to search throughout the worlds of the ten directions, such a person could not be found, for there is no second person.
Because he is pure and undiluted, continuing the lineage of the Patriarchs, he is also called a member of the Śākya clan; thus he is termed a 'King'."
When he attains Buddhahood, the Prince will also follow him into the monastic life. This meaning is extremely difficult to understand; I simply instruct you: do not seek it.
To seek it is to lose it, like a foolish man who, upon hearing a single cry from within a mountain, sees the echo emerge from the valley and then runs down the slope.
When you have caught up with it, you cannot find it; yet you cry out once more, and the mountain echoes. You respond again and run up the mountain to pursue it.
Thus for a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas, you are merely a person seeking sound and chasing echoes—a man of empty life and vain death.
If you had no sound, there would be no echo. Nirvana is without hearing, without knowing, without sound, and where all traces and footprints are severed.
"If you attain such [realization], you will be quite close to the Patriarch.
[The student] asked: "In the royal treasury, there is no such sword at all. I humbly pray that you will instruct me. The Master said:
"The royal treasury is the nature of space (*ākāśa*). It encompasses the empty worlds of the ten directions, yet none of them ever transcend you."

The mind is also called the "Space Bodhisattva. Whether you say it exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist—it all results in the horns of a black goat.
These horns of a black goat are precisely what you are seeking. Question: "Is there a real sword in the King’s treasury?
The Master said: "This, too, is the horns of a black goat. [The student] said: "If [there is no real sword] in the King’s treasury..."
Originally there was no real sword. Why, then, do you say that the prince took the real sword from the royal treasury and went to another country?
How can you say it does not exist? The Master said: "As for 'taking the sword and going out,' this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s messengers.
If you say the prince took the real sword from the royal treasury and departed, then the treasury should have been empty when he left. The original source is void."
"Nature cannot be taken away by another person. What kind of words are these? Even if you had it, it would all be called 'goat's horn.
Question: "Kāśyapa received the Buddha’s mind-seal; is he permitted to enter as a messenger? The Master said: "Yes. [The questioner] said:
"If he is a messenger, he should not be separated from the goat's horn. The Master said: "Kāśyapa leads it himself."
One attains the original mind; therefore, it is not like the horn of a black sheep.

If one were to grasp the mind of the Tathāgata, perceive the intent of the Tathāgata, or perceive the physical marks of the Tathāgata, one would belong to the Tathāgata’s retinue as a messenger who transmits words.
This is why Ānanda served as an attendant for twenty years yet saw only the physical marks of the Tathāgata; thus he was rebuked by the Buddha, who said: "You have only observed..."
The Savior cannot avoid obtaining the horn of a black sheep. Question:
As for "holding a sword before Gautama," what does this mean? The Master said:

Five hundred bodhisattvas have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) and see the karmic obstructions of their past existences. These five hundred are none other than your own five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Because they see these past...

Because it is an obstruction. One seeks the Buddha, seeking enlightenment and nirvana; therefore, Mañjuśrī took the sword of wisdom and insight to strike down this mind that views the Buddha as a substantial entity.
Thus he said, "You must skillfully strike. [The student] asked, "What is this sword? The Master said, "The mind of insight is the sword.
[The student] asked, "If the mind of insight is the sword, then in severing this mind that views the Buddha as a substantial entity, what is it that performs the severing?"

Question: "How can one eliminate this mind that perceives existence? The Master said: "Use your own non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to sever this discriminative mind that perceives existence.
Question: "If one acts with the perception of existence and possesses a mind seeking Buddhahood, how does one use the sword of non-conceptual wisdom to sever it?"

"But what can be done, since there is the sword of wisdom? The Master said, "If there were no non-conceptual wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*), it would destroy both the view of existence and the view of non-existence;
yet even this non-conceptual wisdom cannot be apprehended. [The student] said, "One cannot use wisdom to further sever wisdom, nor can one use a sword to further sever a sword.
The Master said, "The sword destroys itself; sword and sword destroy each other. Thus, even the sword cannot be [apprehended]."
[It is] attained. Wisdom harms wisdom; wisdom and wisdom harm one another, such that even wisdom itself cannot be apprehended. It is just like this when both mother and son perish together.
[The student] asked: "What is the seeing of nature? The Master said: "Nature is seeing; seeing is nature. It cannot be..."
Nature further perceives nature; hearing is itself nature. One cannot use nature to further hear nature.
It is simply because you conceive of nature as an object of perception that there arises the duality of subject and object—of one who can hear and see and a nature that is heard and seen.
He spoke clearly: "That which is already visible cannot be seen again. Why do you place a head upon your own head? He spoke clearly: "It is like scattered pearls within a bowl."
The large is a great circle; the small is a small circle. Each is unaware of the other; each does not obstruct the other.

When arising, it does not say, "I arise"; when ceasing, it does not say, "I cease. Therefore, among the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, there is nothing that does not accord with the timing [of phenomena].

Furthermore, sentient beings do not see the Buddha, and the Buddha does not see sentient beings. Those in the four fruits do not see those in the four stages of approach (srotāpanna-pratipannaka), nor do those in the four stages of approach see...

The four fruits of the path are not seen; the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood do not see the two types of enlightenment—the equal and the wondrous—and the equal and wondrous enlightenments do not see the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.
Even so, water does not see fire, and fire does not see water; earth does not see wind, and wind does not see earth.
Sentient beings do not enter the Dharma-realm, and the Buddha does not emerge from the Dharma-realm. Therefore, the nature of phenomena has no coming or going.

There is neither subject nor object of seeing. Since this is so, for what reason do you say, "I see" and "I hear"? It is at the place of the *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) that one attains realization;
it is the *kalyāṇamitra* who expounds the Dharma for me. When the Buddhas appear in the world, they expound the Dharma for sentient beings.
Kātyāyana merely used a mind of arising and ceasing to transmit the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*), and was consequently rebuked by Vimalakīrti, who spoke clearly: [the Dharma is beyond words].
All dharmas are fundamentally unbound; what need is there for liberation? They are fundamentally unstained; what need is there for purification? Therefore it is said:
"The true mark (*dharmatā*) is thus; how can it be spoken of? You now merely cultivate a mind of right and wrong and a mind of defilement and purity.
Having acquired a bit of knowledge and understanding, you travel about the world, intending to fixate upon and seize things as soon as you see someone. Who possesses such discernment?
Who is strong and who is weak? If it were truly thus, heaven and earth would be as vastly different as they are;

what more could be said regarding the "seeing of nature"? Question: Since you say that nature is seeing and seeing is nature, and since nature itself is without obstruction and without limit, why is it that one does not see when an object intervenes?
Furthermore, within empty space, why is it that one sees when near but does not see when far away? It is like this:
The Master said: "This is you generating false and divergent views.

If you say that one does not see when an object intervenes, yet sees when there is no object, and thereby claim that the nature possesses obstruction, you are entirely out of touch with the truth. The nature is neither seeing nor non-seeing;
phenomena are likewise neither seeing nor non-seeing. For one who perceives the nature, where is there that is not my own fundamental nature? Therefore—"
The six realms, the four modes of birth, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are the essence of my own pure and luminous nature. Therefore it is said:

"To see form is to see the mind," for form and mind are not different. Yet, because one grasps at appearances and forms views through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one attempts to see the mind only after removing external objects;
such a person falls into the category of those of the Two Vehicles who rely on supernatural powers for their understanding. Within empty space...
"If it is near, it is seen; if it is far, it is not seen. This belongs to the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). It is clearly stated:
'It is neither internal nor external, neither near nor far. As for that which is near yet cannot be seen—this is the nature of all things.
If it cannot even be seen when it is near, what purpose is served in further saying that it cannot be seen when it is far?"
Question: "The student does not understand; how does the Master instruct? The Master said: "I possess nothing.
From the beginning, I have never given anything to anyone. Since time without beginning, you have merely been instructed by others to seek the seal [of realization] and seek understanding.
Is this not a case where both disciple and teacher fall into royal calamity? You need only know that in a single thought-moment..."
Feeling is itself the body without feeling. A single thought-moment of non-conceptualization is the body without perception.

To be definitively free from shifting flux and volitional activity is the body without mental formations. Not to engage in deliberation, conjecture, or discrimination is the body without consciousness.
As soon as you now give rise to a single flickering thought, you immediately enter the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions formations; this is both cause and...

From the fruit up to old age and death, each is both cause and fruit. Therefore, when the youth Sudhana sought spiritual friends at one hundred and ten locations, he sought them solely within the twelve links of dependent origination. Finally, he met Maitreya, who in turn directed him to see Mañjuśrī.
This Mañjuśrī is none other than your own fundamental ground of ignorance. If you perceive the mind as something separate and distinct, you will seek it outwardly.
Good friends (kalyāṇamitra) arise in a single thought-moment and immediately perish; having perished, they arise again.
Therefore, you bhikṣus, are born, age, fall ill, and die. From the time one repays causes and answers effects, this is precisely the arising and perishing of the five aggregates.
The "five aggregates" refers to the five *skandhas*. When not a single thought arises, the eighteen *dhātus* are empty;
the very body is the flower and fruit of *bodhi*, and the very mind is numinous wisdom, also called the "numinous terrace.
If one dwells in attachment, then the body is a corpse, and one is also called a "ghost guarding a corpse."
Question: When Vimalakīrti remained silent, Mañjuśrī praised him, saying, "This is the true entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
How is it that the Master says, "The Dharma-gate of non-duality is your own original mind"? Whether one speaks or does not speak, there is arising and ceasing;
when there is no verbal expression, there is nothing to be displayed. Therefore, Mañjuśrī praised him, saying, "When Vimalakīrti did not speak, sound existed..."

"Is there cessation or extinction? The Master said: "Speech is silence; silence is speech. Since speech and silence are non-dual, it is said that the true nature of sound is also without cessation or extinction.
Mañjuśrī’s primordial hearing is likewise without cessation or extinction. Therefore, the Tathāgata constantly says:"
There has never been a time when he did not speak. What the Tathāgata speaks is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the speaking.

Because the Dharma and its speaking are non-dual, even the two bodies of recompense and transformation, the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, the waters, birds, and forest trees—all at once preach the Dharma.
Therefore, speech is preaching, and silence is also preaching. Though he preaches all day long, he has never spoken. Since this is so...
It is so. It is simply that silence is the foundation.
Question: "As for the śrāvaka who can conceal his form within the triple world but cannot conceal it from bodhi, how is this so?
The Master said: "Form refers to substance. The śrāvaka is merely able to sever the views and cultivations of the triple world; having already abandoned afflictions..."
Because it can be concealed within bodhi, the Māra King is consequently able to seize it within that very bodhi while one is sitting in meditative seclusion in the forest;

thus, it becomes a subtle view regarding the bodhicitta. A person who is a Bodhisattva has already reached a definitive certainty regarding the bodhi of the triple world, neither abandoning nor grasping it.
Because they do not grasp it, they cannot find "other" within the seven great elements; because they do not abandon it, external Māras [cannot seize them].
Furthermore, you cannot find another [subject] elsewhere. You need only intend toward a single dharma, and the seal is already accomplished.
If you seal existence, the script of the six realms and four modes of birth immediately emerges. If you seal emptiness, the script of signlessness appears.
Now, simply know that it is certain not to seal any thing; this seal is space—neither one nor two. Emptiness is fundamentally not empty; the seal is fundamentally...
There is nothing that exists. The appearance of Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions throughout empty space is like seeing a flash of lightning.
Contemplating all wriggling and sentient beings is like hearing an echo. Seeing the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, is exactly like a single drop of water in the ocean.
Hearing all most profound teachings is like a phantom or a transformation; mind after mind is no different from the Dharma.
The Dharma is not different; even the thousands of sutras and myriads of treatises are solely for the sake of your single mind.
If you can refrain from grasping at any signs, it is said that within this single mind, you should diligently adorn it through skillful means.
Question: "As it is said, 'In the past, when I was King Kali, my body was cut to pieces. How is this so? The Master said: "The 'sage' is your own mind.
King Kali represents the fondness for seeking. Not guarding the royal throne is called 'craving gain.
As for students today who accumulate merit and virtue, as soon as they see something, they immediately attempt to imitate it; how are they any different from King Kali? It is like seeing..."
When seeing forms, it destroys the seer’s eyes; when hearing sounds, it destroys the seer’s ears; and so it is even up to the point of sensory cognition.
This is called "being dismembered limb by limb. It is said: "If the seer were truly patient, there should be no further dismembering limb by limb;
one cannot be both single-mindedly patient and single-mindedly impatient. The Master said: "You..."
[The student] said: "To cultivate the view of non-arising, the patience of understanding, and the absence of seeking—all of these are injuries.

He asked: "When the immortal was being cut, did he still know the pain? The Master said: "He felt pain. He asked: "In this state there is no experiencer; who is it that feels the pain? The Master said:
"Since you yourself do not feel pain, what are you looking for by poking your head out [of the water]?"

Question: Was the prediction (vyākaraṇa) bestowed by Dīpaṃkara Buddha given within five hundred years [of the teaching], or outside of five hundred years? The Master said: The prediction was not received within five hundred years.
What is called "receiving a prediction" means that your own fundamental mind is resolute, neither forgetting nor losing it;
that you do not grasp at bodhi amidst conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), but simply realize that the world is not the world. This does not even occur within five hundred years.
[The student] asked: "Is it that one receives a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) externally and separately, or does one receive such a prediction within five hundred years?

[The teacher] said: "Can the characteristics of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—be apprehended as being either 'the world' or 'not the world'? [The student] asked: "If so, can they be apprehended at all? [The teacher] said: "Not a single dharma can be apprehended. [The student] asked:

"For what reason do you say that one must pass through five hundred lifetimes, such that the duration from beginning to end is exceedingly long? [The teacher] said: "Five hundred lifetimes are indeed long and distant; however, when one realizes that there is not even a single dharma to be attained..."
[The Master said: "To know that it is still the same as when the Immortal [Dīpaṃkara] bestowed the prediction:

at that time, there was truly not even the slightest dharma to be attained. Question: "The scriptures state: 'Having eliminated my inverted conceptions over billions of kalpas, I shall attain the Dharma-body without passing through the stages of the śrāvakas.
How is this so? Master: "If one were to attain something through cultivation over three incalculable kalpas, it would be as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

It cannot be attained through eons. If one were to attain the Dharma-body within a single kṣaṇa and directly perceive one's nature, this would still be considered the ultimate discourse of the Three Vehicles' teachings.
Why? Because it implies that the Dharma-body can be obtained; thus, it is all subsumed under the category of teachings of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
Question: "One who suddenly realizes the Dharma—does such a person see the meaning of the Patriarchs? The Master said: "The mind of the Patriarchs lies beyond the limits of empty space.
Question: "Is there a finite measure to it? The Master said: "There is both a finite measure and an infinite measure.
These are all dharmas of numerical quantity and relative opposition. The mind of the Patriarchs is neither finite, nor infinite, nor is it 'neither finite nor infinite.'"
As for the measure [of realization]: because it is absolute. You practitioners today have not yet been able to transcend the teachings of the Three Vehicles;
how can you call yourselves Chan masters? I tell you clearly: all are studying Chan equally, so do not recklessly give rise to heterodox views.
Just as when a person drinks water, they know its temperature for themselves; in every movement and stillness, in every single kṣaṇa, thought after thought is no different. If...
It is not so; one will not escape saṃsāra. Question:
The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories. For what reason do the relics of the Buddha’s body amount to eight *hu* and four *dou*?
The Master said: "If you hold such a view, you see only the provisional relics and do not see the true relics. He said: "Relics..."
"Is benefit the original existence? Or is it the result of meritorious effort? The Master said: "It is neither the original existence, nor is it the result of meritorious effort.
[The interlocutor asked: "If it is neither the original existence nor the result of meritorious effort, for what reason are the Tathāgata’s śarīras so refined and pure?"
[The monk said: "The golden bones remain forever. The Master then rebuked him, saying: "If you hold such a view, how can you be called a student of Chan?
Have you ever seen bones in empty space? The minds of all Buddhas are identical to the great void; what 'bones' are you looking for? [The monk asked:
"Since there are currently śarīras (relics), what dharma is this? The Master said: "This arises from your own deluded mind."
When Sheng saw the śarīra, he asked, "Does the Master have any śarīra? Please bring it out so that I may see it.
The Master said, "True śarīra is difficult to see. You should simply take Mount Sumeru and, with your ten fingers, crush it entirely into fine dust."
One immediately beholds the true śarīra. Now, in practicing Chan and studying the Way, one must ensure that the mind does not arise in any situation whatsoever.

It is said that when the workings of the intellect are forgotten, the Buddha-way flourishes; when there is discrimination, the demonic armies flourish. Ultimately, not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma can be obtained.
Question: "The Patriarchs transmitted the Dharma; to whom did they entrust it? The Master said: "There is no Dharma to give to anyone. [The questioner] asked:

"For what reason, then, did the Second Patriarch request the Master to 'settle his mind'? The Master said: "If you had said that there was [a mind], the Second Patriarch would have been able to find it."

Because the mind cannot be found when sought. Therefore it is said: "I have finished granting you peace of mind. If there is anything attained, it entirely falls within the realm of arising and ceasing.
Question: Does the Buddha exhaustively attain ignorance? The Master says: Ignorance is precisely that which all Buddhas attain.

As for the locus of the Way: it is because dependent origination is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When one perceives a single speck of dust or a single color, it immediately accords with the boundless principle of nature.
Whether lifting the foot or setting it down, one does not depart from the site of enlightenment. As for the "site of enlightenment," it is non-attainment.
I have told you before that it is precisely because of non-attainment that it is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment. [The questioner] asked: "Is ignorance light or darkness?"
The Master said: "It is neither light nor darkness. Light and darkness are phenomena of alternation. That which is without light is neither bright nor dark.
This lack of brightness is precisely the fundamental brightness. Neither bright nor dark—this is precisely the fundamental brightness. Neither bright nor dark."
This single phrase confuses the eyes of people throughout the world. Therefore it is said:

"Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they all exhausted their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. His unimpeded wisdom transcends empty space;
there is no place for speech or debate to reach it. Śākyamuni’s capacity is equal to that of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system. Suddenly, there was one...
The Bodhisattva comes forth and takes a single stride, yet he does not step outside a single pore of Samantabhadra.
With what capacity do you intend to emulate him now? [The student] says:
"If it cannot be learned, why is it said that 'the source of returning is non-dual, though the gates of expedient means are many'? What is to be done? The Master says: "Return."
Wisdom. That unimpeded wisdom transcends empty space; there is no place for you to speak or debate.

Śākyamuni’s measure is equal to a trichiliocosm, yet suddenly a single Bodhisattva emerges and takes a single stride, spanning the entire trichiliocosm without leaving a single pore of Samantabhadra. What resources do you have now that you intend to emulate him?
The student asked: "If it cannot be attained through study, why do you say that 'the source to which all return has no duality, yet the expedient means have many gates'?
How is this so? The Master said: "'The source to which all return has no duality' means that the true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature."
Regarding the many gateways of skillful means: Śrāvakas perceive the arising of ignorance and also perceive the cessation of ignorance.
Pratyekabuddhas perceive only the cessation of ignorance and do not perceive its arising; they realize quiescence in every thought-moment.
The Buddhas perceive sentient beings as being born all day long yet without birth, and ceasing all day long yet without cessation. This absence of birth and absence of cessation is the Mahāyāna.
The Fruit. Thus it is said: "When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower blooms, the world arises. Lifting the foot is the Buddha; setting the foot down is the sentient being.

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, are those who are fully endowed with principle, fully endowed with transformation, and fully endowed as sentient beings—fully endowed in all things, whether birth-and-death or nirvana.
Because they are already complete, they seek nothing. This is you, right now, moment by moment, learning from the Buddha; yet you harbor resentment and attachment.
Sentient beings. If you harbor aversion or attachment toward sentient beings, you are slandering the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Therefore, since the Buddha appeared in the world, he carried a refuse basket to sweep away the filth of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). He taught only that you must eliminate the mind of learning and the mind of views from the past;
if these are eliminated completely, you will no longer follow conceptual proliferation. This is also called "carrying out the filth," which means teaching you not to give rise [to them].
Mind. If the mind does not arise, one naturally attains great wisdom. One who possesses great wisdom is definitively free from discriminating between Buddhas and sentient beings;
when there is no discrimination regarding anything at all, only then has one entered the gate of our Caoxi school. Therefore, the ancient sages of old said:
"Few people practice this Dharma-gate of mine. Thus, the Dharma-gate of non-action is simply the single mind.
Gate. When all people arrive here, none dare to enter. It is not that there is none at all; it is simply that few obtain it.
Now, this is precisely the Buddha. Take care! The Master passed away at his native mountain during the Dazhong era.
Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Duanjian, and his stupa was named Guangye.
*The Extensive Record of the Lamp*, Volume Eight;
*The Extensive Record of the Lamp*, Volume Nine. [Compiled by] Shi [Daoxuan].
Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai of Mount Daxiong in Hongzhou. Now, in speech, one must distinguish between the black and the white; one must recognize the general and...

A separate discourse: One must recognize the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and those of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). The teachings of definitive meaning clarify and purify; the teachings of provisional meaning clarify and purify through turbidity.
Speaking of the defilements at the margins of impure dharmas distinguishes the ordinary person; speaking of the defilements at the margins of pure dharmas distinguishes the noble one.

According to the ninefold division of the teachings (*navāṅga-śāsana*), sentient beings of the past lacked the eye [of wisdom] and required human refinement. If one were to speak before an ordinary person who is deaf, one must simply...
Instruct them to leave the household life, uphold the precepts, cultivate dhyāna, and study wisdom.
Even if they are laypeople of great capacity, one must not speak to others in such a manner [as if they were already enlightened], as was done by those such as Vimalakīrti and Master Fu.

If one speaks before śramaṇas who have already completed the *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of fourfold motion) and are fully endowed with the power of morality, concentration, and wisdom, then to speak further to them...
To speak in such a manner is called untimely speech; to speak when it is inappropriate is also called frivolous chatter (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).

If one is a śramaṇa, one must speak of the purity of the Dharma and its boundaries and defilements; one must speak of the Dharma that is free from existence and non-existence, and free from all cultivation and realization, as well as free even from that freedom itself.
If, among those who are śramaṇas, one strips away habitual defilements yet the śramaṇa does not eliminate the diseases of greed and hatred, this is also called [frivolous chatter].
Even for those of deafening ignorance, one must teach them to cultivate dhyāna and study wisdom.

If they are monks of the Two Vehicles, once their diseases of greed and anger have been extinguished and eliminated, they will rely on non-greed as their standard of correctness. Now, the formless realm obstructs the Buddha’s radiance;

it is like shedding the blood of the Buddha’s body. One must also teach them to cultivate dhyāna and study wisdom. One must distinguish between pure and turbid speech. As for turbid dharmas, they are greed...

Although there are many names such as hatred, craving, and grasping, regarding both the pure and turbid streams—the dharmas of ordinary beings and sages alike; the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena;
and all mundane and supramundane dharmas—one must not harbor even the slightest bit of craving or grasping. One should instead return to non-craving and non-grasping.
To rely on and dwell in non-attachment while taking it as the ultimate is "good at the beginning. This is dwelling in the taming of the mind; this is the person of the Śrāvaka;

this is the person who clings to the raft and does not let go; this is the path of the Two Vehicles; this is the fruit of *dhyāna*. To take refuge in non-attachment while also not relying on or dwelling in non-attachment is "good in the middle.
This is the teaching of the "half-letters"; it still pertains to the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is merely a means to avoid falling into the two [extremes].
Riding the path [of the vehicles] to avoid falling into the realm of the māras is still a sickness of *dhyāna*; this is a bondage for a bodhisattva.

To return to non-reliance, non-abiding, and non-clinging, and likewise not to form a conceptual understanding of non-reliance and non-abiding—this is the "subsequent goodness. This is the teaching of the full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*).

It avoids falling into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), avoids falling into attachment to *dhyāna*, avoids falling into the bodhisattva vehicle, and avoids falling into the rank of the Māra kings; it constitutes wisdom.
Because of the obstacles of hindrances, stages, and practices, one perceives one's own Buddha-nature as clearly as seeing forms at night.

It is said that on the Buddha-stage, two types of ignorance are severed: first, the ignorance regarding subtle objects of knowledge; second, the ignorance regarding extremely subtle objects of knowledge. Thus it is said:

"A person of great wisdom breaks through the dust to reveal the sutra scroll. If one penetrates the three phrases, one encounters [the truth] and is no longer governed by the three sections. This is what the Teaching School cites.
Metaphor: It is like a deer that, having leaped three times, escapes the net; this is called a Buddha outside of entanglement. Nothing can restrain him;
he belongs to the Buddhas subsequent to Dīpaṃkara. This is the Supreme Vehicle, the most supreme wisdom. He stands upon the path of the Buddha;
such a person is a Buddha, possesses the Buddha-nature, is a guide, and has attained the wind of non-obstruction—this is unimpeded wisdom. Regarding this...
Later, one will be able to attain mastery over cause and effect, merit and wisdom. This is like a carriage that transports cause and effect;

dwelling in birth, one is not detained by birth; dwelling in death, one is not obstructed by death; dwelling amidst the five aggregates (*skandhas*), one is like a door opening, unimpeded by the five aggregates.
Going and staying are free; entering and exiting are without difficulty. If one can act in this manner, then—
Discussing the gradations of superiority and inferiority, even down to the bodies of ants—if they can simply act in this way, all such places are entirely pure and wondrous lands, inconceivable.
This is still speech that binds; since they have no sores themselves, do not wound them.

To speak of the sores of Buddhas or the sores of Bodhisattvas, and to merely discuss the existence or non-existence of phenomena—all of these are wounds. Existence and non-existence govern everything.
The Dharma. These ten stages are a river of turbid currents; [the Buddha] makes them clear by explaining the characteristics of vertical purity and the faults of turbidity.
He addresses the ten great disciples of former times: Śāriputra, Pūrṇa, Ānanda of right faith, Sunakṣatra of wrong faith, and the others.
Each one has their own model; each one has their own standard. One by one, they are exposed by the Teacher.

These are not the Arhats of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis who dwell in meditative absorption for eighty thousand kalpas; they are those who cling to what they practice and are intoxicated by the wine of pure dharmas.
