Therefore it is said that when śrāvakas hear the Buddha-dharma, they are unable to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. For this reason:

Those who have severed their roots of goodness possess no Buddha-nature. The Teaching says: "To call this the 'fearful abyss of liberation'—if the mind retreats for even a single thought-moment, one falls into hell like an arrow shot from a bow. Yet, one must not say that there is exclusively regression, nor must one say that there is exclusively no regression.
Consider, for instance, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; they returned to the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The ground is one of mutual induction; one cannot say that others have regressed. At such a time, one is simply called a *srotāpanna*.
It is just like present discernment, only that it is not governed by any phenomena of existence or non-existence.

Having penetrated through the three propositions and all conditions of favor or opposition, even hearing of hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas appearing in the world is like not hearing them at all.
It is similar. Furthermore, one does not rely on or dwell upon non-hearing, nor does one produce a conceptual understanding based on non-reliance;

such a person is said to have regressed, and their number cannot be calculated, for they cannot be managed. This refers to the Buddha abiding eternally in the world yet remaining unstained by worldly dharmas.

To say that the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma and then regresses is to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. To say that the Buddha does not turn the wheel of Dharma and thus does not regress—[this is the correct view].
This is also to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Zhaò says: "The Way of Bodhi cannot be schemed or measured; it is high with nothing above it, vast beyond limit;
it is deep with nothing below it, profound beyond fathoming. To speak thus is like setting up a target only to invite an arrow.

To say that even this present discerning awareness (*jñāna*) is not [the truth]—to distinguish the clear from the turbid—is to grant that there exists something external and separate from this present discerning awareness. All of this is [mere conceptualization].
The Māra says: "If one maintains a state of present-time discernment and awareness, this too is the teaching of Māra; it is also called the teaching of the Natural Heretics (Svabhāvavādins).
This present-time discernment and awareness is one's own Buddha—this is but a limited description, a conceptualized description, resembling the howl of a jackal."
It is like being attached to sticky glue. Fundamentally failing to recognize that self-knowing and self-awakening are one's own Buddha, one rushes outward in search of a Buddha.
A true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) provides the teaching of self-knowing and self-awakening as medicine to treat this disease of rushing outward in search.
Once the disease of rushing outward has been cured, the medicine must be discarded. If one clings to self-knowing and...
Awakening is a sickness of *dhyāna*. This is the track of the *śrāvaka*, like water turning into ice; though the ice is entirely water, it is difficult to hope for it to quench thirst.

It is also called a terminal illness for which worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness. "From beginningless time, one has never not been a Buddha"—do not form a conceptual understanding of Buddhahood.
The Buddha is a medicine for the side of sentient beings; when there is no illness, there is no need to take medicine. When both medicine and illness have vanished, it is likened to clarity.
Water. It is like mixing licorice with water, or like mixing honey with water; it is extremely sweet and delicious.

If one counts it alongside clear water, it does not appear as such, yet it is not non-existent. It is inherently present. This principle is also said to be that which is inherently possessed by all people.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas call him the "person who shows the pearl. From the beginning, he has never been a thing. There is no need to know him or understand him;
there is no need for "it is he" or "it is not he. Simply sever the dualistic phrases; sever the phrase of existence and the phrase of non-existence.
Severing both the state of no-phrase and the state of not-no-phrase, the traces of both extremes do not appear.
Neither can you be grasped by either extreme, nor can any measure or calculation govern you. It is neither deficient nor complete; it is neither ordinary nor holy; it is neither light nor dark.
It is not possessing knowledge; it is not lacking knowledge. It is not bondage; it is not liberation. It is not any designation whatsoever.

Why is this not true speech? If one were to carve the void to produce the physical form of a Buddha, or if one were to say that the void is blue, yellow, red, or white and thereby make it so—just as it is said that "the Dharma has no peer" and is beyond comparison.
Because it is an analogy: the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories. Therefore it is said: "The holy body is nameless;

the reality (*yathābhūta-artha*) cannot be described, and the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*) is difficult to approach. This is illustrated by the analogy of the great moth (*pataṅga*), which can alight anywhere but alone cannot alight upon a flame.
Sentient beings are likewise: they can take as objects (*ālambana*) all things, yet alone cannot take Prajñā as an object.
First: To go to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and seek even a single bit of knowledge or understanding is the demon of the spiritual friend, because it gives rise to verbal views.

If one makes the Four Great Vows, saying, "Only after I have saved all sentient beings shall I begin to attain Buddhahood," this is the demon of the Bodhisattva’s dharma-wisdom, because of the refusal to abandon one's vows. If one observes the fasts and precepts, cultivates meditation, and studies wisdom—this is...

If one possesses tainted roots of goodness—such as even sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), manifesting the attainment of perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), delivering beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or realizing the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha*—these are the "demons of roots of goodness," because they give rise to craving and attachment.

If, regarding all phenomena, there is no defilement whatsoever, yet the spiritual principle remains solitary and one dwells in profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without further ascending or progressing, this is the "demon of samādhi. Long...
Because of indulgence and attachment, even reaching the ultimate *nirvāṇa*—the tranquility of freedom from desire—is itself a work of Māra.

If one does not depart through wisdom from the various nets of Māra, then even if one has mastered a hundred volumes of the *Veda*, they are all but dregs of hell. It is impossible to find anyone who resembles a Buddha;
yet now, upon hearing this teaching, one does not cling to any phenomena such as good and evil, existence and non-existence, and so forth.

This is precisely falling into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Not knowing to abandon the secondary for the fundamental, one instead falls into emptiness. To seek the Buddha, to seek Bodhi, and to seek all dharmas of existence and non-existence—this is to abandon the fundamental and pursue the secondary.
Simply now, using coarse food to sustain life, patching clothes to ward off the cold, and scooping up water to drink when thirsty—for these matters alone;
as for everything else, all dharmas of existence and non-existence are utterly nonexistent.

If one has even the slightest lingering attachment, this person will gradually develop a degree of lightness and clarity. A true spiritual friend does not cling to existence, nor do they cling to non-existence.
Having escaped the ten phrases of demonic speech, their words do not bind people; whatever they say, they do not claim themselves to be a teacher.
To speak like an echo in a valley, such that one’s words fill the world without any verbal transgression, is worthy of being relied upon.
If one says, "I can speak and I can explain; I am the Upādhyāya and you are the disciple," this is no different from the speech of Māra; it is groundless talk.

The Way exists within direct perception. Whether one is a Buddha or not a Buddha, whether it be Bodhi, Nirvana, or liberation—these are all without cause for being described as "one knowledge" or "one understanding.
To see someone raise a hand or point a finger and say, "This is Chan, this is the Way"—such words bind people;
they have no time to settle, merely adding further ropes to the monk’s feet. Even if one does not speak, they still exist.

This is an error of speech. It would be better to take the mind as one's teacher than to let the mind be one's teacher. Regarding teachings of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*), there are those who act as teachers for gods and humans, and there are those who act as guides.

Within the teachings of complete meaning (*nītārtha*), one does not act as a teacher for gods and humans, nor does one take the [conventional] phenomena as one's teacher; rather, one must attain profound insight through reliance [upon these teachings].
Furthermore, according to the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*), there still remains a degree of conceptual affinity.

If it were merely the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), they would only be fit to be spoken before ignorant laypeople. Now, simply not abiding in any phenomena that exist or do not exist, yet not abiding in non-abiding either—neither forming a conceptual understanding of "abiding" nor "not abiding"—this is called a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); it is also called "only."
The Buddha alone is the Great Good Spiritual Friend; there is no second person. All others are merely called "outsiders" (tīrthika) and their words are called "the teachings of Māra.
At present, they do nothing but explain the dualistic phrases concerning all phenomena such as existence and non-existence.

They teach people nothing other than the matters of not becoming attached through craving or being liberated from bondage. If one were to say that they have separate phrases to teach people, [it would be false].

Those who claim there is a separate dharma to be given to others are called outsiders (*tīrthika*) and are also termed those who preach the Māra-doctrine. One must recognize the language of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
One must recognize prohibitive language and non-prohibitive language. One must recognize the language of saṃsāra. One must recognize the language of medicine and disease.
One must recognize analogies of the inverse and the direct. One must recognize general and specific language. It is said that by practicing the Way one attains Buddhahood; there is cultivation...
There is evidence for this: "This mind is Buddha; this very mind is Buddha.

This is a teaching spoken by the Buddha that is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), a non-exclusive statement, a general statement, a statement that blends [different levels], a statement concerning the margins of defiled phenomena, a figurative statement, a literal statement, and a statement directed toward ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
It does not permit attaining Buddhahood through cultivation; it asserts that there is neither cultivation nor realization. It is not...
"The mind is not the Buddha" is also a teaching spoken by the Buddha. It is a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*); it is a prohibitive expression; it is a distinct expression;

it is an expression like a hundred-stone load; it is an expression outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles; it is an expression of inverse analogy; it is an expression that selects the boundary of pure dharmas; it is an expression of arising;
it is an expression used before those on the stages (*bhūmi*), from the stage of *srotāpanna* upward through to the tenth stage. There is only...
Words and phrases are entirely defilements of the dharma-object (*dharmārambaṇa*). Wherever there are words and phrases, they are all subsumed under the side of affliction (*kleśapakṣa*).

Wherever there are words and phrases, they are all included within the teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). The teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is upholding; the teaching of provisional meaning is transgression.

In the stage of Buddhahood, there is neither upholding nor transgressing; even the teachings of definitive and provisional meaning are not permitted [there]. One discerns the field from its sprouts; one discerns [the nature of] turbidity [from its manifestations].
Purity. As for this present discerning awareness (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*): if one counts it from the side of purity, discerning awareness is not purity;
non-discerning awareness is also not purity; nor is it non-purity. It is not even "not [being] pure. It is not holy, nor is it non-holy; it is not even that.
When one sees water is turbid, one speaks of the faults and afflictions of the turbid water. If the water were clear, there would be nothing at all to say. Now, however, you are making it turbid.
Water. If there is a question that is neither existent nor non-existent, there is also a teaching that is neither spoken nor unspoken. The Buddha does not teach the Dharma for the sake of a Buddha;
in the equal and true *dharmadhātu*, there is no Buddha and no sentient beings to be received. The Buddha does not abide as a Buddha; this is called the true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

One must distinguish between the host and the guest: when greed and defilement cling to all phenomena of existence and non-existence, one is deluded and distracted by all phenomena of existence and non-existence.
One's own mind is the Demon King; its illuminating function belongs to the subjects of Māra. It is simply like the awareness of a golden mirror:

one merely does not rely on or dwell in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, whether mundane or supramundane; nor does one form a conceptual understanding of "not relying," nor does one rely on a conceptual understanding of "non-reliance.
One's own mind is the Buddha; its illuminating function belongs to the Bodhisattvas. Every moment of mind is...
The Sovereign. Illumination and function belong to adventitious dust; it is like describing water by means of its waves.

To illuminate the myriad phenomena without artifice—if one can achieve still illumination—this is not due to some profound principle, but is naturally penetrating throughout past and present. As it is said: "The spirit has no merit of illumination, yet its ultimate merit ever abides.
Thus, one can act as a guide in all places. Regarding the nature and consciousness of sentient beings, others have never yet trodden the steps of the Buddha.
This is the nature of sticky glue: for a long time it clings to all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent. Suddenly encountering the medicine of the profound principle, one cannot take it;
suddenly hearing words that transcend the ordinary, one cannot believe them. This is why, beneath the Bodhi tree, he remained silent in contemplation for twenty-one days.
His wisdom was dark and obscure, difficult to explain and beyond all analogy. To say that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha.
To say that sentient beings lack the Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. If one says there is a Buddha-nature, it is called the slander of attachment;
if one says there is no Buddha-nature, it is called the slander of falsehood. As it is said: to say the Buddha-nature exists is the slander of exaggeration (*samāropa*);
to say the Buddha-nature does not exist is the slander of denigration (*apavāda*); to say the Buddha-nature both exists and does not exist is the slander of contradiction.
To say that the Buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent is idle speculation and slander. If I were not to speak at all, sentient beings would have no opportunity for liberation.
Yet if I were to speak, sentient beings would again give rise to interpretations based on the words, resulting in more harm than benefit. Therefore, it is said:
"I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana. However, looking back later, one finds that all Buddhas of the past have indeed taught the Three [Vehicles].
The Vehicle of Multiplication (*yāna-prajñapti*). Originally he was not a Buddha, yet we provisionally designate him as "Buddha" for his sake;
originally he was not *bodhi*, yet we provisionally designate for him *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, liberation, and so forth.

Knowing that he could not lift a load of one hundred *shi*, we first give him a load of one *sheng* or one *he*. Knowing that he finds it difficult to believe the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), we for now...

He teaches the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*). While these may cause wholesome dharmas to circulate and are superior to unwholesome dharmas, once the limit of the wholesome fruits is exhausted, the fruits of evil arrive.
When Buddhahood is attained, sentient beings arrive; when Nirvāṇa is attained, birth and death arrive.
When clarity is attained, darkness arrives; this is merely the overturning of the causes and effects of outflows (*sāsrava*). There is nothing that does not reciprocate.
If you wish to escape such matters of overturning, simply sever the two ends of the statement. Do not measure or calculate; do not concern yourself with them.
Be neither Buddha nor sentient being; neither intimate nor distant; neither high nor low; neither level nor uneven; neither going nor coming.
Yet, do not cling to words. Separated by these two extremes, you cannot be grasped. You are free from the mutual conditioning of suffering and pleasure;
you are free from the reciprocal response of light and darkness. True principle is neither truly real nor unreal; it is neither false nor non-false.

It is not a thing subject to measurement or calculation; it is like empty space, which cannot be cultivated or contrived. If the mind harbors even the slightest conceptual interpretation, it is immediately caught within the realm of measurement.
They are frequently constrained, much like the omens of the hexagrams. Being constrained by metal, wood, water, fire, and earth is like being stuck with sticky glue;

when all five points are adhered, the Demon King seizes them and carries them home at will. Generally, the words of instruction consist of three successive parts that are good in the beginning, middle, and end.

First, one must directly cause them to give rise to a virtuous mind. Second, one breaks their attachment to that virtuous mind. Finally, one clarifies what is truly good. This is the Bodhi [teaching].
A bodhisattva is not a bodhisattva; this is what is called a "bodhisattva. Dharma is non-dharma, and it is not the present dharma. This is the total *yamaka* (twofold) [teaching].

If one were to utter only a single phrase, it would cause sentient beings to enter hell; if one were to utter all three phrases at once, they would enter hell themselves—it does not concern the task of the Teacher.
To say that present discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is one's own Buddha is the "initial goodness" (*ādau kalyāṇam*). It is not.
Maintaining the present discernment is "good in the beginning. Not forming any conceptual understanding of this maintenance is "good in the end.
This is as previously mentioned regarding the Buddha after Ratnaprabhāsa: he is neither extraordinary nor holy. Do not mistakenly say that the Buddha is now neither ordinary nor holy.
The First Patriarch of this land said: "Being without ability and without holiness is the holiness of the Buddha. If one says the Buddha is holy, [it is a misconception].
As for spirits of the nine grades, such as those among dragons and beasts, as well as Śakra and Brahmā, they are all capable of supernatural transformations.
Even spirits of the highest grade can know events from the past and present across hundreds of kalpas; how could they possibly be Buddhas?

For instance, when the King of the Asuras, whose body was immense—equaling twice the size of Mount Sumeru—fought with Śakra, he realized his strength was insufficient and led a hundred... [thousand] [soldiers].
Ten thousand soldiers enter and hide within the fibers of a lotus root; their transformative eloquence is not slight. Furthermore, these are not Buddhist terms;
their gradations are relaxed and expansive, and their ascents and descents differ. When one has not yet awakened or attained understanding, it is called greed and anger;
once awakened, it is termed the Buddha-wisdom. Thus it is said: "It is not a different person from before; it is only that the place of one's conduct has changed."
Question: "Is there a karmic retribution for cutting grass, felling trees, digging the earth, or breaking ground? The Master said:
"One cannot definitively say there is retribution, nor can one definitively say there is no retribution. Whether there is retribution or not depends on the person themselves.
If one is greedily attached to all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—and possesses a mind of grasping and rejecting, such a person has not yet passed through the three phrases."
If one definitively says there is sin, yet the mind transcends these three propositions and is like empty space—even then, do not form the conception of "empty space.
Such a person may definitively be said to be without sin. Furthermore, it is said: "If a sin has been committed, to claim that one does not see the sin is impossible."
If one does not commit a transgression, yet the Way possesses transgression, such a thing is impossible.
As stated in the Vinaya, even when one fundamentally deludes another or causes them to kill each other in succession, one still incurs no guilt for murder;

how much less so in the Chan school’s lineage, where the mind is like empty space, not retaining a single thing and lacking even the characteristic of emptiness—where could a transgression be placed? This is also called the "Chan Way."
As for practice: simply do not allow defilement. It is also said that by merely melting away and refining both the surface and the interior until the mind is exhausted, one attains it.

It is also said that it concerns only the illumination of objects; right now, when illuminating all phenomena such as existence and non-existence, there is no grasping at all, nor should there be any attachment.
It is also said: "It is like polishing and studying together. Now, this is what is originally possessed; the defilements are adventitious.
When you hear it said that all existence consists of sounds and forms, regard them as if they were filthy grease; do not allow the mind to settle upon them at all.
Under the Bodhi tree, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics belong to form (*rūpa*); the twelvefold teachings belong to sound (*śabda*).
Right now, cut off the flow of all existence—sounds and forms—and let the mind be like empty space. This is what is meant by "conforming to and rubbing against" (*mārga*).
Study must be undertaken as if one’s head were on fire before it can be mastered. At the moment of death, one follows the old, familiar path; yet even there, one cannot reach the end.

When the time for rebirth arrives, one is still newly trained and just beginning to learn—how then could one possibly succeed? At the point of death, all habitual thoughts manifest as powerful objects of experience;
according to what the mind cherishes, that which is most weighty will first be experienced. Therefore, do not commit evil deeds even now.
At this time, there are no evil objects; even if there were evil objects, they would transform into good ones.
If you fear that at the moment of death you will become frantic and lose your self-mastery, you must attain mastery right now.
Simply by being free from all attachment to every object and phenomenon right now, and by not dwelling upon intellectual understanding, you are indeed free.
A person’s present life is the cause, and the moment of death is the fruit. Since the karmic fruit has already manifested, why fear it? Fear is a matter of past and present.
If there was a "past" in relation to the "present," there must likewise be a "present" in relation to the "past. If there were Buddhas in the past, there are Buddhas in the present as well.

If you attain realization now, you will continue to attain it until the very end of the future. It is simply this single thought-moment after thought-moment that is not obstructed by any existence or non-existence.
The Equal Dharma-pipe: from antiquity to the present, the Buddha is merely a person, and the person is merely the Buddha.
This is also the samādhi of concentration: one does not use concentration to enter concentration; one does not use dhyāna to contemplate dhyāna; one does not use the Buddha to seek the Buddha.

As it is said: "The Dharma does not seek the Dharma; the Dharma does not obtain the Dharma; the Dharma does not practice the Dharma; the Dharma does not see the Dharma. Spontaneously, one attains the Dharma."
One does not attain what has already been attained. Therefore, a bodhisattva should maintain right mindfulness of all phenomena in this way:

they exist in utter solitude, yet there is no phenomenon that exists in solitude. The nature of wisdom is suchness (*tathatā*); it is not something established by causes, and it is also termed the "knot of the essence."

It is also called the "Accumulation of Essence. It is not known by wisdom (*jñāna*), nor is it cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is a realm beyond thought and deliberation, where the essence of stillness is consummated and all calculation has forever perished.
It is like the great currents of the ocean being exhausted, so that waves no longer arise; it is also said to be like the waters of the great ocean.
When there are no rippling waves stirred by the wind, one suddenly perceives those very ripples; this is the coarse within the subtle.
When the perception of perception vanishes, it returns to being the subtle within the subtle—this is the realm of the Buddhas.

From this initial awareness, it is called the summit of samādhi, also known as the King of Samādhis, and also known as the wisdom of *jñeyāvaraṇa* (the obstruction to the knowable); it gives birth to all samādhis and bestows [realization] upon one.

He is honored by the crowns of all the Dharma-princes. Regarding all forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, as well as all Buddha-lands, he has attained equal and perfect enlightenment;

he penetrates both the internal and external without any obstruction whatsoever. A single form and a single atom, a single Buddha and a single form, all Buddhas and all forms, all atoms and all Buddhas—all forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are likewise thus.
It is so. Each one pervades all buddha-fields; this is the coarse within the subtle. This is a virtuous realm.
It is that which all those who stream upward perceive, hear, and see; it is also that from which all those who stream upward are born and die.
It transcends all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and is what is taught by those who stream upward. It is also the nirvana of those who stream upward; it is the unsurpassed path.
This is the peerless mantra; it is the foremost teaching. Among all teachings, it is the most profound, such that no one can reach its depths.

It is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas. Just as clear waves can reveal the clarity or turbidity, the depth, the currents, and the vast utility of all waters, so too is this protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, if one can act in this manner, I shall at that time manifest purity for them.
The body of pure radiance. Furthermore, it is said: "Just as your own [body], speech, and so forth are, mine are likewise.

The sounds of a single buddha-field, the fragrances of a single buddha-field, the tastes of a single buddha-field, the tactile sensations of a single buddha-field, and the phenomena of a single buddha-field—all are exactly thus."
From here upward to the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), the vertical and horizontal dimensions are all likewise.

If one clings to this initial cognition as the ultimate understanding, it is called the "summit-knot" (*mūrdha-granthi*), also known as the "falling summit-knot. This is the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

One’s own arising of knowledge and views binds oneself without a rope; because of what is known, one is fettered to the mundane world in twenty-five ways. Furthermore, it scatters all various afflictions.

The gate of affliction binds one to others; this is first understood. When the practitioners of the Two Vehicles perceive this, it is called *eryan-shi* (the consciousness of burning flame) and also termed "subtle affliction.

They immediately sever and eliminate it. Once it has been severed, they are said to have "turned their spirits to dwell in the empty cave," also called "being intoxicated by the wine of samādhi," and "being liberated from the bonds of Māra.
Regarding the formation and destruction of worlds, this is due to the power of meditative concentration.

Holding [this], one does not perceive at all that the outflows are heading toward other lands; this is also called the "fearful place of the deep pit of liberation," which Bodhisattvas keep far away from.
Now, when reading scriptures or examining the teachings, all words and phrases must be turned back and brought to oneself.
However, all verbal teachings merely clarify the self-nature of present-time awakening; it is simply that one must not be obstructed by anything.
The shifting of all realms of existence and non-existence—this is your guide. It is the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-prajñā*) that can illuminate and shatter all realms of existence and non-existence;

it possesses a state of sovereign independence. If you cannot attain realization through this, then even if you should recite the twelve Vedas, you will merely become a person of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); this is actually slandering the Buddha rather than practicing the Way. However...
To be detached from all sounds and forms, yet not to dwell in that detachment, nor to dwell in conceptual understanding—this is true cultivation.

To read scriptures and study the teachings may be considered a good thing according to worldly standards; however, when reckoned among those who clarify the ultimate principle, such people are merely obstructed.
Even those on the Ten Stages cannot escape this; they flow into the river of birth and death. This applies to all teachings of the Three Vehicles.
To treat the diseases of greed, anger, and so forth: if at this very moment, in every thought-moment, there are diseases such as greed or anger, you must first treat them.
You need not seek out meanings, phrases, or intellectual understanding; for such understanding belongs to greed, and now it has itself turned into a disease.

At this very moment, simply remain free from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and even free from that freedom itself. By passing beyond these three propositions, you will naturally become one with the Buddha.

There is no difference. Since you are yourself a Buddha, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your speech? I only fear that you are not a Buddha, being bound by the dharmas of existence and non-existence and thus unable to attain freedom.
Therefore, before the Principle is established, one must first possess merit and wisdom; it is by being carried by merit and wisdom that [liberation is achieved].

Whether one is lowly or noble, it is not as good as first establishing the principle; subsequently, one will possess merit and wisdom. If you desire merit and wisdom, they can be achieved at any time:
one can gather gold and turn it into earth, or gather earth and turn it into gold; one can transform the waters of the ocean into ghee and curd, or crush Mount Sumeru into fine dust;
one can draw the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore, and manifest immeasurable meanings from a single meaning, or [manifest a single meaning] from the immeasurable...

The meaning is made into a single point. It is also said that one who "loses his footing" becomes a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), causing the people of the four continents to practice the ten wholesome deeds for a single day;
yet even this merit and wisdom cannot be calculated. That which reflects and awakens within oneself is called the King (Rāja).

To conceptually dwell upon and become attached to phenomena as being existent or non-existent is called being a Wheel-Turning King. But right now, within the inner depths of one's own being, one does not admit any existence or non-existence whatsoever.
These dharmas, being beyond the four propositions, are called "emptiness" and are now termed the "immortal medicine. It is not that this so-called immortal medicine was summoned from a former king;
although it is called the immortal medicine, when taken together with the king, it is neither two distinct things nor a single thing.

If one were to interpret it as being either one or two, one would still be called a wheel-turning monarch. It is just as when someone today uses the four requisites of merit and wisdom to make offerings.
For eighty full years, throughout four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds and the six destinies and four modes of birth, [the donor] acts according to their wishes.
Thereafter, he reflects: "Now these sentient beings have all grown old;
I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma, enabling them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to the path of *arhat*. Thus, O donor, merely...

The merit of bestowing all articles of happiness upon sentient beings is already immeasurable; how much more so is the merit of causing them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to and including the path of an *arhat*, which is limitless and boundless.

Yet, this does not equal the merit of the fiftieth person who rejoices upon hearing the sutra. The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: "Queen Māyā gave birth to five hundred princes, all of whom..."
They attained the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood and all entered parinirvāṇa; stupas were erected for each to offer worship, and they prostrated before every one, exclaiming:
"It would not have been as good as having given birth to a single son who attains unsurpassed bodhi.
To reflect upon my own mental power, even if there were but one person among hundreds of thousands of millions who attains it, its value would equal that of a trichiliocosm. This is why—"

I constantly exhort all people: you must have a profound understanding of your own nature. If your understanding of your own nature is profound, it will enable you to attain merit and wisdom—just as a noble person employs the lowly, or like a carriage that does not abide in one place. If you maintain this as your understanding, it is called the pearl within the topknot;

it is also called a precious jewel of value, yet it is also called a dung-carrier. If you do not maintain this as your understanding, it is like giving the king’s bright pearl from his topknot to him.

It is also called the priceless great jewel; it is also called "carrying out the excrement. The Buddha is originally one who stands outside the realm of entanglement, yet he comes within that realm to manifest as a Buddha for us.
He is truly one who belongs to the other shore of birth and death; he is truly one who is transcendent and remote from this side, yet he comes to this shore to manifest as a Buddha for us.
Both humans and monkeys are unable to travel there. Humans are a metaphor for those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Bodhisattva, the analogy of the monkey refers to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Reading the scriptures and examining the teachings to seek all-encompassing knowledge and understanding is not categorically forbidden.
One may understand the teachings of the Three Vehicles, skillfully obtain the ornaments of the *ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (the *Hīnayanālaṃkāra*), and find the cave-dwelling of the thirty-two marks.

Yet, though one seeks the Buddha, one does not find him; for the teaching states that those who indulge in and are attached to the study of the Tripitaka of the Lesser Vehicle are still not permitted [to attain it].
If one would not even associate with them, how much less would one do so for oneself? Such precept-breaking bhikṣus are "bhikṣus in name only" and "arhats in name only.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they are classified among the sixteen types of evil practitioners; they are the same as hunters and fishermen who kill and harm others for the sake of profit and sustenance.
The Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras are like ambrosia, yet they are also like poison. If one can digest them, they are like ambrosia; if one cannot digest them, they are like poison.

When reading the scriptures and examining the teachings, if you do not understand the discourse on birth and death, and certainly cannot penetrate their meaning and phrasing, do not read them as the foremost priority.
It is also said that one must examine the teachings, but one must also consult with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). First...

First, one must possess one's own eyes; only then can one discern the discourse on the birth and death of others. If one cannot discern the white [the pure], one will certainly fail to penetrate through it;
it would merely serve to further increase the shackles of the bhikṣu. Therefore, those who teach the profound essence (xuánzhǐ) are not sent to read written texts.
As it is said: "Speak of the substance, do not speak of appearances; speak of the meaning, do not speak of words. To speak in this manner is called [the true teaching].
This is the true teaching. If one speaks in terms of words and letters, it is all slander; this is called false teaching. When a Bodhisattva speaks, they should speak in accordance with the Dharma;
this is also called the true teaching. They should cause sentient beings to uphold the mind rather than the phenomena, and to uphold practice rather than the teachings.
To speak of persons without speaking of characters, and to speak of meaning without speaking of words—this is the speech of one who possesses but a single eye.

Since it is said that there is no dhyāna in the desire realm, by what means can one reach the form realm? First, by practicing two kinds of meditative concentration on the ground of causes, one subsequently attains the first dhyāna:

the attainment of cessation with perception (saṃjñā-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation without perception (asaṃjñā-samāpatti). Through the attainment of cessation with perception, one is born [in the form realm].

The heavens of the four dhyānas and so forth in the form realm, the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), and the heavens of the four emptinesses and so forth born in the formless realm all possess dhyāna.
It is evident that the desire realm lacks dhyāna; dhyāna belongs to the form realm.
Question: As it is said that there is Chan (meditation) in this land, how is it so? The Master said: "Neither moving nor practicing Chan—this is the Tathāgata’s Chan;
it is free from the conceptualization of Chan."
Question: What is meant by "sentient beings lack Buddha-nature, while insentient things possess Buddha-nature"?
The Master said: From humans up to Buddhas is the attachment of the sacred mind; from humans down to the hells is the attachment of the ordinary mind.

If, at this very moment, one harbors a mind of defiled attachment toward either of these two realms—the ordinary or the sacred—this is called "sentient beings lacking Buddha-nature. If, at this very moment, one merely [remains within] the ordinary...

Regarding the two objects of the sages and all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, there is no mind of grasping or rejecting, nor is there any present cognition or understanding of grasping or rejecting;
this is called "insentient things possessing Buddha-nature. It is simply because they lack emotional attachments that they are called "insentient"; they are not like wood, stone, or empty space.

To take the insentience of yellow flowers and green bamboos as being "possessing Buddha-nature"—if one says it exists— [This passage concludes with a critique of the conceptualization of insentient things as having Buddha-nature.]

Why is it that in the sutras we do not see those who attain Buddhahood without receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)? It is simply because our present mirror-like awareness does not break through the sentient being’s state of transformation;
it is like a verdant bamboo—there is nothing that does not respond to conditions, and there is nothing that does not know the proper time, like a yellow flower.
Furthermore, it is said: "If one has ascended the steps of the Buddha, even insentient things possess Buddha-nature; if one has not yet ascended the steps of the Buddha," [insentient things do not].
"Sentient beings have no Buddha-nature. Question:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten *kalpas*, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
How is this so? The Master said: "'*Kalpa*' means stagnation; it also refers to the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*). Dwelling in a single good [state], one stagnates within the ten."

"Good. In the Western Land [India], it is called "Buddha"; in this land [China], it is called "Awakening. It is the self-reflexive awakening. To become attached to goodness is for those with good roots to lack Buddha-nature;

therefore, it is said that the Buddha-dharma does not manifest before them, and they cannot attain the path of Buddhahood. To encounter evil and dwell in evil is called the awakening of sentient beings;

to encounter good and dwell in good is called the awakening of the śrāvakas. Not dwelling in the two extremes of good and evil, and not relying on or abiding in them—[this is the awakening of the Bodhisattvas].
To act in this manner is called the awakening of the two vehicles, and it is also called the awakening of the pratyekabuddha.

To refrain from relying on or dwelling in either of the two extremes of good and evil, yet also not forming a conceptual understanding of such non-reliance, is called the awakening of the bodhisattva.

When one neither relies nor dwells [in anything], and furthermore does not form a conceptual understanding of "non-reliance," only then can it be called the awakening of the Buddha. As it is said: "The Buddha does not dwell in Buddhahood; this is called the True."
This is a field of merit. If, among ten million people, there should suddenly be one person who attains it, they are called a priceless jewel.
They are able to act as a guide in all places: where there is no Buddha, they proclaim themselves to be the Buddha; where there is no Dharma, they proclaim themselves to be the Dharma;
where there is no Sangha, they proclaim themselves to be the Sangha. This is called turning the Great Wheel of the Dharma.
Question: From the ancestral patriarchs above, there have been secret words transmitted one to another.
How is this? The Master said: There are no secret words. The Tathāgata has no hidden treasury (*guhyakośa*). It is simply the present mirror-like awareness;

when speech is clear, form and characteristics cannot be found at all—this is the "secret word. From the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, right through to the tenth ground (*bhūmi*), it exists only as...
Words and phrases are entirely the dust and dross of the Dharma. Wherever there are words and phrases, they are all subsumed within the realm of afflictions.

Wherever there are words and phrases, they are all of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Wherever there are words and phrases, they are all unacceptable; they are all contrary to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
What further "esoteric language" could there be to seek?
Question: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. How is this so? The Master said: "Emptiness is a metaphor for the bubble;

the sea is a metaphor for the nature (nature). One's own numinous, awakened nature exceeds even empty space; therefore it is said that emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea."
Question: "It is said, 'Clear away the forest, but do not cut down the trees. What does this mean? The Master replied: "The forest is a metaphor for the mind; the trees are a metaphor for the body.
Because one speaks of clearing the forest, fear arises; therefore it is said, 'Clear away the forest, but do not cut down the trees.'"

Question: "Speech is like a target that draws an arrow; one who returns to the target cannot avoid suffering. Now, since the entanglements are identical for both, how can one distinguish between the monastic and the lay?
The Master said: "It is simply a matter of discharging the arrow. If it meets its mark along the way, there will surely be injury.

Seeking an echo in a valley, though one may do so for kalpas, the form remains invisible. The echo is already at the edge of the mouth; whether there is gain or loss depends on the question you have come to ask."
Yet when asked where they were returning to, they were still struck by the arrow. It is also like knowing that an illusion is not [ultimately] an illusion. The Third Patriarch said:

"Not recognizing the profound principle, one's efforts at contemplating stillness are in vain. He also said: "To take objects as the vision is like holding up bricks and pebbles; what can you possibly do with them?"
If you say you do not see them, how are wood and stone any different? Therefore, both seeing and not seeing involve error. This one example serves as an illustration for all others. Question:
If there are no afflictions (*kleśa*), how is it that the thirty-two marks are present now? Master: This concerns the Buddha’s side of affairs.
If there were originally afflictions and the thirty-two marks were present now, they would simply be the ordinary sentiments of the present moment. Question: No.
[The questioner] asks: "How is it that one does not see the Tathāgata’s mark of the crown? The Master says: "It is because one forms views of finitude or views of infinitude;

for this reason, one does not see the Tathāgata’s mark of the crown. Only when, right now, there are no views whatsoever regarding existence or non-existence, and even no view of 'non-viewing,' is it called the manifestation of the mark of the crown."
Question: "Nowadays, all śramaṇas claim, 'I rely on the Buddha's teachings; I have studied a sutra, a śāstra, a dhyāna, a vinaya, and possess some knowledge and understanding.
Is it appropriate for them to receive the fourfold offerings of the *dānapati*? The Master said:

"It simply depends on their present capacity for illumination and function regarding every sound, every form, every fragrance, and every flavor—within all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent."
Upon each and every object, there is not even a speck of dust of grasping or defilement.
Nor does one dwell upon the absence of grasping or defilement, nor is there any conceptual understanding of "not dwelling. Such a person could even digest ten thousand taels of gold daily.
Right now, as you illuminate all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—you must scrub away and sever all craving at the gates of the six sense faculties. Is there even a speck...?

Even if one polishes it with a hair-tip, it will not be removed. Even if one begs from a donor for a single grain of rice or a single thread of silk, every one of them must wear fur and horns, pulling plows and bearing heavy loads; only then can they repay their debt. This is because they do not rely on the Buddha.

The Buddha is one who is without attachment, one who seeks nothing, and one who relies on nothing. Now, you are all busily and greedily seeking the Buddha; you have turned your backs on him entirely. Therefore, it is said:
Having long attended upon the Buddha, they did not recognize the Buddha-nature; they merely perceived the Savior as one who wanders within the six realms of rebirth.

Only after a long time do they behold the Buddha, for whom it is said that a Buddha is difficult to encounter. Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of the seven Buddhas, and is also called the foremost Bodhisattva in this Sahā world.
Yet, without cause, he formed the perception of seeing the Buddha and the perception of hearing the Dharma, and was thereby [afflicted].
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he even brought down the two Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*). It was not that he did not understand;
rather, he specifically provided a standard for all students, so that future learners would not harbor such views or reports.

Simply by being free from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, as well as views of existence and non-existence, and by passing each and every one beyond the three propositions, this is called "acting according to one's will" (*yathākāmam*).
“O Jewel, this is called the ‘Jewel Flower Supporting the Feet. If one forms views of a Buddha or views of dharmas, these are merely views of existence, non-existence, and so forth;
they are called ‘cataracts of the eye’ because one sees what is seen. They are also called the ‘entanglements of view,’ the ‘obstructions of view,’ and the ‘tumors of view.’”

Now, regarding every thought-moment and all that is seen, heard, sensed, and known, once all defilements have been completely eliminated, every single particle of dust and every single form is entirely one Buddha. When a single thought arises, it is entirely two Buddhas.

As for the three periods of time and the five aggregates, who can know the number of their thought-moments? This is called Buddhas filling and obstructing empty space; this is called the Buddhas of manifested bodies.

This is called the manifestation of the jeweled stupa. For this reason, he constantly sighed, saying: "Alas! Behold today’s life upon which I depend—relying on a single grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable.
At mealtime, I cannot eat and die of hunger; I cannot find water and die of thirst; I cannot find fire and die of cold.
Lacking even one day [of food] I do not live; lacking even one day [of food] I do not die. Held fast by the four great elements, it is not as good as before."
The realized one enters fire without being burned and enters water without being drowned; yet if they wish to be burned, they are burned, and if they wish to drown, they drown.
They may live when they wish to live and die when they wish to die, moving and abiding with complete freedom. Such a person possesses this portion of sovereignty.

If the mind is not distracted, there is no need to seek a Buddha, nor to seek Bodhi or Nirvana. If one clings to seeking a Buddha, that belongs to greed; once greed has arisen, it turns into [suffering].
Because of this illness, it is said that "the Buddha's illness is the most difficult to cure. Only those who slander the Buddha and slander the Dharma may take this food.
As for "food," it refers to the food of one's own numinous, awakened nature—the untainted meal, the food of liberation. These words treat the illnesses of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages;
they range from the first stage through the tenth. If, even now, one possesses any mind of seeking at all, one is entirely termed a monk who has broken the precepts.
Those who are merely called "Arhats" by name are all like jackals; it is evident that they cannot digest the offerings made to them.

It is only those who now hear sounds as echoes and smell fragrances as the wind, who are free from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, yet do not dwell even in that freedom, and possess no conceptual understanding of relying or not relying—such a person cannot be burdened by any defilements of sin. This is because they seek...
Even seeking unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa is called "leaving home" [only] because it is still a perverse aspiration;

how much more so is the case of engaging in worldly disputes to seek victory and defeat, claiming "I am capable" and "I understand," coveting a single group of followers, cherishing a single disciple, or being attached to a single dwelling place?
To form a bond with a single patron—relying on them for one robe and one meal, seeking their fame and profit—is to deceive oneself.
To claim, "I have attained all-encompassing non-obstruction," is likewise mere self-deception.

If, even now, you cannot act as the master over your own five aggregates, such that when others cut and dismember you limb by limb, you feel no resentment or stinginess and remain free from affliction—even toward your own younger brother—[then how can you claim such realization]?
Suppose you were whipped by another person, from head to foot; regarding all such matters as these, you do not give rise to even a single thought of "self" or "other.
Yet, you still rely on this state and do not realize that even this single thought is to be regarded as [delusion]. This is called the defilement of dharma-dust (*dharmarajaḥ*).

Even those at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) cannot shed it; they flow into the river of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). For this reason, I constantly exhort all people: you must fear the afflictions of dharma-dust.
If one regards afflictions with the same dread as the three miserable realms, one possesses the portion of independent liberation.

Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvana, one would not give rise to even the slightest thought of cherishing it. Such a person is a Buddha at every step, without needing to tread upon lotus flowers.

Distributing [the teachings] among the hundred officials: if at this very moment one harbors even a hair’s breadth of attachment toward any phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, then even if one treads upon lotus flowers, it is no different from acting as a demon.

If one clings to the notions that one is inherently pure, inherently liberated, oneself being the Buddha, or oneself being the Chan Way and its realization, then one belongs to the naturalistic heretics (*svabhāva-vāda*). If one clings to the idea that [enlightenment] is accomplished through causes and conditions and realized through cultivation...

To assert "existence" belongs to the non-Buddhist schools that cling to causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). To assert "existence" [in an absolute sense] belongs to the non-Buddhist schools of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

To assert "non-existence" belongs to the non-Buddhist schools of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). To assert "both existence and non-existence" belongs to the non-Buddhist schools of extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). To assert "neither existence nor non-existence" [belongs to the same].

This belongs to the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and they are also called the deluded non-Buddhists. Simply put, at this very moment, do not form views such as those of Buddhahood or nirvāṇa.
When there are no views whatsoever regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth, nor even the view of non-existence, it is called right view.

When there is no hearing of anything whatsoever, nor even the hearing of non-hearing, it is called right hearing. This is what is meant by "subduing the non-Buddhists" and being free from the demons of ordinary beings.

It comes; it is a great divine mantra. There is no coming of the māras of the two vehicles. It is a great illuminating mantra. There is no coming of the māras of the bodhisattvas. It is the unsurpassed mantra.
Furthermore, there is not even the coming of the Buddha-māra. It is the mantra of the unequaled with the unequaled. First, it transforms the sycophantic and crooked asuras of ordinary beings;
second, it transforms the sycophantic and crooked asuras of the two vehicles; third, it transforms the sycophantic and crooked asuras of the bodhisattvas. This is it.

The threefold transformation of the pure land refers to all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, mundane or sacred—which are like gold ore. One’s own mind, when accorded with reality, is like the gold itself.

Just as gold and ore are distinct and can be separated so that the pure gold is revealed, it is as if someone seeking money or treasure suddenly transforms the gold into coins to give to them. Likewise, the essence of flour is authentic and free from any grit or saline soil.
When someone asked for *cāpā* (a type of parched grain), he transformed flour into *cāpā* and gave it to him. This was like a wise minister who skillfully understood the king’s intention:
when the king went out on a journey and asked for *saindhava*, he immediately presented a horse; when the king was eating and asked for *saindhava*, he immediately presented salt.

Those who study these profound principles through such metaphors are well able to penetrate them and respond to circumstances without fail; they are also called the "Six Extraordinary Lions. Master Zhigong said:
"They manifest a hundred transformations according to the needs of beings. A Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages is neither hungry nor satiated;
entering water he is not drowned, and entering fire he is not burned. Even if one wishes to burn him, it is impossible to do so. He cannot be measured or constrained by calculations."
The Buddha is not like this. Entering fire, he is not burned; if he wishes to be burned, he is burned; if he wishes to drown, he drowns.
He exercises mastery over the four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind. All forms are the Buddha’s form; all sounds are the Buddha’s sound.
Having exhausted all impurities and the heart of flattery and crookedness, and having passed beyond the three propositions, one may speak these words. Thus is the purity of the Bodhisattva.

Disciple, you have understood clearly. Regarding all speech and expression, do not cling to them as being non-existent. As for all illuminating functions, do not restrict them as being either pure or turbid.
To take medicine when one is ill is the act of a fool; to take medicine when one is not ill is the act of a Śrāvaka. Both involve fixed attachment to a single dharma.
One who is fixed in their nature is called a śrāvaka of fixed lineage; one who is exclusively devoted to extensive learning is called a śrāvaka of overweening pride;

one who knows others is called a śrāvaka still in training (śaikṣa); and one who is submerged in emptiness, stalled in quiescence, and possesses self-knowledge is called a śrāvaka beyond training (aśaikṣa). Greed, hatred, delusion, and the like are poisons.

The twelvefold division of the teachings is medicine. If the poison has not yet been eliminated, the medicine cannot be discarded. To take medicine when one is not ill causes the medicine to turn into illness;
if the illness departs but the medicine does not dissolve, it remains. "Neither arising nor ceasing" is the meaning of impermanence.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: there are three evil desires: first, the desire to be surrounded by the fourfold assembly; second, the desire for all people to become one's disciples; third...
Desiring that all people know me to be a sage and an arhat. Furthermore, the *Kāśyapa Sūtra* states: first, desiring to see future Buddhas;
second, desiring to become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); third, desiring to be born into a great kṣatriya clan;
fourth, desiring to be born into a great brāhmaṇa clan; and even up to: weary of birth and death, seeking nirvāṇa. Such are evil desires. First...
You must sever it. At this very moment, any grasping, defiled mind, or movement of thought is entirely termed "evil desire" (pāpakāma) and belongs wholly to the six heavens of the desire realm;
it is all under the jurisdiction of Pāpīyān.
Question: "For twenty years you constantly ordered him to remove excrement. What does this mean? The Master said: "Simply cease all views of existence and non-existence;
simply cease all greedy seeking. To have each and every one pass beyond the three propositions—this is called 'removing excrement.
As for now seeking the Buddha, seeking Bodhi, or seeking all dharmas such as existence and non-existence—this is called 'carrying away excrement.'"

It is called "carrying out excrement. It is simply seeing as a Buddha and understanding as a Buddha right now. Whatever is seen, whatever is sought, and whatever is clung to—all of these are termed the excrement of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
They are also called coarse speech and dead words. As the saying goes: "The great ocean does not harbor a corpse. Idle talk is not called conceptual proliferation;
it is the discriminating discussion of the clear and the turbid that is called conceptual proliferation. Thus says the scriptural text.

There are altogether twenty-one kinds of emptiness. To sift through and eliminate the defilements and burdens of sentient beings—observing the fasts and precepts as a śramaṇa, practicing patience and gentleness, and cultivating kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity—is the ordinary rule of the monastic community.

If you understand it thus, you will perfectly accord with the Buddha’s teaching; the only thing forbidden is greed, attachment, and clinging. This applies even to the hope of attaining Buddhahood or Bodhi.
The Dharma is like touching fire with one's hand. Mañjuśrī said: "If you give rise to the view of a Buddha or the view of the Dharma, you should harm yourself.
This is why Mañjuśrī brandished a sword at Gautama, and Aṅgulimāla held a blade against the Śākyas.

As it is said, a Bodhisattva may commit the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) yet not enter the Avīci Hell; this is because he possesses the profound penetration of the immediate, which is not shared by ordinary sentient beings.
From the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution to Māra and even unto the Buddha, all are but defilements; there is not even a hair’s breadth of attachment or clinging.

This is what is called the path of the Two Vehicles. How much more so for those who engage in contentious debate to seek victory or defeat, saying "I am able" or "I understand"—these are merely called monks of contentious debate, not monks of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Now, simply do not greedily cling to any existence or non-existence.

Dharma is called non-arising; it is called right faith. To have faith that clings to all dharmas is called incomplete faith, or imperfect faith, or biased and incomplete faith; therefore, one is called an icchantika.

If you now wish to attain direct awakening and understanding, you must simply cause both person and dharma to subside, both person and dharma to be severed, and both person and dharma to be empty, thereby penetrating beyond the three propositions. This is it.

The name does not fall into any numerical category. "Person" refers to faith; "Dharma" refers to precepts, giving, hearing, wisdom, and so forth. Through patience, a bodhisattva does not become a Buddha; through patience, one does not become a sentient being;
through patience, one does not uphold the precepts; through patience, one does not break the precepts. Therefore, it is said that there is neither upholding nor violating.

When wisdom is turbid, it illuminates the pure; when insight is pure, it discerns the turbid. In the Buddha, this is called illuminating insight (*prajñā*); in the bodhisattva, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*).

In relation to the two vehicles and sentient beings, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*) and is also called affliction (*kleśa*). In relation to the Buddha, it is called the cause within the fruit; in relation to sentient beings, it is called the fruit within the cause.
In relation to the Buddha, it is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*); in relation to sentient beings, it is called the wheel of Dharma turning.

In relation to the Bodhisattva, it is called the ornaments of a necklace; in relation to sentient beings, it is called the thicket of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). In relation to the Buddha...
This is termed "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). It is the ignorance that is itself luminosity; therefore, it is said that ignorance constitutes the essence of the Path.
This is not the same as the ignorance that obscures sentient beings. That [latter] is the object, while this [former] is the subject. That is what is heard, while this is the hearing.

They are neither identical nor different; neither interrupted nor eternal; neither coming nor going. These are words of arising; these are words that transcend the tracks [of conventional discourse]. They are not...
Brightness is not darkness. There is neither Buddha nor sentient being; it is all thus. Coming and going, annihilation and permanence, Buddha and sentient beings—these are dead words.
Pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, sameness and difference, annihilation and permanence, and so forth, are the doctrines of the heterodox.
Prajñāpāramitā is one's own Buddha-nature; it is also called Mahāyāna. *Mahā* has the meaning of "great," and *yāna* has the meaning of "vehicle. If...
To maintain one's own awareness is itself to become a naturalist heretic; there is no need to maintain it. To discern and awaken as you do now is sufficient;
there is no need to seek a Buddha elsewhere. If you were to seek it elsewhere, you would again belong to the category of causal heretics.

The First Patriarch of this land said: "If the mind holds something as right, it must hold something as wrong. If you prize one thing, you will be deluded by that one thing; if you value one thing, [you will be bound by it]."
Thus, one is deluded by a single thing: belief is deluded by belief, and non-belief likewise becomes slander. There is nothing to be esteemed and nothing not to be esteemed;
there is neither belief nor non-belief. Even the Buddha is not "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta); yet, though he is not unconditioned, he is also not a dark, silent void.

It is like empty space. The Buddha is a being of great mind who possesses abundant discernment; though his discernment is abundant, that discernment is pure. The demons of greed and hatred cannot seize him.

The Buddha is one who stands outside of the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), without even a hair’s breadth of craving or grasping, yet without the conceptual understanding of "no-craving or no-grasping.
This is called being fully endowed with the six perfections and the myriad practices. If one wishes for the ornaments of adornment, one must plant [the seeds].

All seeds are present; as with what is not required, others do not use them, yet they are not lost. When others cause one to attain mastery over the fruits of cause, merit, and wisdom—that is true cultivation.
It is not a matter of toiling in labor or bearing heavy burdens that is called cultivation; yet it is not otherwise. The three bodies are one essence.
As for the three bodies: first is the Dharmakāya, the Buddha of True Reality. The Dharmakāya Buddha is neither bright nor dark; brightness and darkness...
It belongs to the realm of illusion and transformation. The true mark (*dharmatā*) derives its name from being contrasted with the unreal; fundamentally, it is devoid of all names and designations.

As it is said, "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical categories. Such expressions as "offering a canopy upon attaining Buddhahood" are merely conventional metaphors used for the sake of measurement and comparison.
They derive their meaning only by distinguishing purity from turbidity. Therefore, it is called the "Dharmakāya Buddha of the True Mark," which is the name for the Pure Dharmakāya, Vairocana.
The Buddha is also called the Buddha of the Dharmakāya of Space; he is also called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*); he is also called the Eighth Consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*);

he is also called the School of Nature (*svabhāva-nikāya*); he is also called the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-nikāya*); he is also called the Buddha dwelling in a land that is neither impure nor defiled;

he is also called the Lion in the Cave; he is also called the Subsequently Attained Wisdom of the Vajra; he is also called the Stainless Charity (*vimala-dāna*); and he is also called the Ultimate Emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
It is also called the "Profound Principle" (*xuanzhi*). The Third Patriarch said: "If one does not recognize the profound principle, one's efforts at contemplating stillness are in vain.

The second is the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*), the Buddha beneath the Bodhi tree. He is also called the Illusory Transformation Buddha, the Buddha of Marks and Features, and the Response Body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*).
This is named the Perfect Reward Body Vairocana Buddha. He is also called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) and is also named the Seventh Consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).
He is also called the Buddha who Recompenses Causes and Answers Effects. He is identical in number to the fifty-two stages of *dhyāna*.

He is identical to the *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and identical to all *bodhisattvas* and others. He equally undergoes the suffering of birth and extinction, yet he does not share the suffering of sentient beings bound by karma.
Third, as for the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha: even now, regarding all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—he is entirely free from attachment and defilement. Furthermore...
It is without non-existence or defilement, transcending the four propositions. All verbal expressions and eloquence are called the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha.
This is named the Śākyamuni Buddha of a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million emanations; he is also named the Great Miraculous Transformation, and also named the Playful Supernatural Power.
It is also called the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and it is also called the sixth consciousness. As for the one who makes offerings: they purify the three karmas.
In the past limit, there are no afflictions to be severed; in the middle limit, there is no self-nature to be maintained; in the future limit, there is no Buddha to be realized.
These are the severances of the three limits, the purity of the three karmas, the emptiness of the three wheels, and the emptiness of the three *dānas*. How does a bhikṣu serve?
Regarding the Buddha, that which is called "the non-outflowing of the six sense faculties" is also termed an adornment. It is adorned by the forest trees of emptiness and the absence of all outflows;

it is adorned by the flowers and fruits of emptiness and the absence of all defilements. Although the Buddha-eye is empty and non-existent, the Dharma-eye distinguishes between the clear and the turbid for the sake of practitioners, yet it does not even produce the conceptual understanding of distinguishing between the clear and the turbid. This is what is meant by "even having no eyes. As the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says:
The Dharma-body cannot be sought through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. It is not seen by the fleshly eye, because it is formless.
It is not seen by the divine eye, because it is free from delusion. It is not seen by the wisdom eye, because it is devoid of characteristics.
It is not seen by the Dharma eye, because it is free from all conditioned activities. It is not seen by the Buddha eye, because it is free from all consciousnesses. If one does not [conceptualize]...

To see in this way is called the Buddha-view. That which is identical to form yet not form itself is called true form. That which is identical to emptiness yet not mere vacuity is called true emptiness.
Form and emptiness are also expressions of the mutual treatment of medicine and disease. As the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* says: "One cannot say it is identical to form or not identical to form;
nor can one say it is identical to emptiness or not identical to emptiness. This applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
To encompass all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, is called "entering the seventh stage. Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage do not regress.
For Bodhisattvas of the three stages above the seventh, the mind-ground is so clear that it is easily defiled; if one speaks of fire, they are immediately burned.
From the Form Realm upward, giving is a sickness and stinginess is the medicine. From the Form Realm downward, stinginess is a sickness and giving is the medicine.
Generosity is this medicine. As for the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*), it severs the worldly dharmas; yet, there is no fault in merely not performing [actions] with one's own body or hands.

This unmanifest precept is also called the non-indicative precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) and the untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*). However, if one merely raises a thought or stirs a conceptualization, it is entirely termed breaking the precepts.
It is simply that, at present, one is not deluded or disturbed by any objects of existence or non-existence, nor does one rely upon or dwell in them.
It is not deluded; nor is there any cognition or understanding that does not rely upon it. This is called universal study. This is called diligent mindfulness. This is called wide dissemination.
When one has not yet awakened or understood, it is called the mother; when one has awakened and realized, it is called the child.

Furthermore, there is no absence of awakening, understanding, cognition, or comprehension—this is called the simultaneous loss of both mother and child. There is no entanglement of goodness, no entanglement of evil, no entanglement of Buddha, and no entanglement of sentient beings.

The fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are likewise measured by their number, up until there is a total absence of all measurable fetters; therefore it is said: "The Buddha is one who has transcended the fetters and surpassed all measure.

Regarding the understanding of the meaning of words through craving and attachment, it is like a mother’s love for her child: she gives the child much ghee to eat, yet she knows nothing at all of whether it is digested or not.
This statement is a metaphor for the afflictions of those who have attained the honor and nobility of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). It arises...

The afflictions of the meditative bliss of the form realm and formless realm; the affliction of not attaining mastery over supernormal powers—such as flying, ascending, becoming invisible, or manifesting—and being unable to travel everywhere to the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions to hear the Dharma; the affliction of practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
the affliction of studying emptiness, equality, and the Middle Way; and the affliction of studying the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.

Afflictions. The afflictions of one who studies with the mind of the Mahāyāna and gives rise to the Four Great Vows. The afflictions of clear understanding on the first, second, third, and fourth stages (*bhūmi*).

The afflictions of various knowledges and views on the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages. The afflictions of the Bodhisattvas of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages who simultaneously illuminate the two truths.
And so on, up to the study of the Buddha-fruit, including the myriad [afflictions] of hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Regarding the practice of afflictions: one understands the meaning and phrasing of greed alone, yet does not realize that it is actually a binding affliction;

therefore, it is said that "the river of views can sweep away even the fragrant elephant. Question: Is it seen? Answer: It is seen. Question: What is it like after it is seen? Answer: Seeing is non-dual.
Since it is said that seeing is non-dual, one does not use seeing to see seeing. If there were seeing upon further seeing, [it would be dualistic].
Is it the prior seeing that is this? Or is it the subsequent seeing that is this? As it is said: "When one sees the seeing, that seeing is not seeing;

seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. Therefore, one does not practice the dharma of seeing, one does not practice the dharma of hearing, and one does not practice the dharma of cognition.

The Buddhas swiftly bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). An objection is raised: "Since 'seeing' is not itself the words of the prediction, what further use is there for a prediction? The Master says:
"One who first awakens to the fundamental principle is not constrained by any phenomena of existence or non-existence.

It is like washing a soiled garment; therefore, it is said that being free from characteristics is called Buddhahood. When both the void and the real are entirely absent, the central meaning alone remains profound. Profoundly realizing this oneness—"
The path is the same. Those who follow later accord with its stages; thus it is called "bestowing a prediction" (vyākaraṇa).
Ignorance is the father, craving is the mother. One's own self is the illness; returning to heal one's own self is the medicine. One's own self is the blade;

returning to slay one's own parents—ignorance and craving—is why it is said: "Slaying the father and harming the mother. A single phrase of this kind shatters all dharmas. To consume what is not [proper]...
As for "eating at the proper time," how could it be otherwise? At present, all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—are entirely instances of eating at the improper time;
they are also called "evil food" or "defiled food. To place such [food] in a precious vessel is a violation of the precepts, a form of false speech, and a "mixed meal.
The Buddha is one who seeks nothing; yet now you greedily seek after all dharmas, whether existent or non-existent.
However, all that has been done is contrary [to the truth] and is, in fact, slandering the Buddha. As long as there is greed and defilement, it is entirely called "reaching out the hand.

Now, if one simply does not have greed or defilement, and does not dwell upon that non-greed and non-defilement, and furthermore lacks even the conceptual understanding of such non-dwelling—this is called the fire of prajñā.
This is what burns the finger; this is what does not spare body or life; this is the severing of limb from limb.
Understood. This is the supramundane. This is to hold the world within one's palm and transcend to other realms.

If, even for a moment, there is the slightest lingering attachment toward the twelvefold teachings or any phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—within the depths of one’s being, one has not escaped the net.
Whatever is sought or attained, whatever involves the arising of thought or the stirring of a mind, all such things are termed "wild jackals. It is right here and now.
Within the internal organs, there is nothing sought and nothing attained. Such a person is a great donor and a lion’s roar;
yet they do not abide in non-attainment, nor is there any conceptual understanding of non-abiding. This is called the "Lion of the Six Severances.
