The self and others do not arise, and no evils are produced. This is to contain Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed without it being displaced.
All greed, anger, the eight winds, and so forth—these he can entirely suck up from the four great oceans and swallow into his mouth.
He does not accept any false speech; it does not enter his ears, nor does he allow his body to give rise to any evil toward others.
This is to take all fires into the belly. Just as it is now, with respect to each and every object, one is neither deluded nor distracted, neither angry nor delighted.
At the gateway of one's own six sense organs, one scrapes away and balances them until they attain purity; such a person is one who has nothing to do. This surpasses all intellectual understanding;
it is the asceticism (*dhūta*) of diligence. This is called the "heavenly eye" (*divyacakṣus*), and it is also called the "eye of clear illumination."
This is called the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It functions as a vehicle that carries cause and effect.

When a Buddha appears in the world to deliver sentient beings, one attains the state where the preceding thought does not arise and the succeeding thought does not continue. The cessation of the karma of the preceding thought is what is called "delivering sentient beings.

If the preceding thought is one of anger, one immediately treats it with the medicine of joy; this is precisely what is meant by "a Buddha exists to deliver sentient beings. However, all such verbal teachings are merely...

This is for the purpose of treating illness. Since illnesses differ, the medicines also differ. Therefore, at times one speaks of the existence of a Buddha, and at times one speaks of the non-existence of a Buddha.
These are true words used to treat illness. If the illness is cured, every instance is a treatment by true words;
if the illness is not cured, every instance is a treatment by false words. What is a true word becomes a false word because it gives rise to views; what is a false word is actually the truth.
Regarding speech: it is for the purpose of severing the delusions of sentient beings. Illness is a false construct; there is only the appearance of false medicine to treat it.
When a Buddha appears in the world to deliver sentient beings, these are the words of the ninefold teaching, the words of the provisional teachings.
Hatred and joy, illness and medicine—all are one's own self; there are no two separate persons. Where, then, is there a Buddha appearing in the world? Where are there sentient beings?
Sentient beings can be delivered. As the Sūtra says: "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. It also says:

"Not craving the Buddha’s bodhi, and not being greedily attached to the various dharmas of existence or non-existence, is called 'delivering others. Not remaining fixedly attached to oneself is called 'delivering oneself.
Since illnesses differ, medicines also differ; since prescriptions differ, one must not be dogmatic or adhere to a single approach.
Relying on the Buddha, relying on bodhi, and so forth—all these are modes of reliance. Therefore, it is said that for the wise, one must not adhere to a single direction.
What is analyzed within the teachings is like yellow leaves, and also like an empty fist used to deceive small children.

If a person does not understand this principle, they are said to be identical to ignorance. Thus, a Bodhisattva practicing prajñā must not grasp at my words, nor rely upon the teachings [as ultimate].
Imperial Decree: Hatred is like a stone; attachment is like a river. If, right now, one is simply without hatred and without attachment, this is to penetrate mountains, rivers, and rocky walls.
"Directly" refers to treating the common illness of deafness; "much learning and eloquent discourse" refer to treating the illness of the eyes.
From the human realm to Buddhahood is gain; from the human realm to hell is loss. It is the same with right and wrong. As the Third Patriarch said: "Gain and loss, right and wrong."
At one time, let go completely. Not grasping or dwelling upon any phenomena of existence or non-existence is called "not dwelling on conditions.

Furthermore, not relying on or dwelling in non-reliance is called "not dwelling in the patience of emptiness. To grasp at oneself as being the Buddha, or as one who has realized the path of Chan, is called "internal view.
To grasp at that which is accomplished through the cultivation and realization of causes and conditions is called "external view. — Master Zhizhe.

It is said: To see internally and externally as both erroneous; for the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue to each be free from greed and defilement toward all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent—this is called upholding the four-line verse.
It is also called the four fruits. The six sense bases being traceless is also called the six supernormal powers.
Simply now, one is not obstructed by any phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, yet there is no knowing that does not rely upon them.
Explanation: This is called supernatural power (*abhijñā*). Not abiding in this supernatural power is called being without supernatural power.

As it is said: "The tracks of a bodhisattva who is without supernatural power cannot be sought. Such a person is a superior being above the Buddha; they are most inconceivable. "Human" refers to oneself;
"heaven" refers to the illumination of wisdom. Praising is joy. Joy belongs to the object; the object is heaven, and the praise is the human. Thus, human and heaven [are unified].
The meeting of the two allows them to see one another. It is also said that pure wisdom is heaven and correct wisdom is humanity;

originally they are not Buddhas, yet to claim they are Buddhas is called "binding the essence. Now, simply do not form the conceptual understanding of being a Buddha, nor harbor the conceptual understanding of non-existence or non-reliance.
This is called "extinguishing the knot," which is also called True Suchness (*tathatā*) and also called Essential Suchness. To seek a Buddha...
"Bodhi" is a name for the present body and mind. At this very moment, whatever constitutes the mind of seeking is entirely what is meant by "the present body and mind.
As it is said: "Seeking bodhi," though it is a superior seeking, only increases the accumulation of dust and burdens. Seeking the Buddha belongs to the assembly of Buddhas;
seeking all dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, belongs to the assembly of sentient beings. At this very moment, as you reflect and awaken, simply do not rely upon or dwell in anything at all.

Regarding all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, these do not enter into the reckoning of categories. Simply by now being without attachment toward each individual sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, mental object, and so forth;
by not craving each individual object; and by merely being free from the ten types of turbid minds—this is the realization-cause for attaining Buddhahood.
To study the words and phrases in search of an interpretation is called attaining Buddhahood through conditions. To see the Buddha and know the Buddha is to be able to speak of the Buddha;
yet to have such knowing and seeing is actually to slander the Buddha. If one says, "The Buddha knows, the Buddha sees, the Buddha hears, the Buddha speaks," then it is acceptable.
It is like seeing fire—it is acceptable; but for fire to see, it is not acceptable. It is like a knife cutting an object—it is acceptable; but for an object to cut a knife, it is not acceptable.
Those who know the Buddha, see the Buddha, hear the Buddha, and speak of the Buddha are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. These are what the Buddha knows; these are what the Buddha sees;
these are what the Buddha hears; these are what the Buddha speaks. Yet among ten thousand, there is not one. This is simply because they themselves lack eyes and rely on others to act as their eyes.
In the teachings, this is called "inferential knowledge" (anumāna-jñāna). Even now, when you greedily crave intellectual understanding of the Buddha, that too is merely inferential knowledge.
Worldly analogies are concordant analogies. Definitive teachings and non-definitive teachings are likewise either concordant or discordant analogies.
Sacrificing one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain is a discordant analogy; for instance, the current lack of affection for the Buddha’s bodhi and other such dharmas is a discordant analogy.
It is difficult to relinquish, comparable to one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain. When it illuminates all objective phenomena of existence and non-existence, it is called the "head.

When it is disturbed by the characteristics (*nimitta*) of all objective phenomena of existence and non-existence, it is called the "hands. When it has not yet illuminated any preceding objects, it is called the "marrow and brain."
The Sage dwells in the realm of the ordinary to cultivate the causes for enlightenment; the Buddha enters among sentient beings to guide and transform them through kinship.
When he encounters hungry ghosts whose limbs are ablaze with fire, he preaches the Prajñāpāramitā to them, causing them to resolve their minds toward awakening.

If he were to remain exclusively in the realm of the sages, by what means could he reach those beings and converse with them? The Buddha enters among all classes of beings to act as a boat and raft for sentient beings.
He undergoes suffering along with them; his exhaustion and toil are boundless. When the Buddha enters places of suffering, he likewise undergoes suffering together with sentient beings.
Yet the Buddha alone possesses the freedom to come and go, unlike sentient beings. The Buddha is not empty space; how could he not suffer when undergoing suffering?

If one says that [the Buddha] is not suffering, this statement contradicts the truth; do not speak thus in levity. To speak erroneously of whether the Buddha’s supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are sovereign or not is improper.

A person possessed of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) does not dare to say that the Buddha is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor does he dare to say that the Buddha is autonomous or non-autonomous.
Aside from praising medicinal prescriptions, he does not wish to expose the ugliness of both extremes. This is the teaching.
It is said: "If a person establishes the Buddha’s bodhi within the realm of 'having something' or 'being this,' that person incurs great sin. It is also said:
"Just as there is no fault in speaking thus before one who does not recognize the Buddha, so too can the milk of an untainted cow cure the diseases of those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This cow does not dwell on high plateaus, nor does it reside in low marshes; the milk of such a cow is fit to serve as medicine. High...
The high ground is metaphorically compared to the Buddha, and the low marshlands to sentient beings. As it is said: "The Tathāgata’s true wisdom and Dharma-body likewise possess no such ailments;
his eloquence is unimpeded, his ascent is sovereign, and he is neither born nor extinguished—this is what is called birth, old age, sickness, and death."

Painful afflictions. This was due to secretly consuming mushroom soup, which led to his death from dysentery. This was done secretly to conceal the traces of his enlightened head. Both light and darkness are cast off;
there is no grasping, nor is there even non-grasping. He is neither bright nor dark.
Born in the royal palace, he took Yaśodharā as his wife and attained the Way through the eight signs. These are the conceptual constructions of śrāvakas and non-Buddhists, as it is said:
It is not a body sustained by mixed food. Cunda said: "I know that the Tathāgata will certainly not accept or eat [this offering].
First, one must possess two eyes to illuminate and penetrate matters of both sides; do not merely wear a pair of eyes while walking toward only one side.
If you do so, which side will you reach? The Goddess of Merit and the Woman of Darkness follow one another. A wise host does not accept either."
Receiving [the teaching]: the mind is now like empty space; only when one studies in this way does it begin to bear fruit.
The High Patriarch of the Western Land said, "Clouds and mountains are a metaphor for the Great Nirvana. The First Patriarch of this land said, "The mind is like wood or stone.
The Third Patriarch said, "Utterly forgetting conditions. Caoqi said, "Do not deliberate at all on good or evil. My late teacher said, "It is like a lost person who cannot distinguish [his way]."
Regarding the locus [of this practice], Master Sengzhao said: "To close off the intellect and block the ears, one awakens alone in the profound darkness. Mañjuśrī said:
"Because the mind is identical to empty space, I pay homage to that which has no object of observation. In the most profound sūtras, it is said that one neither hears nor upholds;
it is simply that at present, all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—are neither seen nor heard, and the six sense faculties are sealed shut. If one can...
To study in this way and to uphold the sutras in this way is only then to have the potential for true practice.

These words may be harsh to the ear and bitter to the mouth, yet if one can act accordingly, then in a second or third lifetime, one will be able to sit upon the Great Path of Enlightenment where no Buddha is present.

He manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment; he transforms evil into good and good into evil. He causes unwholesome dharmas to teach and transform bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and causes wholesome dharmas to teach and transform those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts.
He is able to lead toward the realm of light and untie the bonds of light, and able to lead toward the realm of darkness and untie the bonds of darkness.
He can grasp gold and turn it into earth, or grasp earth and turn it into gold; he can accomplish all manner of things through such transformations and displays.
Freedom. Should there be one seeking refuge beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Bhagavān immediately manifests his thirty-two marks and appears before that person.
He speaks with the same vocal resonance as that individual and preaches the Dharma to them, transforming them according to their capacities and responding to their conditions with diverse forms.

He manifests throughout the various realms of existence; yet even this detachment from "self" and "what belongs to self" still pertains to the realm of the other shore. It is but a minor application, and is likewise...
Within the gateway of Buddha-activities, there is the "Great Function": the great body is hidden within the formless; the great sound is concealed within the silent resonance.
It is like fire within wood, or like the sound of bells and drums; when the conditions have not yet converged, one cannot speak of its existence or non-existence.
Rebirth in the heavens as a lateral retribution is cast aside like mucus or spittle. The Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices are like riding upon a corpse.
Having crossed to the other shore, one is as if released from a prison or escaping through a latrine hole.
The Buddha’s thirty-two marks are called "soiled garments. It is also said: "To say that the Buddha never at all receives the five aggregates is impossible;
the Buddha is not empty space, so how could he never receive them? The Buddha simply possesses freedom of coming and going, unlike sentient beings. From...
From one celestial realm to another celestial realm, and from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field—this is the constant law of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, it is said: according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, when a Bodhisattva receives the offerings and alms of others while those others are in the midst of hell, the Bodhisattva practices compassion and transforms them through the guidance of a similar kind to repay their kindness; thus, he cannot remain eternally in nirvana. It is also said: it is like fire seeing fire.
Only do not touch it with your hand; fire does not burn a person. Right now, simply be free of the ten kinds of turbid minds:
the greedy mind, the affectionate mind, the defiled mind, the angry mind, the grasping mind, the dwelling mind, the dependent mind, the attached mind, the seizing mind, and the longing mind.
Each of these single phrases consists of three sub-phrases; let each one pass beyond these three. This is entirely a matter of illumination and function; listen as you please.
Whether horizontal or vertical—indeed, every movement and action, whether speaking or remaining silent, crying or laughing, is entirely the Buddha-wisdom.

Chan Master Yixuan Huizhao of Linji Monastery in Zhenzhou was a native of Nanhua in Caizhou. His secular surname was Xing. From childhood, he was exceptionally gifted.
Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he set his mind upon the Chan school. He served under Master Huangbo for three years, his conduct being consistently pure and singular.
The Head Seat remarked, "This young man is indeed different from the rest. The Head Seat—
The questioner asked, "How long has the Elder been here? The Master said, "Three years. The Head Seat asked, "Have you ever made inquiries [of the Abbot]?
The Master said, "I have never made inquiries. I do not know what to ask.
The Head Seat said, "Why do you not go and ask the Abbot what the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma is? Thereupon, the Master...
He went to ask him. Before the sound of his question had even ceased, Huangbo struck him. The Master came down, and the Head Seat asked, "What was your question?
The Master said, "Before I had finished asking, the Abbot struck me; I do not understand. The Head Seat said, "Just go and ask again.
The Master went to ask again, and Huangbo struck him once more. This continued in the same manner.
He asked three times and was struck three times. The Master came and said to the Head Seat: "I am fortunate to have received your compassion, allowing me to inquire after the Master's well-being.
Having posed my questions three times, I have been struck three times with the staff. I lament my own karmic obstacles for failing to grasp the profound meaning."
"Now I shall take my leave. The Head Seat said, "If you are to go, you must first take leave of the Master before departing. The Master bowed and withdrew.
The Head Seat went first to the Master's quarters and said, "That young man who asked questions was truly in accord with the Dharma.
When he comes to take his leave of you, Master, please receive him with skillful means; later, he will grow into a great tree that pierces through everything."
"The people of the world go about seeking shade," the Master said, and then he went up to take his leave.
Huangbo said, "You must not go elsewhere. Go to Dayu at Gao'an Tan-tou; he will surely explain it for you."
The Master arrived at Dayu’s [place]. Dayu asked, "From where have you come? The Master said, "From Huangbo's place.

Dayu asked, "What words did Huangbo say? The Master said, "I asked him three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I was struck with the staff. I do not know whether I was at fault or not. Dayu said, "Huangbo..."
"You old woman! You have exhausted yourself for my sake, yet you still come here to ask whether there is a fault or not.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So it turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma consists of nothing more than this! Dayu grabbed him and held him fast, saying:
"You bed-wetting child! Just now you were saying, 'Whether there was a fault or not,' and now you say, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma consists of nothing more than this.
What principle have you seen? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master struck Daoyi three times in the ribs.
Daoyi pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business."
The Master took his leave of Dayu and returned to Huangbo. Upon seeing him arrive, Huangbo asked, "This fellow comes and goes; when will there ever be an end to it?
The Master said, "It is precisely because of your grandmotherly concern. Having finished his formal greetings, he stood in attendance. Huangbo asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master said, "Yesterday I received the compassion of the Master; today I am coming to attend upon you."
Regarding "The Fool’s Departure and Arrival," Huangbo asked, "What words did Dayu say? The Master related [the story]:
Dayu asked me, "What words did Huangbo have for you? I then recounted the previous conversation and asked him, "Does he have fault or not?
Dayu said, "Huangbo was so compassionate for your sake that he exhausted himself; yet you still ask whether he has fault or not. I... [said nothing].
Upon these words, Mazu attained great enlightenment. Huangbo said, "How is it that this fellow has arrived?
I shall give him a severe beating! Mazu said, "Why speak of waiting for his arrival? He shall eat [the blow] right now. He then struck him with his palm.
Huangbo said, "This madman comes here to pull the tiger's whiskers! Mazu then shouted. Huangbo said, "Attendant, lead this madman away."

Han entered the hall. Guishan raised the previous karmic cause and asked Yangshan, "At that time, did Linji receive the power of Dayu or the power of Huangbo? Yangshan said, "It was not merely a matter of pulling a tiger’s whiskers; he also knew how to ride upon the tiger’s head. Later, while the Master was planting pine trees, Huangbo asked, "What are you doing planting so many pines in the deep mountains? The Master replied, "I am planting them for the sake of future generations. Huangbo said, "If future generations come here, they will see only these old stumps. The Master said, "If there were no old stumps, what would they see? Huangbo said, "They would see the wind blowing through the pine needles. The Master said, "If there were no wind blowing through the pine needles, what would they see? Huangbo said, "They would see the clouds drifting over the mountain peaks. The Master said, "If there were no clouds drifting over the mountain peaks, what would they see? Huangbo said, "They would see the moon reflected in the pond. The Master said, "If there were no moon reflected in the pond, what would they see? Huangbo said, "They would see themselves. The Master said, "If there were no 'self,' what would they see? Huangbo was speechless. The Master said, "Teacher, you have been defeated. Huangbo said, "I am defeated. The Master said, "If you say 'I am defeated,' who is it that says so? Huangbo said, "If you do not say 'I am defeated,' who is it that says so? The Master said, "If you do not say 'I am defeated' and I do not say 'I am defeated,' then who is it that sees? Huangbo said, "The one who sees. The Master said, "If there is no one who sees, what is it that sees? Huangbo said, "If there is no one who sees, then what is it that sees? The Master said, "If there is no one who sees and nothing that is seen, then what is it that speaks? Huangbo said, "If there is no one who speaks and nothing that is spoken, then what is it that hears? The Master said, "If there is no one who hears and nothing that is heard, then what is it that knows? Huangbo said, "If there is no one who knows and nothing that is known, then what is it that acts? The Master said, "If there is no one who acts and nothing that is acted upon, then what is it that dies? Huangbo said, "If there is no one who dies and nothing that dies, then what is it that is reborn? The Master said, "If there is no one who is reborn and nothing that is reborn, then what is it that attains Buddhahood? Huangbo said, "If there is no one who attains Buddhahood and nothing that is attained, then what is it that is the Buddha? The Master said, "If there is no Buddha and no Dharma, then what is it that is the Way? Huangbo said, "If there is no Way and no practice, then what is it that is the Patriarch? The Master said, "If there is no Patriarch and no transmission, then what is it that is the teaching? Huangbo said, "If there is no teaching and no master, then what is it that is the disciple? The Master said, "If there is no disciple and no teacher, then what is it that is the assembly? Huangbo said, "If there is no assembly and no hall, then what is it that is the monastery? The Master said, "If there is no monastery and no mountain, then what is it that is the world? Huangbo said, "If there is no world and no realm, then what is it that is the void? The Master said, "If there is no void and no emptiness, then what is it that is existence? Huangbo said, "If there is no existence and no non-existence, then what is it that is the Middle Way? The Master said, "If there is no Middle Way and no extremes, then what is it that is the Great Function? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Function and no small function, then what is it that is the Great Matter? The Master said, "If there is no Great Matter and no small matter, then what is it that is the Great Peace? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Peace and no small peace, then what is it that is the Great Nirvana? The Master said, "If there is no Great Nirvana and no small nirvana, then what is it that is the Great Awakening? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Awakening and no small awakening, then what is it that is the Great Enlightenment? The Master said, "If there is no Great Enlightenment and no small enlightenment, then what is it that is the Great Liberation? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Liberation and no small liberation, then what is it that is the Great Return? The Master said, "If there is no Great Return and no small return, then what is it that is the Great Homecoming? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Homecoming and no small homecoming, then what is it that is the Great Rest? The Master said, "If there is no Great Rest and no small rest, then what is it that is the Great Stillness? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Stillness and no small stillness, then what is it that is the Great Silence? The Master said, "If there is no Great Silence and no small silence, then what is it that is the Great Mystery? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Mystery and no small mystery, then what is it that is the Great Truth? The Master said, "If there is no Great Truth and no small truth, then what is it that is the Great Reality? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Reality and no small reality, then what is it that is the Great Suchness? The Master said, "If there is no Great Suchness and no small suchness, then what is it that is the Great Thusness? Huangbo said, "If there is no Great Thusness and no small thusness, then what is it that is the Great Reality-Thusness? The Master said, "If there is no Reality-Thusness and no non-reality-thusness, then what is it that is the Great Unconditioned? Huangbo said, "If there is no Unconditioned and no conditioned, then what is it that is the Great Emptiness? The Master said, "If there is no Emptiness and no form, then what is it that is the Great Non-duality? Huangbo said, "If there is no Non-duality and no duality, then what is it that is the Great Oneness? The Master said, "If there is no Oneness and no many, then what is it that is the Great Totality? Huangbo said, "If there is no Totality and no partiality, then what is it that is the Great Perfection? The Master said, "If there is no Perfection and no imperfection, then what is it that is the Great Completion? Huangbo said, "If there is no Completion and no beginning, then what is it that is the Great Beginningless? The Master said, "If there is no Beginningless and no end, then what is it that is the Great Eternity? Huangbo said, "If there is no Eternity and no transience, then what is it that is the Great Immortality? The Master said, "If there is no Immortality and no mortality, then what is it that is the Great Freedom? Huangbo said, "If there is no Freedom and no bondage, then what is it that is the Great Liberation? The Master said, "If there is no Liberation and no confinement, then what is it that is the Great Unobstructedness? Huangbo said, "If there is no Unobstructedness and no obstruction, then what is it that is the Great Unimpededness? The Master said, "If there is no Unimpededness and no impediment, then what is it that is the Great Unhinderedness? Huangbo said, "If there is no Unhinderedness and no hindrance, then what is it that is the Great Unattachedness? The Master said, "If there is no Unattachedness and no attachment, then what is it that is the Great Ungrasping? Huangbo said, "If there is no Ungrasping and no grasping, then what is it that is the Great Non-acquisition? The Master said, "If there is no Non-acquisition and no acquisition, then what is it that is the Great Non-possession? Huangbo said, "If there is no Non-possession and no possession, then what is it that is the Great Non-ownership? The Master said, "If there is no Non-ownership and no ownership, then what is it that is the Great Non-appropriation? Huangbo said, "If there is no Non-appropriation and no appropriation, then what is it that is the Great Non-seizing? The Master said, "If there is no Non-seizing and no seizing, then what is it that is the Great Non-grasping? Huangbo said, "If there is no Non-grasping and no grasping, then what is it that
Baizhang said, "First, it serves as a scenic feature for the mountain gate; second, it serves as a signpost for future generations.
Having finished speaking, he struck the ground once or twice with his mattock. Baizhang said, "Even so, you have already received thirty blows from me.
The Master again struck the ground twice with the mattock, then sighed, "Heh! Heh! Baizhang said, "My school has reached you."
It flourished greatly in the world. Guishan raised the preceding causal conditions and asked Yangshan:
"At that time, Huangbo entrusted his teachings to Linji alone; were there any others? Yangshan said:
"There were, but the years have been so remote that I do not wish to mention them to you, Master. Guishan said: "Even so, I still wish to know. You simply go ahead and mention them."
Yangshan said: "One person points south; the edict of Wu and Yue is in effect. When it meets a great wind, it stops" (this is a prophecy concerning Fengxue).
Once, while the Master was engaged in communal labor, he saw Huangbo approaching and stood leaning on his hoe. Huangbo said, "This fellow is exhausted.
The Master said, "The hoe has come to lift itself up; what is there to be exhausted? Huangbo then struck him. The Master caught the staff.

As he was being carried out, Huangbo called for the *karmadāna*. The *karmadāna* helped him up, whereupon Huangbo said, "How can you, *karmadāna*, tolerate such a raving madman who is so impolite? Huangbo rose and struck the *karmadāna*.
The Master [Baizhang] pointed his hoe at the ground and said, "In other places they perform cremation; here, we bury everyone alive. Guishan asked Yangshan:
When Huangbo struck the rector, what was his intention? Yangshan said, "The real thief has run away; the one who tracks him down gets the beating.
One day, as the Master was sitting in front of the Sangha hall, he saw Huangbo coming and closed his eyes. When Huangbo saw this, he... [performed a gesture].
Frightened, he returned to the abbot’s quarters. Baizhang followed him to the quarters to pay his respects and offer thanks.

The Head Seat was standing in attendance by Baizhang’s side, and Baizhang said, "Although this monk is but a junior, he knows that such a matter exists. The Head Seat replied: [The text provided ends here.]
The Old Monk, however, exposed this young man. Baizhang struck his own mouth with his hand. The Head Seat said, "If you had known, you would have understood;
if you had known, you would have understood.
While the Master was sleeping inside the hall, Baizhang came down, saw him, and struck the head of the meditation platform once with his staff. The Master—
He raised his head and saw it was Huangbo; he went back to sleep. Huangbo struck the meditation bench once more.
He went up to the hall and saw the Head Seat sitting in meditation. Huangbo said, "The junior monks in the lower quarters are actually sitting in meditation;
what are you doing here, indulging in such discursive thoughts? The Head Seat said, "What is this madman doing? Huangbo struck the head of the wooden board once and then departed.
He went out. Guishan asked Yangshan, "What was Huangbo's meaning? Yang said, "Two colors, one match.
One day, the Master and Huangbo were attending a communal work session together. The Master was walking behind; Huangbo turned his head and saw that the Master was empty-handed.
Huangbo asked, "Where is the mattock? The Master said, "Someone has already taken it away.
Huangbo said, "Come closer; let us deliberate on a matter together. The Master then approached.
Huangbo held up the mattock and said, "This very thing—no one in the world can lift it up. The Master reached out his hand, seized it, and held it up himself.
[The monk] asked, "Why was it in the hands of such-and-such a person? Huangbo said, "Today there is someone else being invited for communal labor," and he then returned to the monastery.
Later, Guishan raised this story and asked Yangshan, "The mattock was in Huangbo’s hand; why, then, was it [taken away] by him?"
Linji snatched [the staff] away. Yangshan said, "The thief is a petty person, yet his cunning surpasses that of a gentleman.
Huangbo entered the kitchen and saw the rice steward. He asked, "What are you doing? The steward replied, "I am sorting the rice for the assembly.
Huangbo asked, "How much do they eat each day? The steward replied, "Two *shí* and five *dǒng*. Huangbo said, "Is that not too much? The steward...
Baizhang said, "I fear there may still be some deficiency. He then struck him. The head cook later recounted this incident to Mazu.
Mazu said, "I shall go with you to examine that old fellow. As soon as they arrived at Baizhang’s place and were standing in attendance, Baizhang brought up the previous cause and condition.
Mazu said, "The head cook does not understand; please, Master, provide a substitute phrase for him. Mazu then asked, "Is it not too much?"
Huangbo said, "Why do you not say, 'Come back tomorrow for another meal'? The Master said, "What are you saying about 'tomorrow'?
I shall eat right now! Having said this, he struck him with his palm. Huangbo said, "This madman has come here again to pull at the tiger's whiskers!
The Master then shouted, "Get out! and left.
Later, Guishan raised this question for Yangshan: "What was the intention of these two venerable masters?
Yangshan said, "What is your own intention, Master? Guishan said, "Only by raising a son does one come to know a father’s compassion.
Yangshan said, "Not so. Guishan asked, "And what do you say, my son? Yangshan said, "It is very much like inviting a thief to ruin the family."
The Master sent a letter on behalf of Huangbo to Mount Gui. Yangshan was serving as the guest prefect at that time;
upon receiving the letter, he asked, "Which of these is Huangbo's, and which is yours, Venerable? The Master then gave him a slap.
Yangshan held him back, saying, "Brother, you know this is all one and the same matter, so let it be. Together they went to visit Mount Gui. Mount Gui then asked, "Huangbo—"
"Brother, how many people are in your assembly? The Master said, "Seven hundred. Miaoyan asked, "Who acts as the leader?
The Master said, "I have already sent the letter just now. The Master then asked Miaoyan, "How many people are in your assembly here, Reverend?
Miaoyan said, "One thousand five hundred. The Master said, "That is quite a lot! Miaoyan said, "Yellow..."
There were also not a few elder brothers like Ba.
When he took his leave of Master Miu-shan, Yang-shan saw him off and said, "If you go north, there will be a place for you to dwell. The Master said:
"How could such a thing be? Yangshan said, "Just go. There will be someone to assist you;
this person has a head but no tail, a beginning but no end."
When the Master arrived at Zhenzhou, Puhua was already there. After the Master settled there, Puhua assisted him; while the Master’s authentic teaching flourished, Puhua cast off his physical body.
The Master took his leave of Huangbo. Huangbo asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "Neither south of the Yellow River, nor north of it.

Huangbo struck him. The Master grabbed him and gave him a slap. Huangbo laughed heartily and called to his attendant, "Bring the meditation board and desk belonging to our late master Baizhang! The Master said, "Attendant, bring fire! —Huangbo.
[Linji] said, "Even so, you must simply take it with you; later on, you shall sit upon the tongues of all people under heaven.
Later, Muzhou raised this story and asked Yangshan, "Did Linji fail to repay Huangbo?"
Yangshan said, "Not so. Miaoshan asked, "And how about you, my son? Yangshan said, "Only by knowing gratitude does one understand how to repay it.
Miaoshan asked, "Did the ancients of old use anything like this? Yangshan said, "They did."
"It is simply that the time has been so long ago that I do not wish to cite it for the Master. Baizhang said, "Even so, I do not yet know.
You just go ahead and cite it. Yangshan said, "For instance, at the assembly of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, Ānanda praised the Buddha, saying:
'To offer this profound mind to every dust-mote world—that is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. Is this not repaying kindness?"

Regarding this matter, Guishan said: "So it is, so it is. If one's insight is equal to that of the teacher, one lacks half the teacher's virtue; only when one's insight surpasses that of the teacher is one fit to receive the transmission."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Upon this lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank who constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face of you all.
Those who have not yet attained verification, look! Look! At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the true person of no rank?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak! As the monk hesitated, the Master pushed him away and said:
"What is the 'true person of no station'? It is a dried-up shit-stick.
Having said this, he returned to his quarters. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk gave a shout. The Master bowed and invited him to sit.
The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him. When the Master saw another monk approaching, he held up his whisk. The monk prostrated himself. The Master—
He struck him. Again, seeing a monk approach, he likewise held up his whisk; the monk paid no heed, so the Master struck him as well.
He ascended the hall. A monk came forward and bowed; the Master immediately shouted. The monk said, "Old Monk, do not poke your head out.
The Master said, "Tell me, where does it fall? The monk then shouted. Another monk asked: "As for such [a matter]..."

The monk said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. The Master said, "If the assembly wishes to understand the Linji phrase of guest and host, go ask the Hall Monitor."

One day, while the Master was attending a meal at a donor’s house together with Puhua, the Master asked Puhua, "A hair swallows the vast ocean."

The next day, the Master again went with Puhua to attend a meal offering. The Master asked, "What is being offered today?"
It was as if yesterday: Puhua, as before, kicked over the rice table. The Master said, “You have succeeded, indeed, but you are far too crude.
Puhua said, “Blind fellow! What ‘coarse’ or ‘subtle’ does the Buddha-dharma speak of? The Master then stuck out his tongue.
One day, the Master was sitting with the Elder Mudata of Heyang inside the hearth in the monks' hall. Because they were discussing this:
Every day, Puhua wandered through the marketplace acting like a madman. No one knew whether he was an ordinary man or a sage.
Before he had even finished speaking, Puhua entered. The Master asked, "Are you an ordinary man or a sage?
Puhua replied, "Now tell me, are you an ordinary man or a sage? The Master then shouted. Puhua pointed his finger and said, "The new bridge at Heyang..."
“Wife and children! The wooden pagoda and the old woman’s Zen! Linji, that little rascal, yet he possesses a single eye!
The Master said, “That thief! Puhua said, “Thief! Thief! and then went out.
One day, while Puhua was eating raw vegetables in front of the Sangha Hall, the Master saw him and said, "You look very much like a donkey.
Puhua then brayed like a donkey. The Master said, "You thief! Puhua replied, "Thief! Thief!

This was because Puhua used to wander through the streets and markets shaking a bell and saying, "If it comes from the bright side, I strike from the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, [I strike from the dark side]."

He struck him on the head. [The monk said: "It comes from the four quarters and eight directions. He struck him with a whirlwind. "It comes from empty space. He struck him as he parried. The Master ordered an attendant to go.
As soon as the attendant saw him speak thus, he seized him and asked, "What if they do not come in this way at all?
The attendant followed his instructions. Puhua pushed him away and said, "Tomorrow there is a meal at the Great Compassion Temple. The attendant returned.
He reported this to the Master. The Master said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
One day, Puhua went into the marketplace and begged people for a monk’s robe; everyone gave him one, yet Puhua would not accept any of them.
The Master ordered the head of the monastery to purchase a coffin. When Puhua returned, the Master said, "I give it to you."
Having finished making the cassock, Puhua carried it out and walked through the marketplace, shouting: "Linji has finished making my cassock for me!
I am going to pass away at the East Gate! The people of the market vied with one another to follow and watch him.
Puhua said, "I will not go today; tomorrow I shall pass away at the South Gate. He continued in this manner for three days.

People no longer believed him. By the fourth day, there was no one following to watch; he went out alone beyond the city walls, entered the coffin himself, and requested a passerby on the road to nail it shut.
News spread immediately, and the townspeople vied with one another to go and open the coffin. Upon opening it, they saw that his entire body had vanished.
An elderly practitioner came to visit the Master; having never engaged in formal greetings before, he asked, "Is it right to prostrate, or is it not?
The Master then shouted. The elder immediately prostrated. The Master said, "What a fine grass-thief! The elder replied: [The text ends here.]
"Thief! Thief! he cried, and then went out. The Master said, "Do not say that there is nothing to it.
While the Head Seat was standing in attendance, the Master asked, "Is there still any fault? The Head Seat replied, "There is. The Master said:
The guest’s house has committed a fault; the host’s house has committed a fault. The Head Seat said, “Both have committed faults.
The Master asked, “Where does the fault lie? The Head Seat then went out. The Master said, “Do not say it is ‘no matter’ (wúshì).
Later, a monk recounted this to Nanquan, who said, “Official horses trampling one another.”
In the evening *samaya*, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not; sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not;

sometimes both person and environment are taken away; and sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away. At that time, a monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'?
The Master said: "The sun shines forth, spreading carpets of flowers upon the ground; the infant’s hair grows long and turns white."
[The student] asked, "What is 'seizing the object but not seizing the person'? The Master said, "The imperial decree has been issued and reached throughout the land;
the General beyond the frontier has cut off all smoke and dust. [The student] asked, "What is 'seizing both the person and the object'?
The Master said, "News is cut off from Bing and Fen; he dwells alone in one place. [The student] asked, "What is 'neither seizing the person nor seizing the object'?"
The Master said, "When the King ascends the jeweled throne, the village elders sing songs of joy.
On one occasion, as the Master entered a military camp for a meal, he saw an officer at the gate. Pointing to a pillar, the Master asked, "Is this ordinary or is it sacred?
The officer was speechless. The Master struck the pillar and said, "Even if you could have spoken, it would still have been nothing more than a wooden peg."
He entered immediately.
The Master asked the head monk, "Where have you come from? The head monk replied, "I went to the prefectural city to sell yellow millet.
The Master said, "Did you sell it all? The head monk replied, "I sold it all. The Master then drew a line before him with his staff.
Huìyuǎn said, "Can you still sell this? The Abbot (Zhǔ) gave a shout; the Master struck him. When the Head Cook arrived, the Master brought up the previous conversation.
The Head Cook said, "The Abbot does not understand the Master’s meaning. The Master asked, "How about you?
The Head Cook then prostrated himself, and the Master struck him as well.
A presiding master (zuozhu) came to visit him. The Master asked the presiding master, "Which sutras and śāstras do you lecture on?
The master replied, "I am a man of shallow learning; I have studied the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas) in a cursory manner.

The Master said, "Suppose there is one person who clearly understands the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, and another person who does not clearly understand the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. Are these two people the same?"
The Master said, "If one understands, they are the same; if one does not understand, they are distinct.
Le Pu stood behind his teacher as an attendant and asked, "Master, what place is this? Are you speaking of sameness or difference?
The teacher turned his head and asked the attendant, "And how about you? The attendant then gave a shout. The teacher then saw the visiting master off on his way back.
He approached and asked the attendant, "Was it you who just now shouted at the old monk? The attendant replied, "Yes.
The Master then struck him. The Master had heard the second-generation Deshan give this instruction: "If you can speak it, thirty blows; if you cannot speak it, thirty blows."
"Thirty blows! The Master ordered Le Pu to go and ask him: "If he can answer, why does he also give thirty blows? Wait for him to strike;
you must catch his staff and give it a shove. See what happens. Le Pu went there and asked exactly as instructed.
Ting Shan struck him immediately. Le Pu caught the staff and gave it a shove. Ting Shan then returned to his quarters.
Zhang Puhui brought this up to the Master. The Master said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Even so, do you see Deshan? As Puhui was about to deliberate, the Master struck him.
The Master arrived at Heyang Prefecture. The Prefectural Governor, Attendant Wang, invited the Master to ascend the seat.

At that time, Mayu stepped forward and asked, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye? The Master said, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Mayu dragged the Master down from the seat and took his place upon it himself. The Master [remained seated].
[Daowu] approached and said, "I hope you have been well. Mazu hesitated. The Master then dragged Mazu down from his seat.
The Master returned to his own seat; Mazu immediately departed, and the Master then descended from his seat.
One day, an attendant visited the Master. While together in the monks’ hall, he asked, “Do these monks in this hall read the sutras?
The Master said, “They do not read the sutras. The attendant said, “Then do they study Chan? The Master said, “They do not study Chan.
The attendant said, “If they neither read the sutras nor study Chan, what exactly are they doing? The Master—
The Master said, "I am teaching him in general to become a Buddha and a Patriarch. The attendant asked, "It is said that 'though gold dust is precious, when it falls in the eye it becomes a cataract.
What then? The Master said, "I take you for a common man."
The Palace Attendant, together with the various officials, again requested the Master to ascend the seat. The Master ascended the seat and said:
"Today, this mountain monk has no choice but to comply with human sentiment and thus mount this seat.

However, if we speak of the Great Matter according to the tradition of our ancestors, it is truly impossible to open one's mouth; there is no place for you to set foot. Today, because the Palace Attendant is so insistent..."
Please. Within this hidden network of the school, there are still veteran generals who, directly unfolding their battle arrays and raising their banners, provide proof before the assembly.
A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master gave a shout.
The monk bowed. The Master said, "This monk is indeed fit for debate."
The monk asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose lineage of the ancestral wind do you succeed?
The Master said, "When I was at Huangbo’s place, I asked three times and was struck three times. As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout and followed it by striking him, saying: "..."
"One cannot drive a stake into empty space.
A presiding master asked, "Are not the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings the clarification of Buddha-nature?
The Master said, "The weeds have never been cleared away. The master said, "Does the Buddha not deceive people? The Master said, "Where is the Buddha?"

The Master remained silent. The Teacher said, "In the presence of the Attendant, you attempt to deceive this old monk. Withdraw quickly! Withdraw quickly! You hinder others from seeking instruction. He spoke again:
"Today’s Dharma assembly is for one great purpose. Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? Come forward and ask quickly.
As soon as you open your mouth, it is already beyond the reach of the truth. Why is this so? Have you not seen?"
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni said: "The Dharma is free from words and letters; it does not belong to causes and does not abide in conditions.
Because you do not believe this, there is this entanglement today. I fear that you, the Attendant, and the various officials will be hindered and remain ignorant of the Buddha-nature.
It would be better for you to withdraw for now. Those with little root of faith will never reach a day of realization. He gave a shout and then descended from his seat.
When the Master arrived at the pagoda of the First Patriarch, the keeper of the pagoda said, "Venerable Sir, will you first pay homage to the Buddha or first pay homage to the Patriarch?
The Master replied, "I pay homage to neither the Buddha nor the Patriarch. The keeper asked, "What grievance do you have with the Buddha and the Patriarch?
Thereupon, the Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master held up his whisk. The monk then shouted. The Master struck him.
Another monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master likewise held up his whisk.
The monk then shouted. The Master also shouted. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
Ascending the hall, he said: "For twenty years I was at the place of my late teacher Huangbo. Three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I received his staff.
It was like a common weed-stick, a whisk, or a pair of chopsticks. Now I am thinking of getting one more blow; who will administer it for me?
At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and said, "I, this person, can do it. The Master [struck him].
The Master brandished his staff toward a monk; as the monk prepared to receive it, the Master struck him.
He asked, "What is the matter on the edge of the sword? The Master said, "A disaster! A disaster! As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him again.
The Master struck him. [The student] asked, "As for the practitioner at Shishui who was treading the mortar, when his will shifted his foot, where did he go?
The Master said, "He sank into the deep spring."
The Master arrived at Xingshan and asked, "What is the white ox in the open field? Xingshan said, "Baa-baa.
The Master said, "Mute! Xingshan said, "How about you, Elder? The Master said, "This beast."

When Zhaozhou was traveling on pilgrimage, he visited a master. Upon encountering the master while he was washing his feet, Zhaozhou asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The master replied, "It happens to be the time when this old monk is washing his feet. Zhaozhou stepped forward and assumed a posture of listening.
The master said, "You want another ladleful of foul water poured over you! Zhaozhou then went down.
Longya asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Give me the meditation board.
Longya then passed the meditation board to the Master. The Master took it and struck him. Longya said, "I am willing to be struck, but there is still no meaning of the Patriarch here.
Later, Longya went to Cuiwei and asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? Cuiwei—
Yangshan said, "Hand me that meditation seat over here. Ya then passed the meditation seat to Cuiwei.
Cuiwei took it and struck him. Ya said, "Strike as you please; however, there is simply no meaning of the Patriarch here. After Ya took up residence at the monastery, [he continued this practice].
A monk entered the room to seek instruction, saying, "Master, regarding the circumstances of your travels when you attended upon two venerable elders, do you approve of them?
He replied, "If I were to approve, I would indeed approve deeply; yet, even so, there is still no meaning of the Patriarchs."
Mount Jing had a community of five hundred followers, yet few came to seek instruction. Huangbo sent the Master to Mount Jing.
Huangbo said to the Master, "How will you act when you arrive there? The Master replied, "I have my own expedient means.
When the Master arrived at Mount Jing and girded his waist to ascend the Dharma Hall to see the Abbot of Jing, the Abbot was just raising his head; the Master then let out a shout. Jing—
As Shanshan was about to open his mouth, the Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Shortly thereafter, a monk asked Jingshan, "What words did that monk just speak that he immediately shouted at you? Jingshan said, "That monk comes from Huangbo’s assembly.
If you wish to know, go ask him yourself. Consequently, more than half of Jingshan’s five hundred followers rushed after him.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To all who come, I owe nothing; I recognize the place from which you all come. To come in such a manner is as if you have lost yourself;
to come not in such a manner is to bind oneself without a rope. At all times, do not engage in confused deliberation. Whether you understand or do not understand, it is all ultimately an error.
I speak clearly and plainly in this way, leaving it entirely up to the people of the world to criticize or disparage me. Long ago...
[The Master] stood up. "Take care.
He ascended the hall and said: "One person stands atop a solitary peak with no way to emerge;
another person stands at the crossroads with neither front nor back. Which one is before? Which one is behind? Not acting as Vimalakīrti..."
[The Master] acted as the Great Master Fu (Fotuo Dashi). After standing for a long time, he said, "Take care. He then ascended the hall and said:
"There is one person whose discourse remains on the road, yet does not leave home; there is another person who leaves home, yet is not on the road.
Which of these two deserves the offerings of devas and humans? Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
When the Master saw the monk approaching, he spread out his two hands. The monk remained silent. The Master asked, "Do you understand?
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This whole lump cannot be split open; I give you two coins."
When the Master was about to pass away, he ascended the hall and said, "After my extinction, you must not extinguish my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Sansheng came forward and said, "How would we dare extinguish the Venerable Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?
The Master said, "In the future, if someone asks you, what will you say to him? Sansheng then gave a shout. The Master said, "Who knew my... [He ceased speaking.]
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was extinguished at the hands of that blind donkey. Thereupon, there is a verse:
Following the current without ceasing, one asks: "How is this? True illumination is impartial; it speaks of self and other.
Transcending form and transcending name, no one receives its transmission. Having used the "blow-off-blade," one must quickly polish it again.
Having finished speaking, he sat upright upon his Dharma seat and manifested parinirvāṇa. This was on the tenth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Xiántóng era (the Bingxū year).
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huìzhào, and his stupa was named Chénglíng.
