[Compiled under the Song Dynasty] By Yìxuán, the Zen Master Huìzhào of Línjì Monastery in Zhènzhōu. The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "In these times, those who study the Buddha-dharma..."
Furthermore, you must first seek a truly authentic insight. If you attain such authentic insight, you will remain unstained by birth and death, and you will possess freedom in going and staying.

You need not seek excellence; excellence will arrive of its own accord. My fellow practitioners of the Way, it is simply that the virtuous predecessors of old all possessed a path for transcending the ordinary.
Just as I, this mountain monk, point the way for others, my sole purpose is to ensure that you are not deluded by others.
Use it when you need to; do not hesitate any further. Why is it that students today cannot attain realization? The sickness lies in their lack of self-confidence.
If you lack confidence in yourself, you will immediately become busily bound by all external circumstances.

You are being turned around by myriad external conditions and cannot attain freedom. If you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly pursues and seeks, you will be no different from the Patriarchs and Buddhas.
Do you wish to recognize the Patriarch? He is simply the one before you who is listening to the Dharma.
If you lack faith, you will pursue it outwardly; even if you were to find something through such pursuit, it would all be nothing but words, names, and conceptual forms.

In the end, you will never grasp the ancestral intent of others; do not err, O Zen masters. If you do not encounter this at this time, you will wander through the three realms for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, pursued by pleasant appearances until you are born within the bellies of donkeys and oxen.

You seekers of the Way, according to my own realization, it is no different from that of Śākyamuni: in all the various ways we act daily, what is lacking? The divine light of the six paths has not yet...
There has been an interruption. If you can see it in this way, you will simply be a person who has nothing to do for the rest of their life.
Venerable Sir, there is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house. This is not a place where you can stay for long.

The demon of impermanence kills in a single kṣaṇa, making no distinction between noble and base, old and young. If you wish to be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, simply do not seek outside. One.
The non-conceptual light within your single thought-moment is the Dharmakāya Buddha within your own house.

The non-discriminative light within your single thought-moment is the Sambhogakāya Buddha within your own house. The light of non-distinction within your single thought-moment is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha within your own house.
These three bodies are the very person listening to the Dharma before you right now. It is simply because...
One does not run outward in pursuit; such is its efficacy. According to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, these three bodies (*kāya*) are taken as the ultimate limit.
However, from the perspective of this mountain monk, it is not so. These three bodies are merely names and also three kinds of garments.
As the ancients said: "The body is established based on meaning; the land is discussed according to essence. Thus, the *dharmatā-kāya* and the *dharmatā-kṣetra* are clearly known to be light.
"O Venerable One, you should first recognize that the person who plays with light and shadows is the fundamental source of all Buddhas.
This is the place where the followers of the Way return as their home. It is not this physical body of the four elements that understands how to preach or listen to the Dharma;

it is not the spleen, stomach, liver, or gallbladder that understands how to preach or listen to the Dharma; it is not empty space that understands how to preach or listen to the Dharma. What, then, is it?"
The expounding of the Dharma and the listening to the Dharma are these very things vividly present before your eyes.
This single, solitary luminosity is this very expounding and listening to the Dharma. If you can see it thus, you will not differ from the patriarchs and Buddhas.

Only do not let it be interrupted at any time; it is everywhere before your eyes. It is only because feelings arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because thoughts transform that the essence becomes distinct. Therefore...

Because one wanders through the three realms of existence and undergoes all manner of suffering, from the perspective of this mountain monk, there is nothing that is not profoundly deep and nothing that is not liberation.
O practitioners of the Way, the dharma of mind is formless and penetrates throughout the ten directions; when it is in the eye, it is called seeing; when it is in the ear, it is called hearing.
With the nose one smells fragrances; with the mouth one engages in discourse; with the hands one grasps and seizes; with the feet one rushes about like clouds.

Originally there was but one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious combinations. Once the single mind is absent, liberation is found everywhere. Where does the meaning of this mountain monk’s teaching lie?
It is simply because you practitioners cannot still the mind that seeks and pursues everything, and thus fall under the sway of the ancients.

"O practitioners of the Way, if you take my perspective, you will cut off the heads of both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas. Those whose minds are perfected in the ten stages are like hired laborers;
those of the two levels of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment are men bearing shackles and chains; Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like excrement in a latrine;
and Bodhi and Nirvana are like hitching posts for a donkey. Why is this so? It is simply because you, practitioners of the Way, do not penetrate the truth."
The three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are empty; it is for this reason that such obstacles exist. If one is a true practitioner of the Way, they will never be like this.
They can simply follow conditions to exhaust past karma, wearing clothes as they happen to come along. When they wish to walk, they walk; when they wish to sit, they sit.
Not for a single thought-moment do they harbor the aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood. Why is this so? An ancient said:
"If you wish to engage in practice seeking Buddhahood, know that the Buddha is but a great omen within birth-and-death. Great Virtue, time is precious;

do not merely intend to wander from house to house, laboring to study Chan and the Way, clinging to names and phrases, seeking Buddhas and Patriarchs, or seeking spiritual friends. Do not let your intentions go astray.
"Followers of the Way, you each have only one set of parents; what more do you seek? Reflect upon yourselves. An ancient said:
'Yajñadatta lost his head. When the seeking mind comes to rest, there is nothing more to do. Venerable sirs, simply maintain your natural state; do not put on a pretense.
There are some who, failing to distinguish between good and evil, immediately see gods and ghosts."

Pointing to the east while drawing in the west; wishing for fine weather or wishing for rain—those of such ilk must all pay their debts. There will come a day when they must swallow hot iron balls before Old Yama.
When the sons and daughters of good families are possessed by these same wild fox spirits and goblins, they immediately begin to act strangely.
You blind, luckless fellows, there will come a day when you must pay for your meal! The Master spoke again: "O practitioners of the Way, take heed!"
Seek the true insight. Act with unimpeded freedom throughout the world, so as not to be deluded by such spectral spirits.
Being without affairs is the state of a noble person; do not engage in further fabrication. It is simply ordinary.

If you intend to seek it outside or rely on others to find a way in, you have gone astray. If you intend to seek the Buddha, know that "Buddha" is merely a name and phrase; do you even recognize the word?

"Seeking the Dharma. The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods and ten directions have appeared solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma. Today’s practitioners of the Way likewise seek only the Dharma;
only upon attaining the Dharma is one finished. Until it is attained, one continues to revolve as before. What is this Way? The Way is the mind-dharma.
The mind-dharma is formless, penetrating through the ten directions, and is manifest and functional right before one's eyes."
People’s faith is insufficient; they merely cling to names and phrases, seeking within words and speculating on the Buddha-dharma.
This is worlds apart from the truth. O practitioners of the Way! When I, this mountain monk, preach the Dharma, what Dharma do I preach?

I preach the Dharma of the Mind-Ground, by which one can enter the mundane and the sacred, the pure and the defiled, the real and the conventional. Yet, fundamentally, it is not your own mundane, sacred, ordinary, or holy self.
One is able to bestow names upon all things—whether true or conventional, mundane or sagely—and yet neither the true, the conventional, the mundane, nor the sagely can bestow a name upon this person.
O followers of the Way, when you grasp it, you use it directly, no longer attaching names to it; this is called the "Mysterious Principle.
My preaching of the Dharma differs from that of everyone else in the world. Suppose, for instance, that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were to appear before you.
At present, each manifests a single body to inquire about the Dharma. As soon as they say, "I ask the Master," I have already discerned them.
While the old monk sits steadily, when there are further seekers who come to meet me, I have discerned them all. Why is this so? It is simply because my realization is distinct:
outwardly, I do not grasp at ordinary beings or sages; inwardly, I do not dwell in the fundamental source. Having thoroughly penetrated the original Dharma, I no longer...

"Do not doubt or err. The Master further said: "In the Buddha-dharma, there is no place where effort is applied; it is simply the ordinary state of having nothing to do. When one must defecate, one defecates; when one must urinate, one urinates;
when putting on clothes or eating, one does so; when weary, one lies down. Fools laugh at me, but the wise understand. An ancient said: "To look outward..."

Those who practice such efforts are all but foolish and stubborn fellows. You should simply take charge wherever you are; wherever you stand is the truth. When circumstances arise, they cannot be exchanged or altered.
Even if you possess habitual tendencies from the past or have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution, these will naturally become the great ocean of liberation.
Nowadays, scholars in general do not recognize the Dharma; they are like sheep that touch their noses: whenever they encounter an object, they place it indifferently into their mouths.

Such people cannot distinguish between master and servant, nor can they differentiate between host and guest. This sort of person enters the Way with a deviant mind, entering wherever there is a bustling place.
One cannot be called a true renunciant; such a person is precisely a true worldly householder. Now, one who has truly left the home-life must be able to discern the ordinary and the authentic view.
One must discern Buddha from Mara, the genuine from the counterfeit, and the mundane from the sagely.
If one can discern in this manner, they are called a true renunciant. If one cannot distinguish between Mara and Buddha, one is merely leaving one family only to enter another.
Those who remain at home are called sentient beings creating karma; they cannot yet be called true renunciants.

Right now, there is a Buddha and a Mara that are of the same substance and inseparable, like water and milk mixed together. When the king of geese drinks the milk, so should you, O enlightened practitioners:
strike both Mara and Buddha. If you love the holy and hate the ordinary, you will drift and sink within the sea of birth and death.
Question: What is the Buddha and the demon? The Master said: "The place where your single thought of doubt arises is the Buddha and the demon.

If you can penetrate the fact that the myriad dharmas are unborn and that the mind is like an illusion or a transformation—such that not a single speck of dust or a single dharma exists, and everything is pure everywhere—that is the Buddha.
Yet, 'Buddha' and 'demon' are merely the two realms of defilement and purity. From my own perspective, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being."
There is no past and no present. One who attains it simply attains it; it does not pass through time or seasons. There is no cultivation and no realization; there is no gain and no loss.
At all times, there is no other dharma whatsoever. Should there be even a single dharma that exceeds this, I would say it is like a dream or a magical illusion.
All that I, this mountain monk, have spoken is for you, O practitioners of the Way, who are now listening with solitary clarity and vivid presence right before your eyes.
This person is unimpeded everywhere, penetrating throughout the ten directions and the three realms. They enter all differentiated objects with sovereign ease, unable to be diverted or exchanged.
In a single kṣaṇa, they penetrate the Dharma-realm; meeting a Buddha, they speak of the Buddha; meeting an Ancestor, they speak of the Ancestor.
Encountering an arhat, he speaks of the arhat; encountering a hungry ghost, he speaks of the hungry ghost.

Traveling through all places and traversing the lands, he transforms sentient beings without ever for a single thought-moment being apart from this. Everywhere he goes, he is pure; his light permeates the ten directions;

the myriad dharmas are of one suchness. O practitioner of the Way! Great man, it is only today that you know there has been no matter from the beginning. It is simply because your faith was not sufficient.
Furthermore, they gallop about in every thought-moment, abandoning their heads only to seek new ones, unable to find rest for themselves.

This is like a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching who enters the Dharma-realm and manifests in a pure land, yet still feels aversion toward the mundane and aspiration for the sacred; such as these have not yet forgotten grasping and rejecting, and the mind of defilement and purity remains present.
According to the insight of the Chan school, however, this is not the case; it is simply seeing that right now there is no further time or occasion.
Wherever this mountain monk speaks, it is all intended as medicine to counteract specific ailments for a particular occasion; there is no real dharma therein at all.
If you can see it in this way, that is true renunciation. Even if one could spend ten thousand taels of gold daily, O practitioners of the Way, do not act recklessly.

To have your faces branded by the seals of teachers from all quarters, claiming "I understand Chan, I understand the Way," and to possess eloquence like a cascading torrent—all such things lead only to the construction of hell.
Regarding karma: if one is a true seeker of the Way, one does not seek worldly excellence; rather, one must urgently seek genuine insight.
Only when one attains the perfect clarity of genuine insight is one finally brought to completion.

Question: What is true and correct insight? The Master said: Simply this—whether entering the mundane or the sacred, entering defilement or purity, entering the lands of all Buddhas, entering Maitreya’s pavilion, or entering the Dharma-realm of Vairocana—in every place there appear lands undergoing formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness;
Buddhas appearing in the world and turning the Great Wheel of Dharma, and immediately entering Nirvana.
He does not perceive any signs of coming or going; seeking the birth and death [of phenomena], they are utterly unattainable.

He then enters the realm of non-arising dharmas (*anutpattika-dharmadhātu*) and travels everywhere through the various lands, entering the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha-lokadhātu*). There he perceives that all dharmas are empty in nature and that none possess substantial reality.
Only the person who listens to the Dharma without reliance—the Way-person (*mārga-pudgala*)—is the mother of all Buddhas. Therefore, the Buddha [arises] from...
Birth is without support. If one awakens to this lack of support, even Buddhahood is not attained. If one perceives attainment in such a manner, that is the true and correct understanding.

Students fail to realize this because they cling to names and phrases; they are obstructed by the names of "ordinary beings" and "sages," which thereby hinder their Dharma-eye, preventing it from becoming clear.
Indeed, the twelve divisions of the teachings are all expressions intended to manifest the truth. As for the student...
It will not. One merely gives rise to understanding based on the names and phrases that manifest [the teaching];

all of this is dependent and falls within the realm of cause and effect, such that one cannot avoid birth and death within the three realms. If you wish to attain freedom in going, staying, departing, and remaining amidst birth and death, you must right now recognize the person who hears the Dharma:
formless and signless, rootless and groundless, without a place of abiding, yet vibrantly alive and alert.
This must be the locus for ten thousand kinds of provisional designations; yet it is simply no-locus. The more you seek to grasp it, the further away it becomes;
the more you search for it, the more you miss it. It is called "the secret. O practitioners of the Way, do not mistake this dream-like, illusory companion.
In the midst of time’s passing, you will soon return to impermanence. What thing do you seek within this world to serve as liberation? You seek—what?
Take a mouthful of rice and eat it; patch your coarse robes and pass the time. For now, you must seek out a true teacher; do not be negligent or pursue pleasures until the time has passed.
Time is precious; every thought-moment is impermanent. On a gross level, one is oppressed by earth, water, fire, and wind;
on a subtle level, one is pressed by the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. O practitioners of the Way, for now you must recognize these four kinds of signlessness.
Regarding "objects" (*viṣaya*): do not allow yourself to be tossed about by objects.
Question: What are the four kinds of signless objects? The Master said: When your single thought-moment harbors doubt, you are obstructed by earth.
If your mind gives rise to a single thought of attachment, you will be drowned by water. If your mind gives rise to a single thought of anger, you will be burned by fire.

If your mind gives rise to a single thought of joy, you will be blown away by wind. If you can discern things in this way, you will not be turned by external conditions; you will employ conditions everywhere:

surging eastward and submerging westward, surging southward and submerging northward, surging in the center and submerging at the edges, or surging at the edges and submerging in the center—treading upon water as if it were earth.
The ground. Treading upon the earth as if it were water—why is this so? It is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and illusions.
O practitioner of the Way, you who are listening to the Dharma right now are not these four great elements; rather, it is that which can employ these four great elements.
If you can see in this way, then you will attain freedom in going and staying. According to my own perspective, do not disparage this teaching. If you cherish it...
The holy loathes the ordinary; thus, they are bound by the realms of the holy and the ordinary.
There is a certain class of practitioners who seek Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai—they have already made a mistake. On Mount Wutai there is no Mañjuśrī. Do you wish to recognize Mañjuśrī?

It is simply the functioning before your eyes, which remains unchanged from beginning to end. When there is no doubt in every situation, this is the living Mañjuśrī. At the very moment of your single thought—
The mind is the light of non-differentiation; everywhere, all is the true Samantabhadra. In a single thought-moment, you can naturally untie your own bonds and attain liberation wherever you are.
This is the dharma of the Avalokiteśvara Samādhi, in which all elements act as both principal and attendant; when they emerge, they emerge simultaneously.
"One is three; three is one. If you can understand it in this way, only then can you begin to study the teachings.
The Master further said: "Those who study the Way today must first have self-confidence; do not seek it outwardly.

Otherwise, you will merely ascend into the mundane realms of others and fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Even such things as 'the Patriarchs' and 'the Buddhas' are matters belonging only to the traces of the teachings."
When a person picks up a single phrase, whether it emerges from the hidden or the manifest, doubt immediately arises.
It illuminates heaven and earth, yet as they seek answers from others, they remain utterly bewildered.

Great men of character, do not merely spend your days in idle talk, debating kings and thieves, right and wrong, or appearances and wealth. Here in my mountain monastery, I make no distinction between monk and layperson; I only—
Should anyone come, recognize them completely, no matter from where they emerge. Whatever names, sounds, or phrases there may be, they are all but dreams and illusions.
Yet, the person who rides upon these conditions is the profound intent of all Buddhas. A Buddha-realm cannot call itself "a Buddha-realm" by its own power;
rather, it is this very person of no dependence who emerges riding upon the realm. If there is one...
When someone comes and asks me for the Buddha, I immediately appear from within the realm of purity.
When someone asks me about the Bodhisattva, I immediately appear from within the realm of compassion. When someone asks me about Bodhi, I immediately appear from within the realm of sublime purity.
When someone asks me about *nirvāṇa*, I respond by manifesting from the realm of quiescence. That realm consists of ten thousand varieties of differentiation, yet the person remains undifferentiated.
Therefore, I manifest forms in accordance with things, like the moon in water.

My followers, if you wish to attain that which accords with the Dharma, you must be true sons of great men; if you are withered and submissive, following along with the ground, then you shall not attain it.

Now, a vessel such as this—cracked and leaking (the character *si* pronounced *xī*, and *shà* pronounced *suòjià*)—is unfit to hold clarified butter (*tíhú*). One who possesses a great vessel simply must not allow themselves to be deluded by others;
they take charge wherever they are, and in every place where they stand, all is true. To anyone who comes before them, they shall accept nothing at all.
If you harbor a single thought of doubt, the Māra will immediately enter your mind. When a Bodhisattva doubts, the Māra of birth and death finds an opening.

You need only cease discursive thinking; do not seek anything externally. Whatever objects arise, simply reflect upon them. You must simply believe that there is not even one thing currently being used.
A single thought of yours gives rise to the three realms; following conditions and being affected by objects, it is divided into the six sense-fields. You, right now—
What is lacking in the place of application? In a single instant, one enters the pure and enters the defiled;
one enters Maitreya’s pavilion and further enters the land of the Three Eyes, traversing everywhere, seeing only empty names.

Question: What is the land of the three eyes? The Master said: "I shall enter with you into the Land of Pure Subtlety, don the robes of purity, and preach the Dharma-body Buddha. Then we shall enter the Land of Non-differentiation, don the robes of non-differentiation."
To speak of the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*), one enters the land of liberation and wears garments of radiance;

to speak of the Transformation Body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*), these three eyes and their lands are all transformations based upon [the source]. According to the masters of the sūtras and śāstras, they take the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) as the root and the Reward and Transformation bodies as its functions.
From the perspective of this mountain monk, the Dharma Body itself does not understand how to preach the Dharma; therefore, the ancients said:

The "body" is established based on its meaning, while the "land" is discussed according to its substance. Thus, the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are clearly known to be constructs of the Dharma.
Relying on the pervasive realm of lands is like using an empty fist or yellow leaves to deceive small children; it is like [seeking] thorns, water chestnuts, and brambles upon a dry bone.
What juice are you seeking? Outside the mind there is no dharma; within, it is likewise unattainable. What thing are you searching for?
You all speak of cultivation and realization—do not be mistaken. Even if there were something to be attained through cultivation, it would all be the karma of birth and death.

When you say that the six perfections and ten thousand practices are to be cultivated together, I see them all as the creation of karma. To seek the Buddha and seek the Dharma is itself the creation of ground [for rebirth].
The karma of the hells. Seeking to become a bodhisattva is also the creation of karma. Reading sutras and studying the teachings is also the creation of karma.
The Buddhas and the Patriarchs are people of no affairs; therefore, they possess both the tainted and conditioned, as well as the untainted and unconditioned, which constitute pure karma.
There is a certain class of blind shavelings who, having eaten their fill, sit in meditation and practice contemplation, seizing upon thoughts and outflows so as not to let them escape.
To let go and arise, to loathe clamor and seek stillness—this is the dharma of the non-Buddhists. The Patriarch said:

"If you dwell the mind to look for stillness, raise the mind to shine outward, gather the mind to clarify inward, or concentrate the mind to enter meditative absorption—all such types of practice are merely contrived efforts.
As for you, who are now listening to the Dharma in this way, how do you intend to cultivate it, realize it, or adorn it?"

That is not something to be cultivated; it is not something to be attained through the accumulation of adornments. If you were to teach others how to adorn it, then all things would be adorned for you.

Do not make a mistake, O traveler! You take the words from the mouths of these ordinary teachers as being the True Path and the inconceivable power of a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), yet you think, "I am but an ordinary person. Do not [think] so.
I dare not fathom that other venerable elder. You, blind from birth, have spent your entire life with only this kind of understanding;
you have brought shame upon those two eyes of yours. You sit there shivering and numb, like a donkey’s back frozen on ice.

I do not dare disparage the good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), for I fear creating verbal karma. O practitioner of the Way! Only a great spiritual friend dares to disparage the Buddhas and the Patriarchs.
This is not the way of the world. You reject the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and insult those who are but children; you seek out people among both the rebellious and the compliant.
Therefore, for twelve years I have sought even a single particle of karmic nature the size of a mustard seed, yet it could not be found.
If you were like the "New Bride" Chan Master, you would immediately be terrified and driven out of the monastery, not being given food to eat, and remaining unsettled and unhappy.
Since ancient times, when the predecessors of old went everywhere and people did not believe them, and they were successively expelled, it was only then that they knew their own worth.
If everyone everywhere were willing to accept you, what would you be capable of accomplishing? Therefore, when the lion roars once, the jackal’s head splits open. O practitioners of the Way! All...
I have just said that there is a Way to be cultivated and a Dharma to be realized. You, however, say: "What Dharma do you realize? What Way do you cultivate?
What is lacking in your practice that you must supplement? Where must it be repaired? Later generations will not understand these petty monks;
they will immediately place their faith in such wild fox spirits and demons, accepting their claims and binding others with talk of "principle" and "practice."
One must guard and cherish the three karmas; only then can one attain Buddhahood. Such a teaching is like a fine spring rain. An ancient said:

"When you encounter a person who has realized the Way on the road, first of all, do not speak of the Way. Therefore it is said: "If a person cultivates the Way but the Way does not proceed," [it is because they have spoken of it].
Myriad delusive states compete to arise; when the sword of wisdom emerges, not a single thing remains. Before the bright side has appeared, the dark side is already luminous.
Thus the ancients said: "The ordinary mind is the Way. O Great Virtue, what are you seeking?
Right now, before your eyes, this man who listens to the Dharma without dependence discerns everything with vivid clarity; nothing is ever lacking. If you wish to attain it—
This is no different from the ancestral Buddhas; simply see it thus and do not allow yourself to be misled by doubt.

When your mind does not differ from moment to moment, this is called the "living ancestral mind. If there were any difference, then essence and appearance would be distinct. Because the mind does not differ, essence and appearance are not separate.
Question: "What is the state where mind and mind do not differ? The Master said: "The moment you intend to ask, it has already become different.
Nature and characteristics are each distinct. O follower of the Way, do not err! All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, lack self-nature and lack the nature of arising;
they possess nothing but empty names, and even these names are empty. You simply take these idle names to be real—this is a great error."

Whatever exists is entirely a realm of transformation based upon something else. There is a basis for bodhi, a basis for nirvana, a basis for liberation, a basis for the three bodies, a basis for object and wisdom, a basis for bodhisattvas, and a basis for buddhas. What do you seek within this realm of transformation based upon something else?
Even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are merely used-up toilet paper. A buddha is an illusory manifestation.
"Body! This patriarch is an old bhikṣu. Are you still merely your mother’s natural flesh? If you seek the Buddha, you will be seized by the demon of the Buddha;
if you seek the patriarch, you will be bound by the patriarch. If you have any seeking at all, it is suffering; it is better to rest in non-action.
There is a certain class of shaven-headed bhikṣus who say to students: 'The Buddha is the ultimate,' and so on for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas..."
Only after fulfilling the fruits of cultivation through *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas does one finally attain the Way.
O follower of the Way, if you say that the Buddha is ultimate, for what reason did he lie down on his side and pass away between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara eighty years later?
Where is the Buddha now? It is clearly known that he is no different from me in birth and death. You say that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute the Buddha;
then a Wheel-Turning Sage King should also be a Tathāgata. It is clearly known that these are but illusory transformations. As an ancient said:

The Tathāgata displays the marks of his entire body merely to accord with the sentiments of worldly beings; fearing that people might give rise to the view of nihilism, he provisionally establishes empty names.
He speaks of the thirty-two [major] and eighty [minor] marks as a mere hollow sound. To possess a body is not the essence of awakening; formlessness is the true form.
"You say that the Buddha possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and is thus inconceivable.
Yet all the devas, ṛṣis, asuras, and powerful spirits also possess supernormal powers; should they not then be Buddhas? You followers of the Way, do not make such an error! Consider this:
when the asuras fought with Śakra, Lord of Devas, and were defeated, they led eighty-four thousand of their retinues into the hollow of a lotus fiber to hide."

"Is this not the holy one? As this mountain monk has pointed out, these are all instances of karmic supernormal powers (*karmarddhi*) and dependent supernormal powers (*āśrayarddhi*). As for the six supernormal powers of a Buddha, it is not so:
entering the realm of form, he is not deluded by form; entering the realm of sound, he is not deluded by sound; entering the realm of fragrance..."

They are not deluded by fragrance and enter the realm of taste; they are not deluded by taste and enter the realm of touch; they are not deluded by touch and enter the realm of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
They are not deluded by mental phenomena. Thus, they realize that the six kinds—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—are all characterized by emptiness.

They cannot bind this person who walks the path of non-reliance. Although they possess the substance of the five aggregates and outflows, they are nonetheless masters of terrestrial supernatural powers.
O followers of the Way: the true Buddha is formless; the true Dharma is signless. You merely fashion patterns and models upon these illusory transformations.
Even if you were to obtain such a thing, it would all be nothing more than a wild fox spirit or a demon; it is by no means the true Buddha—it is an externalist teaching.
Regarding this view: A true student of the Way does not grasp for Buddhas, nor grasp for Bodhisattvas or Arhats, nor grasp for the excellence of the triple world.
They are utterly and independently liberated, unconfined by external things. Even if heaven and earth were overturned, they would have no further doubts.
The Buddhas of the ten directions appear before me, yet not a single thought of joy arises. The three miserable realms and the hells manifest all at once, yet not a single thought of fear arises.
Why is this so? Because I perceive that the characteristics of all phenomena are empty: they exist when transformed, but are non-existent when untransformed.
The triple world is but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Therefore, as for dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky, what need is there to grasp them? There is only the Way.
The Dharma currently manifest before one’s eyes causes those who listen to it to enter fire without being burned and enter water without being drowned.
To enter the three miserable realms—the hells—is like strolling through a garden; to enter the realms of hungry ghosts and animals is to remain free from retribution.

Why is this so? Because there is no dharma that can be disparaged. If you love the noble and hate the ordinary, you will float and sink within the ocean of birth and death; for afflictions arise from the mind.
There is [no need for effort]. Without a mind, what can afflictions constrain? Do not trouble yourself with discriminating grasping at signs; you will naturally attain the Way in an instant.
If you intend to learn by following others through a weary, laborious process, you will ultimately remain within birth and death throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
It would be better to have no concerns and sit cross-legged in a corner of a bed within a forest thicket.
"Followers of the Way, it is like when students from various quarters come here. Once the host and guest have met, there is immediately a single phrase that precedes all else.

When a student brings forth a word of expedient means and hurls it toward the corner of the good teacher's mouth, look and see whether you recognize it or not. If you recognize it as an objective state, seize it and cast it away."
"Into the pit! The student immediately acts as usual; thereafter, he seeks the words of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who again seizes him as before.
The student says, "What superior wisdom! You are a great spiritual friend. [The teacher] then says, "You truly do not know good from evil.
It is as if the spiritual friend were to take up a piece of earth as an object and play with it before you; you, however, fail to discern it."
Having attained mastery over the lower [realms], he was no longer deluded by external objects. The Good Friend (Kalyāṇamitra) then manifested half his body; the student let out a shout.
The Good Friend further entered into all paths of differentiated speech to provoke him; the student said, "I do not recognize you, you old bald-headed fellow!
The Good Friend sighed in praise, saying, "A truly authentic seeker of the Way."
Suppose there are spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in various directions who cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

When a student comes to ask about bodhi and nirvāṇa, or the three bodies (trikāya), the objective realm, and wisdom, these blind teachers proceed to explain them for him. When they are rebuked by that student, they take up their staffs and beat him, saying he lacks propriety.
This is simply because you, as a spiritual friend, lack eyes; you must not be angry with him. There is a certain class of people...
"You ignorant bald slave who cannot distinguish good from evil! You point east and mark west; you favor fine weather and fine rain;

you favor the lanterns and the pillar! Look at your eyebrows—how many hairs do they have? This [exchange] possesses the spark of an opportunity; yet the student does not understand it, and his mind immediately goes mad.
People of this sort are all nothing but wild fox spirits, enchantments, and demons. When those who truly seek the Way encounter them, they laugh heartily and say:
"Blind old bald-pated fellows! You delude and confuse the people of the world."
"Followers of the Way, those who have left the household life must first study the Way.

Just as I myself, in days past, devoted my attention to the *vinaya* for several decades and also sought its meaning within the sutras and śāstras, I only later realized that these were medicinal prescriptions for saving the world."
Having thus cast aside all conventional explanations, he went forth to seek the Way and study Zen. Later, upon meeting a great *kalyāṇamitra*, his eye of the Way finally became clear;
only then did he recognize the elder monks of the world and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. This was not something he understood from birth;
rather, it was attained through investigation and refinement. One day, he realized this for himself. "O practitioners of the Way! If you wish to attain [this],..."
View and understand according to the Dharma; simply do not allow yourself to be deluded by others. Whether facing inward or outward, kill whatever you encounter.

Kill the Buddha when you meet the Buddha; kill the Patriarchs when you meet the Patriarchs; kill the Arhats when you meet the Arhats; kill your parents when you meet your parents; kill your kinsmen when you meet your kinsmen.
Only then will you attain liberation, no longer constrained by external things, but penetrating through to freedom and self-mastery, just as those who study the Way in all quarters do.

Flowing forth—there has never been anything that does not emerge in dependence upon an object. Here in this place, I strike from the very beginning: when it emerges from the hand, I strike at the hand;
when it emerges from the mouth, I strike at the mouth; when it emerges from the eyes, I strike at the eyes.
I have yet to see a single thing emerge in total independence. All of these are merely following the idle conceptual realms of those ancients. I have none of this.
This single Dharma given to people is nothing other than for curing illness and untying bonds. You practitioners from all quarters, try to come forth without relying on external things;
I wish to deliberate with you. For ten or five years, not a single person has appeared.
They are all merely spirits of grass, leaves, bamboo, and wood, or wild solitary demons, who blindly gnaw at all manner of dung-heaps—nothing but blind fools wasting their efforts.
Wasting the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions, you claim to be a renunciant and hold such views as these:
you tell others there is no Buddha and no Dharma, nothing to cultivate and nothing to realize. What do you hope to seek by wandering about in this manner? You blind fellow!
To place a head upon a head—what is it that you lack, O practitioner? That which you employ before your very eyes is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Yet you do not believe this, but seek further outwardly; do not err. There is no dharma to be found outside, nor can it be obtained within.
Rather than grasping at the words from my mouth, it would be better for you to cease your activities and go about without concern. As for those who have already set out...
Do not continue. As for those who have not yet arisen, do not attempt to make them arise; this would surpass ten years of your traveling on pilgrimage.
From the perspective of this mountain monk, there are not so many varieties as you imagine; it is simply the ordinary matter of wearing clothes and eating food, passing the time without affairs.
You who come from all quarters all have the intention to seek the Buddha, to seek the Dharma, to seek liberation, and to seek deliverance from the three realms—how deluded you are!
Person, where do you wish to go out from? The Buddhas and patriarchs are merely names and phrases used for binding. Do you wish to recognize the triple world?
It does not depart from the very mind-ground upon which you are listening to the Dharma right now. A single thought-moment of greed in your mind is the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*);
a single thought-moment of anger is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); a single thought-moment of delusion is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is yours.
The furniture within a house does not itself say, "I am the house.
It is you, O Great Virtue, the person who right before your eyes is luminously aware and illuminates all manner of things, who bestows names upon the triple world. O Great Virtue!
The physical body composed of the four great elements is impermanent—down to the spleen, stomach, liver, and gallbladder, as well as the hair, fur, nails, and teeth.
One perceives only the empty nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*). When your single thought-moment comes to rest, it is called the Bodhi tree;
when your single thought-moment cannot come to rest, it is called the tree of ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance has no place of abiding; ignorance has no beginning or end. You...

If you cannot bring your mind to rest in every thought-moment, you will immediately ascend the tree of ignorance and enter the six realms and four modes of birth, with fur upon your body and horns upon your head.
If you can bring it to rest, this is the realm of the pure body. When not a single thought arises, you have ascended the Bodhi tree;

there you possess the supernatural powers and transformations of the three realms, manifesting bodies through the power of intention, enjoying the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, and radiating light from your body.

Self-illumination. One thinks of garments of a thousand layers of fine silk; one thinks of food with a hundred flavors complete; furthermore, there are no incidental ailments. Enlightenment has no dwelling place;
therefore, there is no one who attains it. O practitioner of the Way! Great man, what else could you possibly doubt? As for the functioning before your eyes, who else is it?
Seize it and use it immediately; do not cling to names. This is called the Mysterious Principle (*xuanzhi*). The Principle.
Do not disdain the Dharma that you have seen and attained. An ancient said: "The mind turns with the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound.
Following the flow and recognizing one's nature, there is neither joy nor sorrow. O practitioners of the Way! According to the insights of the Chan school, life and death are but natural occurrences.
Those who study must be extremely careful. It is like the meeting of host and guest, where there is immediately an exchange of words.
Sometimes he manifests a form; sometimes his entire body acts; sometimes he employs skillful means through expressions of joy or anger; sometimes he appears as half his body;
sometimes he rides a lion, or sometimes he rides an elephant king. If there is one who has attained true and correct awakening, he may suddenly shout and first pull out a lacquer basin.
The good teacher (kalyāṇamitra) fails to discern it as an objective condition and, stepping onto that very condition, puts on airs and makes a display, seeking to learn from him.
The person then shouts. The one before him refuses to let go. This is a terminal illness; it cannot be cured. This is called "the guest looking at the host.
Alternatively, it may be that a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) does not bring forth any object, but seizes [the student] immediately according to the point of their inquiry.
When the student is seized, they refuse to let go even unto death. This is "the host looking at the guest. Or there may be a student who should be one who is pure.
When an object appeared before the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the spiritual friend discerned it and seized it, throwing it into a pit.
The student said, "Excellent! The spiritual friend then exclaimed, "Alas! You do not distinguish between good and evil! Thereupon, the student prostrated himself.
This is called "the master looking at the master. There may be a student who comes before a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) already wearing a cangue and shackles;

the spiritual friend then places another layer of cangue and shackles upon them, and the student rejoices. Since neither can distinguish between themselves, this is called "the guest looking at the guest.
Venerable sir, what I have thus set forth is entirely for the purpose of discerning demons from the authentic, and knowing the false from the true.
"Followers of the Way, the true reality is truly difficult to grasp. The Buddha-dharma is profound and mysterious;

even when one understands it to some extent, I, this mountain monk, spend the entire day explaining it to them, yet the students pay no heed. Though they have trodden over it ten thousand times underfoot, it is pitch black and void, without a single form or trace.
It is vividly and singularly luminous, yet the students cannot believe it, and so they instead cling to names and phrases."
He developed an understanding. Having reached fifty years of age, he had spent his time merely carrying corpses for others, wandering all over the world with his pack on his back;

the day will surely come when he must pay for his straw sandals. "Virtuous One," the mountain monk says that there is no dharma outside, yet the student does not understand and instead forms an understanding within.
He then leans against the wall and sits, pressing his tongue against the upper palate, remaining in a state of profound stillness and motionlessness.
To take this as the Buddha-dharma of our ancestral gate is a great error.
If you take this unmoving, pure state to be it, you are identifying ignorance as the master. As the ancients said: "A deep pit of profound darkness."
This is indeed truly terrifying. If you were to identify that which moves as being it, then all grasses and trees would understand movement, and they should therefore be the Way.
However, that which moves is the element of wind, while that which does not move is the element of earth. Both movement and non-movement are devoid of intrinsic nature.
If you try to seize it at the place where it moves, it stands at the place where there is no movement.
If you try to seize him while remaining in the unmoving state, he will stand in the moving state; it is like a fish hidden in a spring that stirs up waves and leaps forth of its own accord.
Venerable Sir, movement and non-movement are two kinds of objects. Does the man who walks without reliance employ movement or non-movement?
It is like when students from all quarters come here; I, this mountain monk, sever them according to their three types of faculties.
If one with middling or inferior faculties comes, I immediately seize their object but do not remove their dharma.

If one with middling or superior faculties comes, I simply seize both their object and their dharma. If one with the highest faculties comes, I seize both their object, their dharma, and their person.
If someone with extraordinary insight comes, I, this mountain monk, manifest my total functioning here, without passing through stages.

"Root-capacity. Venerable Sir, when one arrives here, the place where the student exerts effort does not admit even a breath of air; the flash of a stone-fire or a bolt of lightning has already passed.
If the student’s eye wavers for a moment, there is no connection. To conceive a thought is to err; to stir a single念 (mental state) is to go astray.
If there is anyone who understands, it is not apart from what is before one's eyes. Venerable Sir, you are carrying a beggar’s sack and a burden of dung by the side of the house."
Go! Seek the Buddha, seek the Dharma. Do you recognize that very one who is now thus rushing about in search? It is lively and alert; it has no roots or branches.
It cannot be gathered by blocking it, nor can it be dispersed by pushing it away. If you seek it, you move further from it; if you do not seek it, it is already before your eyes.
Its spiritual resonance addresses your ears. If a person does not believe this, their hundred years of toil will be in vain. O followers of the Way, in a single kṣaṇa—
In an instant, he entered the Flower Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*). He entered the realm of Vairocana; he entered the realm of liberation;
he entered the realm of supernormal powers; he entered the realm of purity. He entered the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); he entered the defiled and the pure; he entered the mundane and the sagely.
Entering the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, one searches everywhere, yet finds neither birth nor death;
there is only an empty name, like a phantom or a flower in the sky—do not trouble yourself to grasp it. Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once.
O practitioners of the Way! This mountain monk’s Buddha-dharma has been transmitted directly and authentically from Master Mayu, through Master Danxia, to Daoyi of this land.
Master [Nanyue] Huishan trod upon stones at Mount Lu; traveling this path throughout the world, no one could believe him, and all raised slander.
As for Master Daoyi’s way of acting—pure and without admixture—though there were three hundred or five hundred students, none of them perceived the Master’s intent.
As for Master [Dongshan] of Mount Lu’s sudden, authentic application in both favorable and adverse circumstances, the students...
Its limits are unfathomable, and all are utterly bewildered. Take, for example, Master Danxia, who played with the pearl, appearing and disappearing;

whenever a student approached, he would invariably scold them—his application was as bitter as Huangbo’s, and one could not get near him. Or take Shigong’s application: he sought the person upon the arrowhead, so that all who came were struck with fear.
As for my own application today: [The text here implies a contrast with the preceding masters, suggesting a different pedagogical approach.]

Truly accomplishing creation and destruction, playing with spiritual transformations, entering all realms, remaining unburdened wherever one goes, and not being swayed by external objects—yet whenever someone comes seeking me, I immediately go out to look at them.
They do not recognize me, so I put on several kinds of robes and act like an ordinary person to lead them toward understanding. Alas!
They follow my words and phrases exclusively; what a pity! These blind shaven-headed ones, these sightless people, are grasping [at shadows].
I am wearing clothes; I recognize blue, yellow, red, and white. I take them off and enter the realm of purity.
As soon as the student sees this, he gives rise to longing and desire. I take them off again, and the student loses his mind, wandering about in a frantic daze, saying, "I have no clothes!
I then say to him, "Do you recognize me, the person who was wearing clothes? Suddenly, he turns his head back and recognizes me.
"I have understood, Venerable One. Do not mistake the robe for the truth; the robe cannot move. It is the person who can wear the robe.
There is the robe of purity, the robe of non-arising, the robe of bodhi, the robe of nirvana, the robe of the patriarchs, and the robe of the Buddhas, Venerable One."

All sounds, names, and phrases are merely transformations of clothing. They are stirred up from the ocean of vital energy at the navel wheel, and through the clashing of the teeth, their meaning is formed. It is clear that these are illusory manifestations.
Venerable sir, external vocal karma and internal mental factors arise through volition and mindfulness—all of them are but clothing. You simply recognize them as such and wear them.

This is considered a true understanding. Even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would still be nothing more than the "penetration of clothing"—merely wandering through the three realms and cycling through birth and death.

It is not as good as being free from affairs, where upon meeting one does not recognize the other, and conversing together, one does not know the other's name. This is because contemporary students fail to attain this;
they take names and words to be understanding, copying the speech of dead old men onto their great tablets, layer upon layer, five times over.
To hide it within one's bosom and not allow others to see it, claiming it is the profound essence and treating it as something to be cherished—this is a great error. You blind fellow!
What kind of juice are you seeking on a withered bone? There is a certain class of people who do not distinguish between good and evil;
they take the meaning from the teachings and speculate upon them to construct phrases and meanings. It is like taking a lump of excrement into one’s mouth, spitting it out, and giving it to another.
Such people are like worldly folk playing the game of "whispered commands. They have wasted their entire lives in vain.

Though they say they have left the household life, when questioned about the Buddha-dharma, they immediately remain speechless and at a loss for words. Their eyes are like pitch-black pits, and their mouths are like wooden planks.
Those of this sort, when Maitreya appears in the world, shall be transported to another world-system and made to undergo retribution in hell.
"Alas, Venerable Sir! Why do you travel to all quarters seeking some external thing? Your footstool is wide enough;
there is no Buddha to be sought, no Way to be realized, and no Dharma to be attained. To seek outside for a Buddha with form is not like you.
If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separated. O seeker of the Way, the true Buddha has no form; the true Way has no [attributes]."

The essence is the true Dharma without marks; the three dharmas blend and fuse, merging into a single place. Since they cannot be distinguished, such beings are called the "busy-busy sentient beings of karmic consciousness."
Question: What are the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Path? We beg the Master for instruction. The Master said: "The Buddha is the purity of the mind.
The Dharma is the luminosity of the mind. The Path is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere. These three are one."
All these are merely empty names and lack substantial reality. For instance, when Master Zhi was a practitioner, his mindfulness was uninterrupted from moment to moment.
Since the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he sought only a person who would not be deluded by others.

Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he attained realization in a single word; only then did he realize that all his previous efforts had been in vain. Today, I, this mountain monk, see it clearly.
The state [of realization] is no different from that of the patriarchs and Buddhas. If one attains it within the first phrase, one serves as a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas.
If one attains it within the second phrase, one serves as a teacher to humans and devas. If one attains it within the third phrase, one is unable to save even oneself.
Question: "What is the meaning of coming from the West? The Master said: "If there were a meaning, you would not even be able to save yourself. Question:
"Since there is no meaning, how did the Second Patriarch obtain the Dharma? The Master said: "To 'obtain' it is precisely not to obtain it. Question:
"If it is indeed not obtained, what is the meaning of this non-obtaining? The Master said: "It is because you have been running and seeking everywhere, and your mind has been unable to rest."
According to the words of the Patriarch: "Alas, O man! You are seeking your head with your head.

If you, upon hearing these words, immediately turn the light back upon yourself and reflect within, seeking nothing else, and realize that your own body and mind are no different from those of the Patriarchs and Buddhas—being thus free from affairs in this very moment—only then can it be called "attaining the Dharma.
Venerable Sir, at this time, this mountain monk has no choice but to speak; I have exhausted my meager talent to deliver these words.
Do not make a mistake. According to my own perspective, there are truly not so many varieties of principles. When you need them, you use them; when you do not, you simply let them rest.

For instance, what is preached everywhere as the "six perfections and myriad practices" being the Buddha-dharma—I say these are merely the gate of adornment and the gate of Buddha-activity, not the Buddha-dharma itself. This even extends to observing fasts and precepts, or carrying oil without spilling a drop. I say:
The eyes do not see clearly; one must exhaustively repay one's debts. The day will come when you must pay for the food provided. Why is this so?
Because you have entered the Way without penetrating its principle, you must return the offerings of the faithful to their bodies. At eighty-one years of age, the elder’s tree will no longer grow.

Even such practices as sleeping alone on a solitary peak, eating only one meal before noon, sitting long without lying down, and practicing the Way during the six periods of the day—all these are merely the accumulation of karma.
People—even their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains; their kingdoms, cities, wives, and children; their elephants, horses, and the seven treasures—all these they give away in charity.
Such views as these arise because they perceive the body and mind as suffering, yet they still invite evil retributions. It is better to remain in a state of non-action, pure and unadulterated.
Even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Grounds who have reached the fullness of their resolve all seek this. O practitioner of the Way, its traces are utterly unfindable.
For this reason, the devas rejoice and the earth deities support his feet; there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not offer praise.
Why is this so? Because the path of the person who now listens to the Dharma leaves no trace behind.
Question: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he did not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
I do not yet understand the meaning of this; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said: "Mahābhijñā (Great Penetration) refers to oneself.
To penetrate everywhere that the myriad dharmas are without nature and without marks is called 'Great Penetration. Jñānābhibhū (Victorious Wisdom) refers to all..."

Abiding without doubt and not grasping at a single dharma is called "supreme wisdom. A Buddha is one whose mind is pure and luminous, penetrating throughout the Dharma-realm; thus, they are named "Buddha.
As for "sitting at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas," this refers to the ten pāramitās. Regarding "the Buddha-dharma not appearing before one":
since the Buddha is fundamentally unborn and the Dharma is fundamentally unceasing, how could there be anything further that appears? One cannot achieve [realization] in such a manner.
Regarding the Buddha-way: a Buddha need not become a Buddha again. As the ancients said: "The Buddha is always in the world, yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
O practitioner of the Way (*dōryū*), if you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not follow the discrimination of objective conditions. Therefore, when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. The world and...
It transcends the world. There is no Buddha and no Dharma; it does not manifest before one, nor has it ever been lost.

Should there be such things, they are all merely names, phrases, and sentences used to guide the young, established as a prescription for the illness to reveal names and terms. Yet names and terms do not constitute themselves as names and terms;
rather, they are simply that which is bright and vivid, the discerning awareness, the hearing and knowing, and the illuminating light right before your eyes. Rest here.
"O Virtuous One, one must commit the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) before one can attain liberation.

Question: "What are the five acts of immediate retribution? The Master said: "Killing one's father, harming one's mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and burning scriptures and images—these are the five acts of immediate retribution. Question: "What is the father? The Master said: [The text continues from here].

Ignorance is the father. If you, in a single thought-moment, seek the place where it arises and ceases and cannot find it—like an echo in space, being without concern wherever you go—this is called "killing the father.
[The student asks: "What is the mother? The Master says: "Craving is the mother.
If you, in a single thought-moment, enter into the realm of desire and seek that craving, you see only the empty nature of all phenomena; being without attachment everywhere, this is called..."
[The questioner asked: "What is meant by 'harming one's mother'? The Master said:

"If, within the pure *dharmadhātu*, you do not give rise to a single thought of conceptual understanding, and thus remain without discrimination in every situation—this is what is meant by 'shedding the Buddha’s blood. [The questioner asked:

"What is meant by 'breaking the harmonious Sangha'? The Master said: "When a single thought-moment of yours directly penetrates the fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*), such that they are like space and non-existent."
[Question: "What constitutes the breaking of the harmony of the Sangha? And what is meant by 'burning the scriptures and images'? [The Master] said:

"To see that causes and conditions are empty, the mind is empty, and dharmas are empty—to reach a definitive realization in a single thought-moment where all is transcendent and without affairs—this is precisely what it means to burn the scriptures and images.
Venerable One, if you can penetrate this way, you will avoid being obstructed by the names of 'ordinary' or 'saintly. For you have been merely pointing with an empty fist."
Superior birth is true liberation. Within the phenomena of the faculties and their objects, you have falsely fabricated delusions;
you disparage yourself and become disheartened, saying, "I am an ordinary person; he is a sage. You have been born many times as a bald-headed monk, yet what urgency do you feel toward death?
Donning the skin of a lion while still howling like a jackal, you, a great man, fail to manifest the breath of a great man. You refuse to believe in the very things within your own house.
Thus you merely seek outwardly, following the idle names and phrases of the ancients. Relying on the dark to gain the light, you are unable to maintain penetration;
whenever you encounter an object, you become conditioned by it, and whenever you encounter a defilement, you grasp at it. Delusion arises at every touch, and you have no standard of your own.

You practitioners of the Way, do not take what this mountain monk says as authoritative. Why? Because these words have no foundation. For a single moment, they paint over the entirety of empty space, like a work of colored painting.
"O followers of the Way, do not take the Buddha as the ultimate. My view is that [the Buddha] is like a latrine hole;
Bodhisattvas and Arhats are all merely shackles and fetters used to bind people. This is why Mañjuśrī took up his sword to slay Gautama, and Aṅgulimāla brandished his blade to harm the Śākyas.
O followers of the Way, there is no Buddha to be attained—not even the Three Vehicles or the Five Natures. Thus it is said. Perfectly...
The traces of the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) all constitute a single occasion where medicine and disease treat one another; there are no real dharmas whatsoever.
Even if such things were to exist, they are merely conventional expressions set forth through written characters, arranged and provisionally explained in this way.

O followers of the Way, there are a certain class of shaven-headed ones who apply their efforts toward that inner realm, intending to seek the dharma that transcends the world; they have erred. If a person seeks the Buddha, it is...
If a person seeks the Buddha, they lose the Buddha; if a person seeks the Way, they lose the Way; if a person seeks the Patriarchs, they lose the Patriarchs.
Venerable Sir, do not err! For now, I shall not accept your mastery of the sutras and treatises, nor will I accept you as a king or a great minister.
I do not take your eloquence that flows like a rushing river; nor do I take your cleverness or wisdom. I require only your true and correct understanding. O practitioner of the Way!
Even if you could explain a hundred volumes of sutras and treatises, it would not equal a single master who is free from concerns.

If you possess such intellectual understanding, you will look down upon others with contempt, fostering the strife of victory and defeat, the demon of *asura*, and the ignorance of self and other. Long...
Regarding the karma of hell: Take for example the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra, who, despite his understanding of the twelvefold teachings, fell into hell in his very body;

the great earth could not contain him. It would have been better to simply rest in non-action: when hunger comes, eat; when sleep comes, close your eyes. Fools may laugh at me, but the wise alone understand.
O followers of the Way, do not seek within words and letters; the mind becomes weary and exhausted by such efforts—just inhale the cool air.
It is of no benefit. It is not as good as realizing in a single thought that dependent origination is unborn, thereby transcending the Three Vehicles.

You provisional practitioners and Bodhisattvas of great virtue, do not let the days pass by in negligence. When I, this mountain monk, had not yet attained insight in the past, everything was pitch black;
I could not let my time pass in vain. With a burning belly and a restless mind, I hurried about seeking the Way. Only after returning with strength did I finally arrive today.
I have been conversing with fellow practitioners in this manner. I urge all you practitioners: do not seek out the world for the sake of food and clothing.
The world is easy to pass through, but a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is difficult to encounter; they appear but once in an age, like the udumbara flower.

You have heard from various quarters that an old man named Linji has appeared, and you immediately intend to pose difficult questions to him. But you shall not succeed; I, this mountain monk, will respond to you with my entire being.
When a student attempts to open their eyes to the emptiness of phenomena, their mouth is rendered entirely unable to move; they remain dazed, not knowing how to answer me.
I say to them: "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure. Yet everywhere you go, you do nothing but point to your chest and nod in agreement.
"You claim you understand Chan and understand the Way; three or two of you have reached this point and can do nothing about it. Alas!
With this very body and mind, you travel everywhere flapping those two pieces of skin, deceiving the common folk. The day will come when you shall eat iron rods!"
Such are not the sons of the renunciant; they are all subsumed within the realm of the asuras. As for the Way of ultimate truth, it is not sought through contentious debate.

While vigorous discourse and resonant eloquence may be used to crush the heterodox, when it comes to the successive transmission from Buddha to Buddha and Patriarch to Patriarch, there is no other intent whatsoever.

Should there be verbal teachings, they fall within the scope of transformative ritual; the Three Vehicles and Five Natures, or the causes and effects of humans and devas—these are not like the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
Furthermore, the youth Sudhana did not seek out faults. Great Virtue, do not misapply your mind.
Just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, you carry such [faults] about, intending to wander through the world, thereby giving rise to the obstacle of views which hinders you.
In the mind, the sun rises without clouds; it adorns the heavens and shines everywhere. In the eyes, there is no film; in the sky, there are no flowers.

O practitioner of the Way, if you wish to attain accord with the Dharma, simply do not give rise to doubt. When extended, it encompasses the entire dharma-realm; when withdrawn, not even a hair’s breadth is established.
It is vividly and individually luminous, never lacking anything. The eyes do not see it, and the ears do not hear it—what thing can you call it?
An ancient said: "To describe it as a single thing is to miss the mark. You need only look for yourself; what more is there?
Even speaking of it would be inexhaustible. Each of you must exert yourselves. Be careful."

While the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at Longgang. When Longgang ascended the hall, the Master stepped forward and asked, "Without deploying any sharp edge or blade, how does one achieve victory?
Longgang remained seated. The Master said, "Great Teacher of Wisdom, surely you have some skillful means?
Longgang stared at him with wide eyes and said, "Ha! The Master pointed his finger and said, "This old fellow has met his defeat today."
When he arrived at Sanfeng, he asked Master Ping, "Where have you come from?
The Master said, "From Huangbo. Ping said, "What words or phrases did Huangbo speak? The Master said, "Last night, the Golden Ox was covered in mud and mire;
even until now, his tracks are nowhere to be seen. Ping said, "The golden wind blows through the jade flute; who is it that knows this sound? The Master said, "[He] is here."
Directly penetrating ten thousand layers of barriers. Not dwelling within the azure heavens. Píng said: "Your question, sir, was far too high. The Master said:
"A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick; it breaks through the surging green waves. Píng said: "Sit for a while and drink some tea.
He asked again: "Where have you recently departed from? The Master said: "Lóngguāng (Dragon Light). Píng said: "How has Lóngguāng been lately?"
The Master [Zhaozhou] then went out and arrived at Daci.
Daci was sitting within the abbot’s quarters. The Master asked, "What is it like when one sits upright in the abbot's quarters?
Daci said, "A cold pine tree, one color, a thousand years of separation; a village elder, withered flowers, ten million springs. The Master said, "Now..."
Gucheng said, "The eternal wisdom-body transcends the nation; the three mountains lock away ten thousand layers of barriers. Chuanzi gave a shout. The Master also shouted.
Chuanzi asked, "What are you doing? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
When he arrived at Huayan in Xiangzhou, Huayan leaned on his staff and made the gesture of falling asleep. The Master said, "Old monk, why are you dozing off?
Huayan replied, "An adept Chan guest is truly not like others. The Master said, "Attendant, bring some tea for the old monk to drink.
Huayan then called for the *vinaya-dhara* (chant leader) and said, "Arrange for this *upadhyaya* (senior monk) to take the third seat."
The Master asked a nun, "Welcome? Or ill-welcome? The nun then shouted. The Master raised his staff and said, "Speak further!
Speak further! The nun shouted again, and the Master struck her.
He arrived at Cui-feng. Cui-feng asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from Huangbo.
Cui-feng asked, "What words or phrases did Huangbo use to instruct people? The Master said, "Huangbo had no words or phrases. Cui-feng asked, "Why is there none?
The Master said, "Even if there were, there would be no place to bring them up. Cui-feng said, "Just bring one up for me. The Master said, "One."

The Arrow passed through the Western Heavens and reached the Elephant Field (Hastikṣetra). The Master asked, "Neither ordinary nor holy—please, Master, speak quickly. Xiangtian said, "I, this old monk, am just like this.
The Master then gave a shout and said, "With so many bald-headed monks here, what bowl are you looking for?"
Upon arriving at Minghua, Minghua asked, "What are you doing coming here and going there? The Master said, "I am merely treading my straw sandals to pieces.
Minghua asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "Even this old fellow does not recognize the head of the matter.
Later, while traveling on the road to Fenglin, he encountered an old woman. The woman asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going to Fenglin. The woman—
The nun said, "It happens that Fenglin is not here. The Master asked, "Where has he gone? The nun then departed.
The Master called out to her, "Nun! She turned her head back. The Master then walked away.
Upon arriving at Fenglin, Lin asked, "I have a question to ask you; may I do so? The Master said, "Why do you gouge out flesh to create a sore?
Lin said, "The sea moon is clear and without shadow; the roaming fish alone is deluded. The Master said, "Since the sea moon has no shadow, how can the roaming fish be deluded?
Lin said, "Observing the wind, one sees the waves rise; gazing at the water, the wild sail drifts."

The Master said: "The solitary wheel shines alone as the rivers and mountains fall silent; a single laugh from within stirs heaven and earth. Lin said: "Let the three-inch tongue illuminate heaven and earth; try to speak a phrase on the spot. The Master said:

"When meeting a swordsman on the road, you must present your sword; if you are not a poet, do not offer your verse. Lin then desisted. The Master then offered this verse: The solitary wheel shines alone, the rivers and mountains are still; A single laugh from within, heaven and earth are startled.

Let the three-inch brilliance illuminate the world; Try to speak a phrase when the moment arrives. When meeting a swordsman on the road, you must show your blade; If you are no poet, do not offer your verse. Lin then ceased. The Master then composed a verse.
The Great Way transcends sameness; let it lead you west or east. The spark of a flint cannot be overtaken; a flash of lightning is a futile communication.
Miaoshan asked Yangshan: "The spark of a flint cannot be overtaken; a flash of lightning is a futile communication. What do the sages of antiquity use to point to people?
Yangshan said: "What is your intention, Master? Miaoshan said: "As long as there is verbal expression..."
"It has no real meaning whatsoever. Yangshan said, "Not so. Muzhou said, "And what about you, my son?
Yangshan said, "In official matters, not even a needle is permitted; in private affairs, a carriage and horse may pass."

The Master then spread out his sitting mat; Jie threw down his whisk and withdrew the mat.

My teacher Dengniaoliang, beyond the mundane world, had severed all pursuit and travel;
Dongshan then offered him this verse in reply.
Poetry describes the affairs of men; why should it not be excised from the Empty Gate? In seeking pearls, one should calm the waves;
if the water is stirred, they are difficult to obtain. The mind for fame and profit must be pruned. Do not associate with those who are not true friends.
Abandon the heterodox and return to the Right Path; then what need is there to worry about not finding tranquility?
The Master then took his straw rain hat, waved it three times, and departed.

"Why do you not know? The Master said, "This old monk has never received your kōan. The monk asked, "What is the Way?
